  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Philadelphia, PA sale

Philadelphia at a glance

  • Philadelphia is in Philadelphia County.
Selling in Philadelphia?
We buy Philadelphia houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which sales routes are open to a Philadelphia homeowner?

Three routes cover most sales: hire an agent, handle the sale yourself, or take an offer from a buyer paying cash. They all finish at the Department of Records with a recorded deed and the city's transfer tax. What changes is the calendar, the repair list and the amount you keep.

The city is also its own county. Philadelphia and Philadelphia County have shared one government since 1854, so the assessment office, the tax collector and the deed recorder are all city departments, and no outside courthouse comes into a typical sale.

  • An agent listing suits a rowhouse in sound shape that can handle weeks of showings and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Selling it yourself saves the commission but puts the contract and settlement details on your desk.
  • A cash purchase suits deferred repairs, a clouded title, a tenant in place or an estate closing out.

What will a sale cost me in Philadelphia?

The largest single cost that the city sets is the realty transfer tax. Since July 1, 2025 the combined rate has been 4.578%, made up of 3.578% for the city and 1% for the Commonwealth. According to the Department of Revenue the rate had last changed in 2018, and the increase is earmarked for affordable housing programs.

On a $200,000 sale the combined rate comes to $9,156. The sales agreement decides which side pays it, so read that clause before you sign. Payment falls due at deed recording. The city allows up to 30 days to pay after the purchase, but the Department of Revenue suggests having it paid in full at closing, and you can pay online through the Philadelphia Tax Center.

Philadelphia transfer tax and recording charges (Department of Revenue and Department of Records, rates in effect from July 1, 2025)
ChargeAmount
City realty transfer tax3.578% of price or assessed value
Commonwealth realty transfer tax1%
Combined transfer tax4.578%
Recording a deed$277.75
Recording a mortgage$247.75
Recording a mortgage satisfaction$230.75

When there is no sale price, such as a transfer between relatives, the tax is figured on the value that the Office of Property Assessment has set for the property.

Which transfers in Philadelphia are exempt from the transfer tax?

A transfer to a spouse, child or grandchild is exempt, and so is a transfer under a will. Every family exemption needs supporting documents filed with the deed, so gather them before the settlement date and do not assume the settlement agent will chase them for you.

The estate rule catches people out. A property passing under a will to several heirs is exempt on that transfer, but when those heirs then sell the house to a buyer, the sale is taxed. Anyone who inherited a Philadelphia house and plans to sell should budget for the full rate on the second step.

What is Philadelphia like for someone selling a home?

Philadelphia is the state's largest city, with an estimated 1,574,281 residents in July 2025, about 1.8% fewer than the April 2020 base. It covers 134.36 square miles of land and fits roughly 11,937 people into each of them, which is the density that makes rowhouse blocks the normal housing type. William Penn's charter dates to 1682, and the first row houses of the early 19th century earned the style the name Philadelphia rows.

Much of the housing stock dates to the 18th, 19th and early 20th centuries. Federal-style blocks stand in Old City and Society Hill, Victorian homes fill North Philadelphia, and twin houses are common in West Philadelphia. Wikipedia notes that this old stock has left vacant lots and decay in some areas, while Northern Liberties and Society Hill have been rehabilitated. A buyer or investor looking at an older rowhouse will price in the roof, the party walls and the plumbing, which is why condition drives offers more here than in newer suburbs.

  • Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 put the middle home value at $243,100 for owners, with 51.8% of households owning.
  • Rent runs a median $1,397 a month across 679,428 households of 2.26 people on average.
  • Commutes average 31.7 minutes.
  • Summers are hot and humid, with about 30 days a year at or above 90 degrees, and winters average 22.4 inches of snow.

Large employers in the city include the University of Pennsylvania and the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and Temple University is the largest school by enrollment. Hospital and university jobs anchor demand in University City and the nearby rowhouse neighborhoods.

How do Philadelphia property taxes affect the sale?

The Office of Property Assessment sets values, and the Department of Revenue bills them. Bills for tax year 2027 go out on December 1, 2026, new assessments take effect January 1, 2027, and the payment is due March 31, 2027. For that year the First Level Review deadline was September 1, 2026 and the Board of Revision of Taxes deadline was October 5, 2026, so both windows have closed. Ask the Office of Property Assessment how to dispute a value for the following year.

The Homestead Exemption takes $100,000 off the taxable portion of an owner-occupied home's assessed value, and most owners save $1,399 a year. A mortgage or delinquent taxes leave eligibility intact, while a 10-year abatement rules it out. An accepted application keeps working until the deed changes, so a buyer who will live in the house files their own application. The final date to apply is December 1 each year, and applying by October 1 puts the credit on the first bill.

  • An heir without their name on the deed can ask for a conditional Homestead Exemption, granted for up to three years, using a paper application marked Tangled Title.
  • Seniors and income-qualified owners can pay in eleven monthly installments if they apply by March 31.
  • The owner-occupied payment agreement can set a monthly payment as low as zero for past-due tax.

For a house with back taxes, ask the Department of Revenue for a payoff figure before you accept an offer, because delinquent tax is paid from the proceeds.

What does state law make a Philadelphia seller put in writing?

Chapter 73 of Title 68, the Real Estate Seller Disclosure Law, calls for a signed statement about known defects, handed over before any agreement of transfer is signed. Seventeen subjects appear on the form, among them the roof, basement, wiring, drainage and title questions. Nothing forces you to hire testers, yet you cannot assert what you know is untrue.

Act 74, signed October 22, 2026, adds section 7305.2, a flood insurance notice that goes to the buyer once the Insurance Department publishes its flood information page. Suits over a violation must start within two years of final settlement, and an executor selling for an estate stands outside the chapter.

Where should a Philadelphia seller begin?

Begin with the deed and the tax account, because those two records set the pace of a closing. The city's property search shows the assessed value, any homestead credit and the balance owed, and the deed shows who must sign.

  • Pull together the deed, the newest bill and a mortgage payoff letter if one exists.
  • Keep family-relationship papers handy if the transfer could be exempt.
  • Weigh each repair against what it adds to the price.
  • Put the transfer tax split in writing with every buyer, whether a listing buyer or a cash buyer.

A good buyer walks you through the tax, the recording charge and the payoff before you commit, and leaves you free to decline.

More questions about Philadelphia, PA

What is the transfer tax rate for a Philadelphia house sale?

The rate is 4.578%, made of 3.578% for the city and 1% for the Commonwealth, and it has applied since July 1, 2025. It is figured on the price, or on the assessed value if no price exists. The contract says who pays.

Can heirs sell an inherited house in Philadelphia?

Yes. The passing of the house under a will is exempt from transfer tax, but when the heirs sell to an outside buyer that sale is taxed. An heir whose name is missing from the deed may request a conditional Homestead Exemption lasting up to three years.

Does the Homestead Exemption pass to a buyer?

No, a buyer who will live in the home applies separately, since an accepted application lasts only until the deed changes. December 1 is the yearly cutoff, and October 1 is the date that gets the credit onto the first bill.

When is the Philadelphia real estate tax due?

March 31. The bills are mailed from December 1 of the prior year. Seniors and income-qualified owners may spread payment over eleven monthly installments by applying before March 31, and a payoff figure from the Department of Revenue shows what a closing must clear.

What if a Philadelphia seller omits a known defect?

The seller can owe the buyer actual damages. A buyer may sue a seller who willfully or negligently breaks the disclosure duties, with the case filed inside two years of final settlement. A missed disclosure alone does not undo the sale.

Sell My House Fast in Pittsburgh, PA: Options, Costs and Cash Offers

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Pittsburgh at a glance

  • Estimated population, July 1, 2025: 307,632 (Census Bureau).
  • Pittsburgh is in Allegheny County.
Selling in Pittsburgh?
We buy Pittsburgh houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What are my choices for selling a Pittsburgh house?

Pittsburgh sellers usually weigh three paths: an agent listing, a sale by owner, or a purchase for cash. A listing reaches the most shoppers but leans on showings and a buyer's financing. A cash buyer takes the property in whatever condition it is in and can often close on a date you pick, which helps when the roof leaks, the stairs are failing or an estate wants out quickly.

Three local facts shape every path. The city does not demand a Certificate of Occupancy at sale, Allegheny County gathers the transfer tax at recording, and school tax on the city bill has its own collection rules. Sorting them out early keeps the closing date from slipping.

  • Find out who holds title and whether a mortgage or lien must be cleared from the proceeds.
  • Look up the Certificate of Occupancy record on the city's online search.
  • Have the settlement agent total the transfer tax before you agree to a price.

How much transfer tax comes out of a Pittsburgh sale?

A sale inside the city of Pittsburgh carries a 5% realty transfer tax in most cases: 1% to the Commonwealth, 3% to the city and 1% to the Pittsburgh School District. Allegheny County collects it for all three when the deed goes on record, and it is paid by a separate check from the recording fees. Per the county, residential deeds recorded from February 1, 2020 onward carry the city's full 5%.

A $200,000 sale at 5% comes to $10,000. Part of the city lies in the Baldwin-Whitehall School District, where the school share is one half of one percent instead of 1%, so addresses there total 4.5%. The county's rate table lists each school district, so match your parcel to the right line before you estimate your proceeds.

Transfer tax split for a house in the city of Pittsburgh (Allegheny County Department of Real Estate)
Taxing bodyRateOn $200,000
Commonwealth of Pennsylvania1%$2,000
City of Pittsburgh3%$6,000
Pittsburgh School District1%$2,000
Total5%$10,000

The sales agreement states who pays. Transfers between close family members may need only a statement on the deed describing the relationship, while other exemptions need the state's Statement of Value form.

Does Pittsburgh require a Certificate of Occupancy to sell a house?

No. The city says it does not require a Certificate of Occupancy to sell or buy a property, unlike many municipalities around it. The city also warns that this does not mean a property meets every zoning and building code, and many older single-family homes have no certificate on file because past rules did not call for one.

A buyer may have to apply for an Occupancy Permit if the use of the building differs from the use on the latest certificate. The city tells parties to complete a Zoning Certificate request so the transaction meets Pennsylvania law. The most recent certificate is the current legal use, and two certificates can together cover a building approved in stages.

  • Search the Permits, Licenses, and Inspections online occupancy tool by address, parcel number, permit number or ward.
  • If a certificate should exist but does not appear, email the records office and expect a reply within five business days.
  • If you hold a certificate that is missing from the city's files, send a copy so it is added to the library.

What is it like to own and sell a home in Pittsburgh?

Pittsburgh sits where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers join to form the Ohio, and the Golden Triangle of downtown points at that meeting. The Census Bureau counted 302,971 residents in 2020 and estimates 307,632 for July 2025, a gain of 1.5%. The city is divided into 90 neighborhoods, and more than a quarter of their names refer to hills, heights or similar features. That hints at the terrain: many streets are steep two-lane roads, and the city keeps about 800 sets of public stairways.

The city grew around Fort Pitt after General Forbes took the forks in 1758 and became known as the Steel City. The economy now centers on health care, education and technology, with UPMC and Allegheny Health Network as the two biggest health systems and the University of Pittsburgh and Carnegie Mellon University in the Oakland and Shadyside area. The city counts 446 bridges, more than Venice.

  • For 2020 to 2024 the Census Bureau reports $205,800 as the middle home value among owners.
  • Only 47.7% of households own, so more rent than own.
  • Median rent is $1,261 across 138,188 households.
  • Bachelor's degree or higher among adults 25 and older: 49.1%.
  • Average snowfall runs about 44 inches a year.

Which property taxes must a Pittsburgh seller settle?

The city, the parks fund, the Carnegie Library and the Pittsburgh School District all bill on the value set by the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments. County values follow a base year of 2012, so the assessed figure is not a current market price. Bills go out in January, the full amount is due at the end of February, and a 2% discount applies for early payment. Installments fall at the end of February, April and July.

If you owe tax from earlier years, the city keeps past-due city, library and parks tax, while past-due school tax sits with Jordan Tax Service, Inc. An unpaid balance can lead to a Treasurer's Sale. Ask the Department of Finance and the collector for payoff figures before closing, since both come out of the proceeds.

The homestead program reduces the taxable value of an owner-occupied home. The city's reduction is $15,000, worth $120.90 a year in city tax, and a county homestead application also activates the city, school and library exemptions. A buyer who will live in the house should apply through the county. Assessment appeals follow an annual window: for tax year 2027 it ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026 and has closed, Check the county's real estate portal for the dates of the next window.

What written disclosures does a Pittsburgh seller owe?

Title 68, Chapter 73 of the state code directs a seller to give the buyer a signed and dated statement on known defects before the agreement of transfer is signed. Its subjects include additions and remodeling, water and sewer service, and land features such as sinkholes, drainage and flood risk indicators. Pittsburgh's slopes make the land and drainage lines worth a careful answer.

No special investigation is required, but a false statement is not allowed. A change in the facts before settlement must be passed to the buyer, a condominium seller covers only the unit, and a fiduciary selling for an estate is exempt from the chapter.

What should a Pittsburgh seller verify before agreeing to a price?

Work out the net. Take the offer, then subtract the 5% or 4.5% transfer tax if you pay it, recording fees, any mortgage payoff, unpaid tax and the repairs a buyer will ask for. The result is the number to compare across a listing, a sale by owner and a cash bid.

  • Is the parcel in the city, or in a nearby borough with a lower rate?
  • Does the certificate on file match how the house is used?
  • Are the city, library, parks and school installments current?
  • Whose name is on the deed, and does probate or a payoff come first?

More questions about Pittsburgh, PA

Is a Certificate of Occupancy needed for a Pittsburgh sale?

No. The city does not require one at sale. A buyer may still need an Occupancy Permit when the intended use differs from the last certificate, and the city points parties to a Zoning Certificate request. The online occupancy tool or the records office shows what exists.

How big is the transfer tax inside Pittsburgh?

Five percent for most addresses: 1% state, 3% city, 1% Pittsburgh School District. Part of the city sits in the Baldwin-Whitehall district, whose half-percent share brings the total to 4.5%. The county takes payment when the deed is filed.

When do Pittsburgh property tax payments fall due?

The full bill is due at the end of February, with installments at the end of February, April and July. Early payment earns a 2% discount, and the city's own FAQ gives two different cutoff dates, so confirm yours with the Department of Finance.

Can I still contest my Allegheny County assessment?

Not for tax year 2027. That window ran July 1 through September 1, 2026. The county portal will announce later windows if you believe the value is wrong.

Does my homestead exemption go with the house?

No. It ends with your ownership and the new owner applies. The city reduction is $15,000, and an application to the county also switches on the city, school district and library exemptions for a resident owner.

Selling in Allentown?

What is Allentown like for someone selling a house?

Allentown is the seat of Lehigh County and the biggest city in the Lehigh Valley, so a seller there deals with older, closely built housing and a city rule that puts an inspection ahead of the closing. The Census Bureau estimates 126,044 residents for July 1, 2025, against 125,845 counted in the 2020 census, which is close to no change at all.

The city covers about 17.55 square miles of land on the Lehigh River, 48 miles north of Philadelphia and 78 miles west of New York City. Jordan Creek and Little Lehigh Creek meet inside city limits before they reach the river, and South Mountain forms a ridge along the southern edge.

How did Allentown's history shape the houses sold there?

William Allen laid out the town in 1762. His first plan held 42 blocks and 756 lots, most of them 60 feet wide and 230 feet deep, between what are now 4th and 10th streets. The Lehigh Canal opened in 1829 to move anthracite coal, and the first railroad arrived in 1855, which pushed the city toward the factory economy that built much of its older housing.

Allentown also holds a footnote in national history. The Liberty Bell sat under the floorboards of Zion Reformed Church on Hamilton Street from September 1777 to June 1778. Heavy industry faded from about 1980, and the city moved toward services, with Air Products and PPL among the companies headquartered here.

Which Allentown neighborhoods have which kinds of houses?

The city describes its housing by area, and the era of construction changes from one side of town to the next.

  • Center City: Victorian and terraced rowhouses, plus loft apartments in converted mills. Old Allentown and the Old Fairgrounds are historic districts here.
  • West Park: mostly Victorian and American Craftsman houses, and also a historic district with its own home tour.
  • West End: begins roughly at 15th Street, with tree-lined blocks of houses built mostly in the 1920s through the 1940s.
  • East Side and South Side: single and twin homes from the 1940s to the 1960s, with some older Victorians. The East Side runs toward Bethlehem and the South Side borders Emmaus.
  • The Wards: residential blocks east of Center City from the late 19th and early 20th century boom.

A buyer reading an inspection report will weigh the house's era, so a seller gains from knowing which of these groups the property belongs to.

What do Census figures say about housing in Allentown?

Renters live in more than half of Allentown's occupied homes, because the owner-occupied rate for 2020 to 2024 is only 43.2 percent. That mix shapes who buys: many sales involve two-family and multi-unit buildings alongside single houses.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts. The median covers every owner-occupied unit in the city, so a single house can land far above or below it.

What does Allentown require before a house can be sold?

Allentown requires a safety and maintenance inspection before a residential or commercial property is sold. The city's pre-sale inspection page says the visit checks the property against the Allentown Property Maintenance Code and the zoning rules.

  • Follow the city's Pre-Sale Inspection Procedure, then apply online for a Pre-Sale permit.
  • An inspector schedules the visit. A property that passes receives a Certificate of Compliance before the sale.
  • If the inspector finds violations, the seller fixes them, unless the buyer agrees to take the repairs on. That agreement goes on the city's Acceptance Form.
  • After settlement, the seller or the agent submits a Buyer's Information Report within three days.

The page lists no exception for cash or as-is sales. Contact the city's Building Standards and Safety office for the current fee and the scheduling time before you set a closing date.

How do Lehigh County assessments and appeals affect a sale in Allentown?

Lehigh County assesses every Allentown parcel, and the county's base year is 2013, the date of its last countywide reassessment, with the assessment set at 100 percent of fair market value at that time. New construction and demolition change a parcel's assessment in between. The Assessment Office is in Room 517 of the Government Center at 17 South Seventh Street, Allentown, and its number is 610-782-3038.

  • Appeal deadline: the Board of Assessment Appeals accepts an original signed appeal received by August 1 each year, with the filing fee. Postmarks and faxes do not count as timely filing.
  • Interim appeals: these follow the date printed on a Change of Assessment Notice instead.
  • Act 29 of 2026: the county says an owner of non-owner-occupied property must submit contact information within 30 days of buying it. Owner-occupants are exempt, so the rule matters mostly to landlords and investors buying from you.

How does Allentown's weather affect a house?

Allentown has four distinct seasons. January averages 30.1 degrees and July averages 75.6, and the Lehigh Valley airport has recorded 105 degrees on July 3, 1966 and minus 15 on January 21, 1994. Seasonal snowfall averages 33.1 inches, with February the snowiest month at just under 11 inches.

Roofs, gutters, basements and heating systems carry that load year after year. The city sits in USDA plant hardiness zone 6b, and rain falls on eight to twelve days in a typical month, so moisture in a basement is a routine question from buyers.

How do schools, jobs and roads affect Allentown buyers?

The Allentown School District covers most of the city and is the fourth largest in Pennsylvania, with 16,510 students in 2023 and 2024. William Allen High School serves the southern and western sections and Louis E. Dieruff High School serves the east and north. A small area near Trexler Park belongs to the Parkland School District, so confirm the district for a specific address.

  • I-78 runs together with PA 309 across the southern part of the city, and US 22 clips the northwest corner.
  • The city maintains 287.94 of its 314.10 miles of public road; PennDOT maintains the other 26.16.
  • LANta buses connect from the Allentown Transportation Center on North 7th Street.
  • Lehigh Valley International Airport is about 3 miles northeast, in Hanover Township.

Lehigh Valley Hospital-Cedar Crest, with 877 beds, anchors a large health care sector. Air Products and PPL have headquarters in the city.

What are the ways to sell a house quickly in Allentown?

An Allentown owner can list with an agent, sell without one, or accept a cash offer. A listing opens the house to the widest set of buyers and brings showings and the buyer's own inspection. A cash sale skips the mortgage approval step, which is usually the part of a closing that runs on someone else's schedule.

Every route passes through the city's pre-sale permit, so request it early and keep the Certificate of Compliance with the sale paperwork. If the house has code violations you cannot afford to fix, ask the buyer in writing whether they will accept the repairs on the Acceptance Form.

More questions about Allentown, PA

Do I need an inspection before selling my Allentown house?

Yes. The city requires a pre-sale safety and maintenance inspection for residential and commercial property, and a house that passes receives a Certificate of Compliance before the sale.

Can the buyer take over repairs the Allentown inspector finds?

Yes. If the inspector lists violations, the seller can repair them or the buyer can agree to do so, and that agreement is recorded on the city's Acceptance Form.

What do I file after an Allentown closing?

A Buyer's Information Report goes to the city within three days of settlement. The seller or the real estate agent can submit it.

Which school district serves my Allentown home?

Most of the city lies in the Allentown School District, but a small area near Trexler Park is in the Parkland School District. Check the exact address with the district.

What is the deadline to appeal a Lehigh County assessment?

August 1 each year. The Board of Assessment Appeals needs the original signed appeal and the filing fee in hand by then, and postmarks and faxes are not accepted.

What makes selling a house in Reading, PA different?

Reading is a dense, rowhouse-heavy city where a sale needs a city Certificate of Transfer, carries a transfer tax of 5%, and often involves a house that has not been updated in decades. Those three facts shape price, timing and who is likely to buy.

Reading is the Berks County seat and the fourth-largest city in Pennsylvania, with 95,112 residents at the 2020 census. It sits on the Schuylkill River, with Mount Penn rising to the east and Neversink Mountain to the south. The Reading Railroad, the Schuylkill and Union canals and an iron industry that supplied Revolutionary War troops built the housing stock, and a good share of it still stands. Outlet shopping and pretzel bakeries remain part of the city's identity.

Sellers here usually weigh a repair-and-list route against a quick sale to an investor. The details below show what each route requires at the city and county level.

What do the Census numbers say about Reading's housing market?

Reading's housing costs are far below those of the Philadelphia suburbs, and most households rent, so the buyer pool leans toward investors and first-time owners.

Reading city housing and population snapshot (U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, 2020-2024 estimates unless noted)
MeasureReading

With only about four in ten homes owner-occupied, a large share of Reading's houses are rentals. Owners of those properties also deal with the city's housing registration and rental inspection cycle, which can matter if tenants are in place at the time of sale.

What is the Certificate of Transfer in Reading?

It is a city document the seller must obtain before a property sale closes, and it applies to every property sold in Reading regardless of use. The City's Property and Codes Enforcement page states that the seller applies before the sale and hands the buyer a property packet with summary sheets.

A Health and Safety Inspection that checks code compliance is part of the process. Either the buyer or the seller may arrange it, and the city allows limited exemptions. The Housing Welcome Packet page lists the forms: a Certificate of Transfer and Property Sale Inspection Application, and a Property Sale Inspection Acknowledgement.

  • Download the sale application from the City's Housing Welcome Packet page and complete it as early as the sales agreement is signed.
  • Ask the City of Reading Property Maintenance division, which works from 815 Washington Street, for the current fee and processing time.
  • Agree in the sales contract who schedules the inspection and who pays for any violations it finds.
  • For help or complaints, the Citizen's Service Center is at 1-877-727-3234.

A seller who sells as-is to an investor should still get the certificate lined up. The document is the city's requirement, so it does not disappear because the buyer is paying cash.

How much transfer tax do sellers in Reading pay?

The Berks County Recorder of Deeds fee schedule states that the transfer tax rate is 5% in the City of Reading, compared with 2% in every other Berks municipality. One percent of that goes to the state, and the Recorder collects the whole amount when the deed is recorded.

On a house at Reading's median value of $121,300, 5% comes to about $6,065. Pennsylvania law makes both parties liable, so the sales agreement should say who pays and how it is split. Splitting it is a negotiation point, so settle it before the contract is signed.

  • Personal checks are not accepted for transfer tax at the Recorder's office, and cash is no longer accepted either.
  • The base recording fee for a deed is $88 for up to four pages, with $4 for each additional page.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) must accompany a deed that does not state the full price, and the Common Level Ratio printed on it is 3.12 for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
  • The Recorder of Deeds is in the Berks County Services Center, 633 Court Street, third floor, phone 610-478-3380.

Certain family transfers and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt under state law, according to the Department of Revenue, so an inherited house passing to an heir may owe nothing.

Which Reading neighborhoods and roads matter to buyers?

Buyers sort Reading by neighborhood and by how quickly they can reach U.S. 422. The city's neighborhood map names areas such as Center City, Callowhill, College Heights, Hampden Heights, East Reading, Glenside, Millmont, Outlet District, Penn's Commons, Queen Anne Historic District, Prince Historic District and Southside.

The historic districts attract owners who want older architecture, while the Outlet District and Center City draw renters and investors. Reading Senior High School, serving grades 9 through 12, had 5,498 students in 2023 and is the largest traditional high school in Pennsylvania. Reading School District runs the city's elementary and middle schools, and Berks Catholic High School is a private option.

For commuting, U.S. 422 circles the west side as the West Shore Bypass, U.S. 222 bypasses the city to the west, Interstate 176 heads south toward the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and PA 61 runs north toward Pottsville. The city maintains about 132 miles of its roads, and the state maintains about 25 miles.

What about property taxes and assessments in Reading?

Reading homeowners are assessed through Berks County and pay the county, the city and the Reading School District. Ask Berks County for the current millage on your parcel rather than relying on a general figure.

Ask the Berks County Assessment Office for the appeal deadline and the form, because the rules for contesting a value are set at the county level. Ask the Berks County Tax Claim Bureau about any unpaid years. A title company will request a tax certification before closing, and unpaid taxes are paid from sale proceeds.

The city's code program adds its own tickets. Reading's Quality of Life program issues immediate tickets that increase with repeat violations at the same property in a year, and the city holds blight hearings for deteriorated properties. Clearing open violations before closing keeps them from becoming a buyer's negotiating point.

Should I list, repair or sell to a cash buyer in Reading?

The answer depends on condition and timing. A house in good repair near a historic district may do well on the open market, but a vacant rowhouse with deferred maintenance may be worth more to a rehab investor than to a retail buyer who needs financing.

  • Get a rough repair estimate before listing. Many Reading buyers use loans that require inspections and appraisals.
  • Work out your net after 5% transfer tax, the sale inspection, commissions and unpaid taxes.
  • If you own rental units, ask the Property Maintenance office how registration and open inspection findings transfer to a new owner.
  • If time matters more than price, a cash sale on an as-is basis avoids lender delays, though the Certificate of Transfer is still required.

More questions about Reading, PA

Is a Certificate of Transfer required for every house sale in Reading?

Yes. The City of Reading says the certificate is necessary for all properties sold in the city regardless of use, with limited exemptions only from the Health and Safety Inspection. The seller applies before the sale.

Who pays Reading's 5% transfer tax?

The law makes buyer and seller jointly liable, and the sales agreement decides who actually pays. The Berks County Recorder of Deeds collects it at recording and lists the rate at 5% in the City of Reading versus 2% elsewhere in Berks.

Can I sell a Reading house with code violations?

Yes, but the sale inspection will surface them, and the contract must say whether you repair them or the buyer does. Open violations that the city has recorded do not go away at closing.

Does an inherited house in Reading owe transfer tax?

Property passed by will or intestate succession is exempt from realty transfer tax under the state's rules. A later sale by the heir to a third party is a normal taxable transfer at the Reading rate.

Where do I record the deed after a Reading sale?

At the Berks County Recorder of Deeds, third floor of the Services Center at 633 Court Street in Reading, or by e-recording through a title company. Your closing agent usually handles it and pays the transfer tax by check.

  • Scranton is in Lackawanna County.

How can I sell my house fast in Scranton, PA?

You can sell a Scranton house quickly by taking a cash offer, by listing it with an agent, or by selling it yourself, and the cash route is the one with the fewest moving parts. Scranton sits in Lackawanna County, and the city has its own rules for permits, rental licenses and transfer tax that can slow a conventional sale.

A listing in Scranton usually depends on a buyer's lender, an appraisal and a repair list. A cash buyer skips most of that, which matters when the house is inherited, has tenants, needs work, or sits on a street where older homes take longer to move. The trade-off is price: a cash offer is normally lower than a fully prepared listing, so compare both before you commit.

What kind of city is Scranton for a home seller?

Scranton is a hilly second class A city and the county seat of Lackawanna County, counted at 76,328 by the 2020 census, with a 2025 estimate of 75,514. That makes it the most populous city in Northeastern Pennsylvania and the sixth largest in the state.

The city covers about 25.4 square miles in the Lackawanna River valley. Inhabited ground runs from roughly 650 to 1,400 feet above sea level, with ridges on both sides, so lot slope, drainage and retaining walls come up often in inspections. The city is usually divided into nine districts:

  • North Scranton and Green Ridge
  • Central City and the Hill Section (Eastside)
  • Westside and West Mountain
  • Southside and Minooka
  • East Mountain

Green Ridge and the mountain neighborhoods read very differently to a buyer than the older streets near downtown, so a price from one district says little about another.

How did coal and rail shape Scranton's housing?

Most of Scranton's older housing stock dates from the anthracite and railroad boom. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad had its hub here and was the largest employer for nearly a century, and the borough became a city in 1866 after absorbing Hyde Park and Providence.

Population climbed from the 1860s until it reached a peak of 143,433 in 1930, then fell to about 76,000 as demand for coal dropped. The 1959 Knox Mine disaster effectively ended mining in the region. The housing left behind is large in number and old in age: narrow lots, brick and frame doubles, steep driveways and basements that have seen decades of freeze and thaw.

The city earned the nickname Electric City from a streetcar system that began running in 1886, and the neighborhoods built around those lines are compact, so houses within reach of downtown and the University of Scranton often draw a different kind of buyer than those up on the mountains.

What does the 3.7 percent transfer tax mean at closing?

On a Scranton sale the combined realty transfer tax is 3.7 percent of the value, compared with 2 percent in most of Lackawanna County, according to the county Recorder of Deeds. The Recorder will not take a deed for recording until the tax is paid.

Pennsylvania's own share is 1 percent, set by the Department of Revenue and collected by the county Recorder, with the rest going to local government and the school district. Who pays is a matter of the sales agreement. In many deals the seller and buyer split it, but the new owner is on the hook if the amount is ever questioned.

  • On a $120,000 sale, 3.7 percent comes to $4,440 in total tax.
  • Some family transfers, such as parent to child or between siblings, are exempt. Non-profit corporations are not.
  • A deed that shows nominal consideration, such as $1, needs a Statement of Value so the state can review it.

What are the key Scranton sale and rental costs at a glance?

Scranton figures. Sources: Lackawanna County Recorder of Deeds, PA Department of Revenue, City of Scranton rental licensing and code enforcement pages.

Total realty transfer tax in the city3.7 percent of value

Rental license renewalDue March 15 each year

What if my Scranton house has tenants?

Every rental property in Scranton needs a city rental license, and renting an unlicensed unit has been a violation since September 16, 2023. Renewals are due by March 15 each year, and a new rental unit must be licensed within 30 days of a tenant moving in.

Fees depend on unit count, from $45 per unit for one to three units up to a $450 flat fee at fifty or more. Family-occupied units still need a license but pay no fee. Inspections run on a three-year cycle, and the first re-inspection is free.

If you plan to sell with tenants in place, have the license current before you list. A buyer's lender or an investor will ask for it, and a lapse can lead to refusal of a license, fines or worse. Ask the city's rental licensing office where your property stands before you pick a closing day.

What if the house is vacant, behind on its mortgage or heading to a tax sale?

Scranton requires registration of any property in the city, occupied or empty, that is in mortgage default, has a lis pendens filed, faces a foreclosure action, is subject to a tax deed application or pending tax lien sale, or has been transferred to the lender by a deed in lieu. Registration carries no fee, and it is done through the city's online portal.

The abandoned designation stays on the property until it sells, the foreclosure is dismissed or the default is cured. Selling before a judgment or tax sale ends that status, and a fast cash closing is one way to do it. Ask the Lackawanna County Tax Claim Bureau for the exact upset sale dates that apply to your parcel.

Do I need permits or repairs before I sell in Scranton?

Pennsylvania does not require a seller to renovate, but any work you start in Scranton needs a permit first. The city says all construction projects require one and no work may begin without it. Painting and gutter installation are the exceptions the city names.

Since January 1, 2026, plans have to follow the 2021 International Code Council series, with the 2024 International Property Maintenance Code applied to existing buildings. Three other checks catch sellers off guard:

  • Homes in a historic district or landmark need a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior changes, even when no building permit is needed.
  • Projects in a FEMA flood zone go through the floodplain administrator, and a substantial improvement of 50 percent or more of market value triggers elevation or flood-proofing.
  • Fences, sheds and pools can need zoning approval even without a building permit.

Code Enforcement moved its in-person counter to 338 N Washington Avenue in October 2026. Open or expired permits on the house are a common reason a title company delays closing, so ask the office for the permit history before you list.

Should I worry about mine subsidence?

Possibly. Scranton grew over underground anthracite workings, and standard homeowner policies usually exclude damage from collapsed mines. The state's Mine Subsidence Insurance program, run by the Department of Environmental Protection, fills that gap.

Coverage runs from $5,000 to $1,000,000, and residential coverage of $150,000 costs $41.25 a year. DEP's MSI Risk map shows whether an address lies over mined ground, and a buyer's lender may ask. A policy does not transfer to the new owner, who has to apply for their own, and a seller who cancels at closing can get unused premium back when the notice arrives inside a month of the sale.

Cracks are sometimes soil settlement or frost rather than mines, and the program lists those as common look-alikes.

How does Scranton's winter affect a house that is for sale?

Scranton has a humid continental climate with 45.1 inches of snow in an average year, 38.72 inches of total precipitation and about 39 days when the high stays below freezing. January averages 28.0 degrees and July 73.7 degrees, measured at the Wilkes-Barre/Scranton airport.

That freeze-thaw cycle is hard on roofs, gutters, chimneys, retaining walls, concrete steps and old foundations, and buyers' inspectors look for exactly those items. A buyer who purchases as-is removes the need to schedule repairs around the weather.

How do schools and commuting affect Scranton buyers?

Public schools are run by the Scranton School District, which serves almost 10,000 students through two high schools, three intermediate schools and twelve elementary schools.

For commuters, Interstate 81 runs along the city's southeastern and northern edges, Interstate 476 (the Turnpike's Northeast Extension) sits along the west side, and U.S. Route 11 passes through downtown. Local buses are run by the County of Lackawanna Transit System. Several colleges sit in or beside the city, including the University of Scranton, Marywood University, Lackawanna College, Johnson College and the Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine.

More questions about Scranton, PA

How long does it take to sell a house in Scranton for cash?

A cash sale can close in a few weeks, since there is no lender underwriting or appraisal to wait on. The remaining steps are title work, payoff of any liens and recording the deed with the Lackawanna County Recorder of Deeds.

Who pays the transfer tax on a Scranton home sale?

The sales agreement decides, and in most deals the seller and buyer split it. The county Recorder says the state and local governments do not care who pays, only that the 3.7 percent total is paid when the deed is recorded.

Can I sell a Scranton rental property without a rental license?

You can sell it, but an unlicensed rental has been a violation since September 16, 2023, and the city can refuse a license or fine the owner. Apply for or renew the license first if tenants are in the unit, since renewals are due March 15.

Does Scranton require an inspection before I can sell?

The city's code enforcement and rental pages describe permit inspections and a three-year rental inspection cycle, and they describe no inspection tied to a sale. Ask the office whether anything is open on your address before you list.

Is mine subsidence insurance required when buying a Scranton home?

It is not required by the state, but a lender may ask for it when the property sits over mined ground. DEP sells the coverage, and the new owner has to apply for a new policy because the seller's does not transfer.

How do I sell a house fast in Lower Merion Township?

The quickest sale in Lower Merion Township is one where the township paperwork is started on day one, because the Resale Certification takes 30 to 60 days to come back. A cash buyer can agree to a closing date as soon as the contract is signed, but the certificate, the tax certification and the deed registration still have to be in hand before settlement.

Lower Merion is a first-class township in Montgomery County and the heart of the Philadelphia Main Line, about 12 miles northwest of central Philadelphia. It is the ninth most populous municipality in Pennsylvania, with 63,633 residents at the 2020 census. Sellers often need speed for ordinary life reasons: an estate with out-of-town heirs, a move, a divorce, a tenant situation, or an older house that needs more work than the owner wants to fund.

  • Order the Resale Certification application first, since it has the longest lead time.
  • Request the tax certification as soon as you have an accepted offer, because it takes two to three days.
  • Ask your buyer or title company to confirm who files the Real Estate Registration form and who pays the transfer taxes.

What is Lower Merion Township like for a seller?

It covers 23.9 square miles between the Schuylkill River on the east and Radnor and Haverford townships on the west. City Avenue, often called City Line, marks the southern edge and separates Montgomery County from Philadelphia, while the borough of Narberth sits entirely inside the township. Its communities include Ardmore, Bala Cynwyd, Bryn Mawr, Gladwyne, Merion Station, Penn Valley, Wynnewood, Rosemont and Villanova, and several of them extend into neighboring Delaware County.

The history is long. Welsh Quakers settled the area in 1682 on land William Penn granted, the township was established in 1713, and it was incorporated as a first-class township in 1900. The Merion Friends Meeting House, in continuous use since 1695, is described as the oldest continuously used place of worship in the United States. After a 2012 federal sign rule, the township declared itself a historic district by ordinance to keep its street signs, some of which date to the early 1910s. After World War II the township changed from farmland to suburb, and the stretch of City Avenue known as the Golden Mile holds offices, shops and condominium towers.

Transportation is a selling point. The Schuylkill Expressway (I-76), the Blue Route (I-476), US 1, US 30, PA 320 and PA 23 all cross the township. Of 240.08 miles of public road in 2018, 204.94 miles were township maintained. SEPTA's Paoli/Thorndale Line stops in Merion, Wynnewood, Ardmore, Haverford, Bryn Mawr and Rosemont, the Cynwyd Line stops at Bala and Cynwyd, and the Norristown High Speed Line serves the western edge. Children attend the Lower Merion School District. The climate sits between humid continental and humid subtropical, in hardiness zone 7b.

What does the Lower Merion Resale Certification require?

The township requires the owner to obtain a Resale Certification before selling. To qualify, the property must meet a short list of conditions, and township staff also review the property file so the buyer hears about any open violations.

  • Sidewalks and curbs must be in good repair.
  • The street address must be posted where it can be seen from the street.
  • Smoke detectors must be installed in each bedroom and on every level.
  • The owner must certify how the building is used.
Lower Merion Township sale paperwork, from township pages

The township no longer requires the original deed to be registered with it before recording at the county, though the Real Estate Registration form is still required for any change in ownership or legal description. If the house has an abandoned underground fuel oil tank, the township says it must be removed by a DEP-certified individual under a building permit, so deal with that before an inspector finds it. Building and Planning answers questions at 610-645-6200.

What does the tax certification cover in Lower Merion?

The township tax collector provides a four-year certification that lists township tax, county tax, school tax, sewer and solid waste, including delinquent amounts. It is accurate only on the day it is issued, free updates run for sixty days for whoever ordered it, and the township does not confirm amounts due over the phone.

Order by emailing the tax collector's office for a credit card invoice or mailing a check payable to Tax Collector, Lower Merion, to 75 E Lancaster Ave, Ardmore. Lien taxes are checked at the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau. Most condominiums and apartments pay sewer and solid waste through their association instead of directly, so those fees may not appear. The township does not take final readings for sewer or solid waste because the certification already carries that data.

What do Census figures show about Lower Merion homes?

The Census Bureau estimated 64,691 residents on July 1, 2025. Of owner-occupied homes, the median value over 2020 to 2024 was $810,400, and 74.7 percent of housing is owner occupied. Median gross rent was $1,893, median household income was $176,512 in 2024 dollars, and 78.7 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Residents aged 65 and over make up 21.0 percent of the population, and the township counted 24,077 households.

High values raise the stakes on transfer tax and carrying cost. The state tax is 1 percent of value and the county Recorder of Deeds collects it with the local tax, and on a house at the median value the state share alone is $8,104. Montgomery County requires two separate checks at recording, one for the recording fee and one for the realty transfer tax, and its fee chart effective June 25, 2026 lists a deed base fee of $87.75. Ask your title company for the local rate that applies to your address.

How do assessment appeals and rentals work in Lower Merion?

Montgomery County takes annual assessment appeals until August 1, and the appeal must be postmarked or delivered by then. The form requires an original owner signature and three copies of supporting documents, and faxed or emailed appeals are not accepted. A single-family residential appeal carries a $50 processing fee, and the county hears all appeals by October 31. The Board of Assessment Appeals can be reached at 610-278-3761.

If you own a rental, the township requires a Rental Unit License from Building and Planning, an inspection against the housing code, a business registration and an annual business privilege tax return. A buyer of your tenant-occupied house will ask whether the license is current, and the township keeps a separate list of approved student homes. For deeds that carry no market price, such as gifts, the state determines value using a common level ratio factor, which Montgomery County lists as 3.36 as of July 1, 2026.

More questions about Lower Merion, PA

Is a resale certificate required to sell in Lower Merion Township?

Yes. The township requires a Resale Certification before a sale, and it takes 30 to 60 days. The fee is $100 if the application arrives 20 or more days before settlement and $150 if it arrives later.

What must be fixed to pass the Lower Merion resale inspection?

Sidewalks and curbs must be in good repair, the address must be visible from the street, and smoke detectors are needed in every bedroom and on every level. The owner also certifies the use of the building.

How much is a Lower Merion tax certification?

The regular certification is $50 with a two to three day turnaround, and the rush certification is $75 and comes back the same day. It covers township, county and school tax plus sewer and solid waste.

When must I file a Montgomery County assessment appeal?

The annual deadline is August 1. The appeal must be postmarked or hand delivered by that date, and faxed or emailed appeals are rejected.

Which school district serves Lower Merion Township?

The Lower Merion School District serves the township, and pupils attend its schools unless they go to a private school. It is also one of the township's largest employers.

What kind of place is Bensalem Township?

Bensalem is a township of about 62,800 people at the southern tip of Bucks County, tucked against the Northeast section of Philadelphia. The Census Bureau puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 62,783, and the 2020 census counted 62,707, which made it the most populous municipality in Bucks County.

Despite the word township, Bensalem has had a mayor and a five-member council since voters chose that form in 1987. It has no incorporated boroughs inside its lines. Villages such as Andalusia, Cornwells Heights, Eddington, Oakford and Trevose are communities within the one township, and each shows up in mailing addresses and listings.

How did Bensalem get its name and its shape?

The name comes from the Manor of Bensalem, the estate of an early settler who combined the Hebrew word for peace with a nod to William Penn. The township was defined by a Bucks County jury in 1692 and carries its present name from a 1701 record, which makes it nearly as old as Pennsylvania itself.

Bensalem covers 21.0 square miles, of which 1.0 is water. Neshaminy Creek marks the eastern edge and Poquessing Creek the western edge, and the Delaware River runs along the southeast border across from Burlington County, New Jersey. The Fall Line, which separates the Atlantic Coastal Plain from the Piedmont, passes through the township near Neshaminy Mall. Population rose from 11,365 in 1950 to 52,368 in 1980, and it has stayed between 56,000 and 63,000 since 1990.

Which roads and rail lines serve Bensalem sellers and buyers?

The township maintains 144.61 of its 195.30 miles of public road. PennDOT looks after 45.89 miles and the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission 4.80.

  • Interstate 95, US 1, US 13 (Bristol Pike), PA 63, PA 132 and PA 513 all cross the township.
  • The Turnpike's Bensalem interchange, exit 351, sits on US 1 in Trevose, and exit 352 at Street Road is E-ZPass only.
  • SEPTA's Trenton Line stops at Cornwells Heights and Eddington, and its West Trenton Line stops at Trevose and Neshaminy Falls.
  • Cornwells Heights also has Amtrak Keystone Service and Northeast Regional trains and a park-and-ride lot reached from I-95 and PA 63.
  • Philadelphia International Airport is about 25 miles away.

What do Census figures show about Bensalem homes?

Bensalem leans toward homeownership, with 62.3 percent of homes owner-occupied for 2020 to 2024 and a median home value of $364,400. About one resident in five was born outside the United States, and 27.2 percent of residents age five and over speak a language other than English at home.

What must a Bensalem seller file before closing?

Bensalem requires a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit whenever a dwelling changes hands. The Building and Planning Department's application form describes it as the permit to occupy a single or multi-family dwelling or condominium through new ownership or new use, and it carries a $100 fee.

  • File the application one month before the settlement date. The form is signed, and a signed copy is required before the permit issues.
  • Attach an electrical panel certificate from one of the approved electrical underwriters named on the form.
  • Attach a maintenance certificate from a registered contractor saying the heating system is in good working condition.
  • Attach a chimney, flue and vent inspection at NFPA 211 Level II, usually done with a camera.
  • Pay in cash, check or money order. The township does not accept credit cards or electronic payments.

The certifications may be obtained up to one year before settlement. Staff search the property's history for open permits, complaints and liens, and unresolved items delay the certificate, so clearing them falls to the seller. Questions go to the Building and Planning Department at 2400 Byberry Road, phone 215-633-3644, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. See the township's resale application.

How does Bucks County assess a Bensalem house?

The Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals, at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown, keeps the assessment rolls for Bensalem. Its office number is 215-348-6219, and the board meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesday of each month.

The county's page gave August 3, 2026 as the deadline for annual appeals that year, and any change from an annual appeal takes effect in the 2027 tax year. That date has passed; the next annual deadline will appear on the same page. The same page lists March 1, 2027 as the homestead and farmstead deadline for the tax year starting July 1, 2027.

It also explains Act 29: a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying a property. Bensalem's sewer service comes from the Bucks County Water and Sewer Authority and its water from Aqua Pennsylvania, since the township sold both systems in 1999, so utility transfers at closing go through those companies. PECO supplies electricity and natural gas.

How does Bensalem's weather affect a house?

Bensalem has a humid subtropical climate. Since 1981 the air temperature has peaked at 103.0 degrees on July 22, 2011, and bottomed out at minus 8.8 on January 22, 1984. July is the wettest month, and thunderstorms peak then.

The wettest single day since 1981 delivered 6.70 inches of rain, on August 27, 2011. The township sits in plant hardiness zone 7a. Houses near Poquessing Creek, Neshaminy Creek or the Delaware are worth checking for drainage and basement moisture, and a buyer can ask the township's engineering and building staff about the flood zone for a specific parcel.

How do schools and employers affect Bensalem buyers?

The Bensalem Township School District runs six elementary schools, two middle schools and Bensalem High School, with a nine-member school board. Holy Ghost Preparatory School is a private Catholic high school in the township, and Catholic elementary schools include St. Charles Borromeo in Cornwells Heights and Saint Ephrem.

  • Rita's Franchise Company has headquarters in Trevose, and Philly Pretzel Factory has headquarters in Bensalem.
  • Healthcare Services Group is headquartered here, as is the United States base for Ibanez guitars and Tama drums.
  • Parx Casino and Racing, which opened as Keystone Racetrack in 1974, and the Penn Community Bank Amphitheater bring regional visitors.
  • Wat Mongkoltepmunee on Knights Road, a Buddhist temple, is a landmark in the township.

What are the options for selling a house fast in Bensalem?

A Bensalem owner can list the house, sell directly, or take a cash offer. A listing exposes the house to the most buyers, while a cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting from the schedule.

All three routes depend on the same township paperwork. Because the use and occupancy application asks for a settlement date and certificates from outside contractors, order the electrical, heating and chimney inspections as soon as a buyer is lined up, and keep the one month filing window in mind when you pick a closing date.

More questions about Bensalem, PA

Does Bensalem require a certificate when a house is sold?

Yes. The township issues a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit for a change in ownership, based on electrical, heating and chimney certificates and a $100 application fee.

How far ahead should I apply for the Bensalem resale permit?

About one month before the settlement date. The township asks for the signed application and all three certifications at that point, and the township accepts only cash, check or money order.

Who inspects the chimney for a Bensalem sale?

A chimney sweep company of your choice, with an NFPA 211 Level II inspection noted on the certification. The township also states that it will not accept certifications from two named companies.

Where do I send a Bucks County assessment appeal?

To the Board of Assessment Appeals at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown. The 2026 annual deadline was August 3, 2026, and the board posts each year's date on its page.

What do new owners of Bensalem property file with the county?

Under Act 29, a new owner submits contact information to the Board of Assessment within 30 days of the purchase, according to the Bucks County page.

What do I have to do before closing on a house in Abington?

Abington Township requires an affidavit at or before settlement on any single-family, two-family or multifamily dwelling. The seller swears that the house shows a clear street address, has smoke detectors and has at least one carbon monoxide detector. Under the township's Resolution 92-008, a deed is not accepted for registration unless this certification comes with it.

The rules in Ordinance 1894 are specific, and a buyer's agent will check them.

  • Address numerals at least three inches high on the street side of the structure, visible from the center of the street
  • A smoke detector on each level and in each bedroom or sleeping area
  • A carbon monoxide detector no more than 40 feet from every sleeping area
  • Detectors that are UL rated and approved

Breaking the ordinance is a summary offense that can bring a fine of $1,000 at most, up to 30 days in jail, or both, and every day of a continuing violation is charged separately. The affidavit form is on the township's document center. Smoke and CO alarms cost little, and installing them before listing removes a closing delay.

Does Abington require a use and occupancy permit to sell a home?

No. The township's permit page states that Abington does not have a use and occupancy permit for residential properties. Use and occupancy review applies to commercial properties, new businesses and business transfers, and includes a Fire Marshal inspection.

That makes a typical Abington house sale lighter on municipal paperwork than in towns that demand a resale inspection. The detector affidavit is the main township requirement. Any building work you did without a permit is a separate question. Ask the Code Enforcement Division before listing if you finished a basement, built a deck or added a bathroom.

What are the real estate and transfer taxes in Abington?

Abington's 2026 tax sheet lists a real estate tax split among the township, the Abington School District, a school referendum levy and Montgomery County with its community college. On a house assessed at $150,000 the sheet shows a total of $7,994 a year. The school district portion, at 39.8992 mills, is $5,970 of that.

The same sheet lists a township realty transfer tax of 1 percent, collected by Montgomery County, on top of the state's 1 percent. Ask your closing agent whether the school district adds a share on your deed. Pennsylvania's Department of Revenue exempts some transfers, such as property passing by will or intestate succession.

Abington does not assess property. The Montgomery County Board of Assessments does, and the last countywide reassessment was in 1998. The township bill, which also covers sewer and refuse, is mailed in the first week of February for a January to December year. The school bill follows in the first week of July and runs July to June.

What is Abington Township like for a seller?

Abington is a first-class township in Montgomery County, incorporated in 1704 and described by the township as a first-ring suburb of Philadelphia. It covers about 15.5 square miles. The township names Willow Grove, Roslyn, Crestmont, Glenside, Rydal, North Hills and Meadowbrook among its neighborhoods.

Easton Road, Huntington Pike (PA 232) and Old York Road (PA 611) run through the township, and I-276 and PA 309 are minutes away. Seven SEPTA stations on three regional rail lines serve it: North Hills on the Doylestown line; Crestmont, Roslyn and Ardsley on the Warminster line; and Meadowbrook, Rydal and Noble on the West Trenton line. The township says the ride to Center City takes less than half an hour.

Most of the township has public water from Aqua Pennsylvania and public sewer maintained by the township. It runs more than 25 parks covering over 375 acres, and its fire protection comes from an all-volunteer department with five stations. The Abington School District is a separate body from the township government.

What do the numbers say about Abington housing?

The Census Bureau's mid 2025 estimate for the township is 58,656 people, compared with 55,310 in 2010. Density comes to roughly 3,769 people per square mile.

  • Owners live in 77.3 percent of occupied homes

  • Rent in the middle of the market is $1,493
  • 22,391 households, averaging 2.56 people
  • Household income in the middle is $103,645
  • 51.1 percent of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree or more
  • Workers spend 28.7 minutes getting to their jobs on average

These come from Census QuickFacts for Abington township and cover 2020 to 2024. The same table shows 92.5 percent of residents in the house they lived in a year before, so turnover is low and a listing with defects or title questions takes more effort to place.

Which sale routes suit an Abington house?

Sellers here generally choose among three routes. An agent listing reaches the widest pool of buyers, and it also means staging, showings and waiting on a buyer's financing and inspection. Selling without an agent saves the commission but leaves the paperwork, from the detector affidavit to the deed, in your hands.

A direct cash sale skips showings and repairs. It suits an inherited house, a tenant-occupied property, a house with code or maintenance issues, or a seller who needs a firm closing date. A cash buyer's price reflects the work the house needs, so weigh it against what a repaired and listed house would net once fees, repairs and months of carrying costs come out.

Whichever route you pick, the same Abington steps apply: the detector certification, the tax figures above and a recorded deed at the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds.

How do I handle an inherited or tenant-occupied Abington house?

With an inherited house, settle first who can sign for the estate, because title must be in order before a deed can be recorded. Title passing through an estate carries no state transfer tax, though the later sale does.

With a tenant in place, read the lease before you list. Showings and possession dates depend on its terms and on Pennsylvania landlord and tenant law. Buyers who plan to keep the tenant will ask for the lease and rent history, and the detector rules cover rentals sold in the township too.

For questions about the township tax sheet, call the Abington tax office at 267-536-1024 on weekdays between 8 am and 4 pm. Owners of a primary residence can apply for a homestead exclusion through the Montgomery County Board of Assessments, and applications must arrive by March 1 to reduce the school tax bill.

More questions about Abington, PA

Does Abington require a smoke and carbon monoxide certification when I sell?

Yes. Ordinance 1894 requires smoke detectors on each level and in each bedroom, plus a carbon monoxide detector within 40 feet of every sleeping area, with a seller's affidavit at or before settlement.

Is there a residential use and occupancy permit in Abington?

No. The township says it has no use and occupancy permit for residential properties. That review applies to commercial buildings and business transfers.

What is Abington's transfer tax?

The township's 2026 tax sheet lists a 1 percent real estate transfer tax, collected by Montgomery County. The state adds its own 1 percent. Ask the closing agent whether any other local share applies.

Who assesses property in Abington Township?

The Montgomery County Board of Assessments, not the township. The township says the last countywide reassessment was in 1998, and interim bills reflect changes such as additions or demolitions.

When must I apply for the homestead exclusion?

Applications must be in the Board of Assessments' hands by March 1 to cut the school tax bill. Approved owners are not asked to refile annually, but a move or a change of title means applying again.

How does selling a house in Lancaster, PA work?

Whether you hire a broker, post a sign yourself or take a cash offer, the same city and county paperwork applies. The city issues its own payoff figures, the recorder collects transfer tax, and a countywide reassessment is something buyers will raise.

Lancaster is a small, dense city. About 58,366 people lived in Lancaster by the Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate. They share barely 7.2 square miles of land, around 8,000 per square mile. Much of the housing is rowhomes on narrow lots, so a sale often turns on the condition of one building.

A cash sale can move faster, since no lender appraisal holds up the closing. It does not remove the city steps below. Someone still has to order the property certification, record the deed and pay the transfer tax.

What kind of city is Lancaster for a home seller?

Lancaster is the county seat and one of the oldest inland cities in the country. It began as Hickory Town, was laid out in 1734, became a borough in 1742 and a city in 1818, and served as the state capital from 1799 to 1812. That age shows up in the housing stock, where nineteenth century brick and early twentieth century rowhouses sit beside factory conversions.

The city sits in the Piedmont region just north of the Conestoga River. Its neighborhoods include the Historic East Side, Chestnut Hill, Cabbage Hill, the West End, Prospect Heights, Musser Park, Mussertown, Woodward Hill and the Gallery Row arts district. Central Market, built in 1889, anchors the downtown core, and Park City Center is the largest enclosed shopping center in south central Pennsylvania.

Jobs come mostly from health care, government, education and retail. Lancaster General Hospital was the largest city employer in the 2018 financial report, with 9,406 employees, followed by the county government and the School District of Lancaster. Franklin & Marshall College and several other schools add rental demand near the center of town.

  • Public schools: the School District of Lancaster, with McCaskey and McCaskey East as the high school campuses.
  • Weather: about 42 inches of precipitation a year, and 72 inches of snow in the winter of 2009 to 2010, which is the record. Older roofs and basements take the strain.

What do the Census numbers say about Lancaster homes?

They describe a city with more renters than owners and home values far below the Philadelphia suburbs. Less than half of occupied homes have their owner living in them, which means many sales involve tenants.

The gap between a $219,500 middle home value and $1,240 middle rent is why investors buy in the city. A seller with a rental can expect offers that price in the rent roll and the cost of the next licensing inspection.

Which City of Lancaster rules can affect a sale?

The ones that matter most are rental licensing, the vacant property registry and the lead safety rules for older rentals. They are run by the Bureau of Property Maintenance and Housing Inspections at 120 North Duke Street.

  • Rental licenses and inspections. The city runs a residential rental program under its Chapter 238 and inspects every licensed rental at least once every six years, with at least three weeks of notice. For a tenant-occupied house, request the license status and open inspection items from the city before replying to any bid.
  • Lead safety. Rentals and child care facilities built before 1978 must meet lead safety requirements every two to four years under rules that took effect in January 2023. The city plans to cover roughly 12,000 older rentals over a four year cycle.
  • Vacant or abandoned houses. An owner must register a vacant building within 10 days. The semiannual fee is $200, with extra charges for buildings vacant two years or longer, and a house actively marketed for sale is outside the definition of vacant. If a registered property is sold, the new owner has 10 days to update the registration and inherits unpaid fees.
  • Short term rentals. The city allows them only in listed zoning districts, with a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, a rental license and an inspection first. A buyer planning an Airbnb use should confirm the district before paying for the house.

The vacant property rule counts a house in mortgage default or under a pending sheriff sale as abandoned, and those properties face monthly inspections. A seller behind on the mortgage should know that before listing.

What does the 2027 Lancaster County reassessment mean for sellers?

It means every parcel in the county, including each house in Lancaster, received a new assessed value for the 2027 tax year. The county mailed the notices on June 15, 2026, and the deadline to appeal a reassessment value was August 3, 2026, so that window has closed. Annual appeals after that point must be filed by August 1 of a given year to take effect for the following tax year.

The old values were based on market conditions from 2018. The new ones draw on arm's length sales from 2022 through 2024, adjusted by neighborhood. For a Lancaster seller this matters in two ways. A buyer may notice a higher assessed value than the one on the old bill. The county points out that every taxing body must lower its millage so that the reassessment alone does not bring in more revenue.

  • County and municipal millage for 2027 gets set around the close of December 2026.
  • School district millage for the 2027 to 2028 school year is set in June 2027, and the reassessment does not change 2026 to 2027 school taxes.
  • The assessment office is at 150 North Queen Street, Suite 310, and property records can be searched free on the county reassessment site.

Have the new assessed value ready when you talk to a buyer. A parcel that jumped will raise questions about the tax bill, and the answer is that the rates reset before 2027 bills go out.

What paperwork does the city require before closing in Lancaster?

The settlement company must send the city a Request for Property Certification with payment, and for a house inside city limits a smoke detector certification has to be completed before the city will release information. The city asks for two full business days to return the figures once the request is complete.

The 2025 version of the city form listed an $18 tax certification, a $5 trash final, a $17 water final and a $40 combined final. It also asks for the meter reading, the new owner's details and the settlement date, and it tells the title agent to escrow estimates if the city does not answer in time. The form flags delinquent city taxes, property violations, police alarm charges, housing licenses and liens.

  1. Order the property certification early, since the smoke detector step comes first.
  2. Have the buyer open a water account using the city application.
  3. Check for delinquent county taxes with the Lancaster County Tax Claim office, which the city form lists at 717-299-8232.
  4. The form also has a line for Downtown Investment District (DID) charges, with a separate DID office number.

What does a Lancaster sale cost at the recorder's office?

The state's cut is 1 percent of the property value. The county recorder gathers it at the same time as any local transfer tax. Buyer and seller are both liable for it. State exemptions cover certain family transfers and property passing by inheritance.

The title agent can quote the exact combined rate for a Lancaster deed, since the local portion depends on the taxing bodies involved. Who pays it is negotiated in the sales contract.

With an as-is purchase, check the contract line by line for who covers transfer tax and the city finals.

Which Lancaster houses suit a cash offer?

It makes sense when speed, condition or tenants matter more than the last dollar of price. A rowhouse with deferred repairs, a rental with an open inspection report, or a vacant inherited house are cases where a cash buyer can simplify the sale.

Compare any offer to a realistic list price less repairs, agent commission, transfer tax, city finals and months of carrying cost. To see what a direct buyer would pay for your Lancaster house, request a quote from Cash Home Buyers and weigh it against the net sheet.

More questions about Lancaster, PA

Do I need a smoke detector certification to sell a house in Lancaster city?

Yes for a house inside city limits. The city's property certification request states that a completed smoke detector certification is required before the city provides settlement information. Have it done before the title company orders the finals.

Can I still appeal my Lancaster County reassessment?

The reassessment appeal deadline for the 2027 tax year was August 3, 2026, so that window has closed. Annual appeals can still be filed each year by August 1 for the following tax year, and an appeal can lower or raise the value.

What happens to a vacant house in Lancaster while I try to sell it?

A vacant house that is not actively marketed must be registered with the city within 10 days and carries a semiannual fee. Properties in mortgage default count as abandoned and face monthly inspections. Check the registry rules with the housing bureau at 717-291-4781 before the house sits empty.

Does a tenant have to leave before I sell a Lancaster rental?

No. Tenants do not have to move out for a rental to sell, because the buyer steps into the lease. The unit still needs a current city rental license, and any open inspection items should be cleared or priced into the sale.

Who collects the transfer tax when a Lancaster house sells?

The Lancaster County recorder takes payment at the moment the deed is filed. The state's piece is 1 percent of the value, with local taxes stacked on top. The title company will show the exact figures on the settlement statement.
