What should sellers know about Lower Paxton Township itself?

The township covers 28.1 square miles in south central Dauphin County. Susquehanna Township is on its west, Middle Paxton on its north, West Hanover and South Hanover on its east, and Swatara on its south. Beaver Creek forms the eastern border, and Blue Mountain, the southernmost ridge of the Ridge and Valley Appalachians in the region, sits along the northern edge. Four unincorporated communities are counted as census designated places: Linglestown in the northeast with 6,334 residents, Paxtonia in the center with 5,412, Colonial Park in the west and southwest with 13,229, and a small piece of Progress in the far west.

The name comes from Paxtang, spelled Peshtank in the original Native American language and understood to mean standing water. Dauphin County was split from Lancaster County in 1785, and what remained of the old Paxtang Township after a 1767 division was renamed Lower Paxton. Harrisburg was formed as a borough in 1791 and Swatara Township followed in 1799. Population jumped from 6,546 in 1950 to 17,618 in 1960 and 26,517 in 1970, which explains why so many neighborhoods date from the postwar suburban boom.

Two interstates meet here. Interstate 83 runs through the west with Exit 50 at US 22 and Jonestown Road and Exit 48 at Union Deposit Road, and I-81 crosses the center from west to east, with Exit 72 between Linglestown and Paxtonia. Children attend the Central Dauphin School District.

What do Census figures show about Lower Paxton homes?

The median value of an owner-occupied home was $284,700 over 2020 to 2024, median gross rent was $1,417, and the township had 22,025 households. Median household income was $91,789 in 2024 dollars, 38.8 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and mean travel time to work was 21.4 minutes. Some 86.0 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

A median value under $300,000 means transfer taxes and closing costs are smaller in dollars than in the Philadelphia suburbs, but they still add up. At the median value, the combined 2 percent transfer tax is $5,694. A landlord selling a rental pays the same percentage, so settle the split before you sign.

What happens to sewer and stormwater accounts when I sell?

Lower Paxton's sewer authority requires settlement agents to request balances on a specific form before a sale or refinance, and it can take up to five business days for the form to be reviewed and returned. Start this the day the contract is signed.

  • The completed Sewer and Stormwater Services Transfer Form goes to the authority's settlements email address or by fax.
  • A new sewer account carries a $15 processing fee collected at settlement.
  • The authority bills in arrears each January, April, July and October, so ask your settlement agent to prorate a mid-quarter sale. Its billing page lists a flat residential sewer rate and a single family stormwater fee on the same quarterly bill.
  • Delinquent accounts can go to a collection law firm, and unpaid charges become a lien that follows the property.

If your account is on automatic withdrawal, call the Sewer and Utilities Department at 717-657-5617 so the draft stops after the sale. Bills stay in the owner's name, which matters when you own a rental and a tenant normally pays the household bills.

How do Lower Paxton property taxes work?

Real estate is taxed by the township, Dauphin County and the Central Dauphin School District, and the school district is by far the largest bill at 18.2934 mills for 2025 to 2026. The township says its assessments rest on a January 2002 base, adjusted for new construction and appeals, so the figure on your bill can differ a great deal from market value. Earned income tax is 2 percent, with 1.5 percent to the school district and 0.5 percent to the township, and the local services tax is $52 for people who work in the township.

Interim notice mailed March 1March 1 to April 30May 1 to June 30July 1 to December 31
Interim notice mailed August 1August 1 to September 30October 1 to November 30December 1 to January 31

Unpaid taxes pass to the Dauphin County Tax Claim Bureau after December 31. Interim bills follow new construction, pools and additions, so a seller who finished a basement or built a deck may owe an interim bill even after the regular one.

How do I appeal a Dauphin County assessment?

Dauphin County accepts annual appeals after June 1 and no later than 4:30 p.m. on August 1, and a late filing is rejected even if it was mailed on time. An appeal from a new or revised assessment must arrive within 40 days of the notice. The filing fee must come with the form and is not refunded, and all delinquent taxes on the parcel must be current before the Board will accept or hear it.

The Board of Assessment Appeals sits in the Administration Building at 2 South 2nd Street, Harrisburg, and takes filings by mail or in person on weekdays. The aggrieved party must appear at the hearing, and anyone representing an owner must be a Pennsylvania attorney who brings a power of attorney.

What closing costs should a Lower Paxton seller expect?

The state realty transfer tax is 1 percent, the township levies one half of one percent by ordinance, and the Central Dauphin School District levies one half of one percent. Together that is 2 percent of the sale price, collected at settlement by the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds. Both parties are jointly liable under state law, so allocate it in the contract. Exempt transfers include certain moves between close family members and property that passes by will or intestacy.

Add pro-rated real estate tax, sewer and trash charges, any agent commissions, and payoff of any mortgage or lien. Ask the township codes office whether any sale-related inspection or certificate applies to your address.

More questions about Lower Paxton, PA

How much is the transfer tax in Lower Paxton Township?

The total is 2 percent of the sale price: 1 percent to Pennsylvania, one half percent to the township and one half percent to the Central Dauphin School District. The county Recorder of Deeds collects it at settlement.

Does the Lower Paxton sewer authority need anything before closing?

Yes. The settlement agent must send the Sewer and Stormwater Services Transfer Form and allow up to five business days for balances, and the authority charges a $15 new account fee at settlement.

What is the Dauphin County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 at 4:30 p.m., with filing allowed after June 1. A new or revised assessment can be appealed within 40 days of its notice.

Who collects real estate tax in Lower Paxton Township?

An elected tax collector handles real estate tax payments for the township, county and school district. Unpaid taxes go to the Dauphin County Tax Claim Bureau after December 31.

Which interstates serve Lower Paxton Township?

Interstate 83 runs through the west and Interstate 81 runs across the center. I-83 has Exits 50 and 48 in the township, and I-81 has Exit 72 between Linglestown and Paxtonia.

What should I know before selling a house in Middletown Township?

Middletown Township in Bucks County requires a Level 2 chimney inspection on every home that is sold, and Levittown sections add a heater compartment wall inspection. That fire marshal rule is the main local step, followed by a 2 percent transfer tax paid at recording.

The township has 46,040 residents, according to the 2020 census, spread across about 19 square miles in the Philadelphia metropolitan area. It surrounds the boroughs of Langhorne, Langhorne Manor, Penndel and Hulmeville, which is why many addresses read Langhorne even though they sit in the township. Do not confuse it with other Pennsylvania townships that share the Middletown name; this page covers the Bucks County one only.

Sellers can list, sell without an agent or accept a cash purchase. The township rules below apply whichever route you choose.

How did Levittown shape Middletown Township?

The township was formally established in 1692 and stayed farmland for most of its history. In 1930 it had only 2,095 residents, and in 1950 it had 4,987. Then William Levitt began his second Levittown, which reached into four municipalities including Middletown, and the 1960 census counted 26,936 people, a 440 percent jump.

That history explains the housing mix you will find on a listing search:

  • Levittown sections in the south, built in the 1950s, with hundreds of similar homes per development.
  • Parkland, where houses date from every decade of the 20th century and the 21st.
  • Newer townhouses and condominiums around the Oxford Valley Mall, along with assisted living and 55-plus housing.
  • A few older farm properties; Edgemont, Harewood and Beechwood carry National Register listings.

The township later preserved hundreds of acres, now Core Creek Park with Lake Luxembourg, and saved Styer's Orchards from a plan for 632 homes in the late 1990s. Sesame Place and part of Cairn University are also inside the township.

What inspection does Middletown Township require when a house sells?

Every home sold in the township needs a Level 2 chimney inspection, and the Fire and Emergency Management office keeps a copy. The rule follows NFPA 211, which calls for the inspection any time a property is sold or transferred.

The inspection covers any appliance that vents combustion gases, including oil-fired and gas-fired heaters with a metal B-vent chimney, fireplaces, wood stoves and pellet stoves. A certified CSIA chimney sweep must do it, and the township website keeps a courtesy list of local sweeps. The requirement does not apply to a home heated and cooled only by electric devices or one with a vent-less fireplace, and plastic PVC exhaust pipe does not need a Level 2 inspection.

Middletown Township resale and tax facts. Source: Middletown Township Fire and Emergency Management, Bucks County Recorder of Deeds and Board of Assessment.

How much are property taxes in Middletown Township?

The 2026 combined millage in Middletown Township is 252.2674 mills, according to the Bucks County millage list effective July 1, 2026. Three taxing bodies make up that number: the county at 29.65 mills, the Neshaminy School District at 198.0124 mills and the township at 24.605 mills.

The township's own 24.605 mills break down into a general fund of 7.025, a debt service fund of 5.115, fire protection of 4.75, parks and recreation of 3.25 and fire apparatus of 2.5, plus smaller street light, ambulance, road machinery and hydrant levies. One mill equals a dollar of tax on each thousand dollars of assessment. The Bucks County Board of Assessment sets each property's assessed value.

Because Neshaminy carries most of the load, the school district millage drives the difference between Middletown and nearby municipalities in other districts. For comparison, the same county list shows Falls Township at 250.763 total mills and Lower Makefield at 265.786.

What is the transfer tax on a Middletown sale?

The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds describes a 2 percent transfer tax on property sales in Pennsylvania, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. Payment is made at recording, and the value that is taxed can differ from the sales price.

Neither state nor local government says who pays, and in most agreements the buyer and seller divide it. The new owner is responsible if the amount paid turns out to be wrong. Starting in January 2026, the recorder's office stopped accepting personal checks for the tax. Payment options are cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card, so tell your title company early.

  • Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings can be exempt.
  • A one-time transfer between former spouses is allowed.
  • A $1 deed or a transfer with no tax paid needs a statement of value so state investigators can check the real worth.

The recorder's office can be reached at 215-348-6209 for exemption questions.

When can I appeal a Bucks County assessment?

The 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, and it has passed. Any change from that cycle takes effect for the 2027 tax year.

The Board of Assessment Appeals sits at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown and can be reached at 215-348-6219. It meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesdays of each month. Appeal forms and rules for both residential and commercial properties are posted on the county site.

Two other county items apply to sellers and buyers. The homestead and farmstead exclusion application is due March 1 for the tax year beginning the following July 1, and a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying, under Act 29.

What affects a Middletown Township house's value and appeal?

Location along the Philadelphia and Trenton corridor, school assignments and weather exposure all shape buyer interest. Interstate 295 runs through the east side of the township, and U.S. Route 1 crosses the middle. Pennsylvania routes 213, 413, 332 and 513 also touch it. The township reports 189.70 miles of public roads, of which the township maintains 139.07 miles.

SEPTA's West Trenton Regional Rail line stops at Woodbourne station in the township, and Langhorne station is just across the line in Langhorne Manor. SEPTA also runs City Bus route 14 and suburban routes 127, 128, 129 and 130 through the area.

Neshaminy School District serves the township. Albert Schweitzer, Herbert Hoover, Pearl S. Buck, Tawanka and Walter Miller elementary schools cover kindergarten through fourth grade, Carl Sandburg and Maple Point middle schools take grades five through eight, and Neshaminy High School serves grades nine through twelve.

NOAA's 1991 to 2020 normals for the Neshaminy Falls station show 50.7 inches of rain and melted snow per year plus 19.9 inches of snowfall, and July is the wettest month. The township record wet day was 6.60 inches on August 27, 2011, so basements and drainage are a fair question for any buyer inspection.

Is a listing or a cash sale the better fit in Middletown?

A cash sale suits a property with deferred repairs, while a listing suits one a lender will finance as it stands. Either way, the chimney inspection comes first, and a failed inspection can change what you can ask.

  • Book a CSIA chimney sweep before you list and send the report to the fire marshal.
  • If the house is in Levittown, ask the fire office what the heater compartment wall inspection involves.
  • Compare offers after the 2 percent transfer tax, your mortgage payoff and the school and township tax proration.

More questions about Middletown, PA

Does Middletown Township require a chimney inspection when I sell?

Yes. A Level 2 chimney inspection by a certified CSIA sweep is required for homes with combustion appliances, and a copy goes to Fire and Emergency Management. Levittown homes also need a heater compartment wall inspection.

What is the transfer tax in Middletown Township?

The Bucks County Recorder of Deeds lists 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district. The tax is paid at the time of recording.

Which school district serves Middletown Township?

Neshaminy School District. Five elementary schools, two middle schools and Neshaminy High School serve the township.

What is the total property tax rate in Middletown Township?

The county's July 1, 2026 list shows 252.2674 mills combined: 29.65 for the county, 198.0124 for Neshaminy School District and 24.605 for the township.

Can I still file a Bucks County assessment appeal for 2026?

No. The 2026 annual appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, and it has passed. Call the Board of Assessment at 215-348-6219 to ask about the next annual cycle.

What should I know before selling a house in Manheim Township?

Manheim Township is a Lancaster County municipality of 43,977 people where the biggest issue for sellers is the countywide reassessment that takes effect for the 2027 tax year. A certificate of use and occupancy and a 2 percent transfer tax round out the local rules.

This page covers Manheim Township, which sits directly north of Lancaster city. Lancaster County also has a separate borough named Manheim, so check the municipality on your tax bill before relying on any local rule. The township has no ZIP code of its own, so owners carry a Lititz, Lancaster or Leola mailing address depending on where the house sits.

A retail listing, a sale by owner and a direct cash purchase are all open to a seller, and the paperwork below applies to each.

Where does Manheim Township sit in Lancaster County?

The township covers about 24 square miles and ranks as the second largest municipality in Lancaster County, behind the city itself. It was established in 1729, and its southern boundary meets the Lancaster city limits.

The township's communities include Neffsville, Dillerville and Landis Valley. Population counts show how steadily it has grown:

  • 9,289 residents in 1950.
  • 21,539 in 1970.
  • 33,697 in 2000.
  • 43,977 in 2020.

The 2000 census put the median age at 43, with 21 percent of residents 65 or older.

How does the Manheim Township School District affect a sale?

The school district is coterminous with the township, so a home inside the township boundary is in the district and a home outside it is not. That clean match makes the address check simple for a buyer.

The district runs Manheim Township High School, a virtual high school, Manheim Township Middle School, Landis Run Intermediate School and six elementary schools: Brecht, Bucher, Neff, Nitrauer, Reidenbaugh and Schaeffer. Buyers with children usually ask which elementary school serves a street, and the district office can confirm that from an address.

The township itself does not bill or collect property taxes. Lancaster County assesses the property, while the elected tax collector and the school district collect the bills.

What is the 2027 Lancaster County reassessment?

Lancaster County reassessed every parcel at current market value, and the new values apply to the 2027 tax year. The previous assessments were based on 2018 values, and the county says the new notices should land near what a property would sell for today. Notices were mailed on June 15, 2026.

The county used valid arm's-length residential sales from 2022 through 2024, adjusted for acreage, square footage, porches, garages and bathrooms. State law requires each taxing body to adjust its millage so it does not collect more revenue only because values moved, but the tax on an individual house can still rise or fall. County and municipal millage for 2027 is set near the end of December 2026, and school millage for the 2027-2028 year is set in June 2027. The reassessment does not change 2026-27 school taxes.

The reassessment appeal deadline was August 3, 2026, the first business day after August 1, and it has passed. The county says the next opportunity for an annual appeal is 2028. Ask the Property Assessment Office at 717-299-8381 what applies to a house that sold or changed after the notices went out.

Does Manheim Township require an inspection to sell?

No. The township states that it does not require an inspection before settlement. A certificate of use and occupancy can still be requested by the parties to the deal, and the zoning ordinance has required one for every structure since 1944.

If you need a copy, contact the Code Compliance Department with the property address, the home type (single-family, townhouse or duplex) and whether any part of the basement is finished. Staff check the records and send a copy if one is on file. If none exists, the owner or an agent applies in person at the township office, pays a $50 residential filing fee and books an inspection with a code official.

Manheim Township sale paperwork. Source: Manheim Township website and Lancaster County Property Assessment Office.

What does the realty transfer tax cost in Manheim Township?

The township Treasurer's Office FAQ puts the realty transfer tax at 2 percent of the value transferred. The Commonwealth receives 1 percent, and the township and school district share the other 1 percent.

The Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds, at 50 North Duke Street, takes payment as part of recording the deed. The state notes that both buyer and seller are liable for it, and the sale contract decides how it is split. Certain family transfers and property passed by inheritance are exempt from the state portion, so ask the recorder before assuming a deed is taxable.

Real estate tax bills combine the county and township taxes and go out by March 1. If a lender pays your taxes from escrow, send the lender a copy of the bill.

What rules apply if I am selling a rental in Manheim Township?

Manheim Township has licensed rental properties since 2022, and an annual license costs $50 per building. Each rental unit is inspected at least once every five years, and one- and two-unit buildings have every unit inspected.

  • Owners living more than 25 miles from the township must name a responsible local agent.
  • Inspection fees run from $40 for one unit to $250 for buildings with 51 or more units.
  • The code compliance office handles applications, renewals and de-registration.

A landlord who sells should ask the code office how to de-register or transfer the license, and should hand the buyer the latest inspection results.

Which route suits a Manheim Township seller?

The right route depends on the house's condition and your moving date. Putting it on the market reaches more buyers but brings showings and inspection haggling, while a direct cash sale can be timed around your move.

  • Request your certificate of use and occupancy early so a missing certificate does not delay the closing.
  • Look up your 2027 reassessed value on the county property search site and compare it with the price you are weighing.
  • Subtract the 2 percent transfer tax share you agree to, plus any mortgage payoff, to estimate net proceeds.

If a buyer asks for repairs, compare the cost against a quote for selling as-is.

More questions about Manheim, PA

Is Manheim Township the same as the borough of Manheim?

No. Manheim Township is a separate municipality that borders Lancaster city and has its own school district and township government. Lancaster County also has a borough named Manheim.

Does Manheim Township require a certificate of use and occupancy when I sell?

Not as a condition of settlement. The township does not inspect before closing, but buyers or lenders may ask for a copy. If none is on file, the residential filing fee is $50 and an inspection is scheduled.

What do buyers and sellers owe in transfer tax in Manheim Township?

The combined rate is 2 percent of the value transferred. The state gets 1 percent, and the township and school district share the other 1 percent. The Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds collects it.

When did the Lancaster County reassessment take effect?

The elected tax collector and the school district collect the bills. Lancaster County sets the assessment, and the township does not bill or collect property taxes itself.

Altoona at a glance

  • Altoona is in Blair County.
Selling in Altoona?

What is Altoona like for someone selling a house?

Altoona is a railroad city of about 42,300 people in Blair County, built on hillsides in the Allegheny Mountains at 1,161 feet. The Census Bureau estimates 42,347 residents for July 1, 2025, down 3.6 percent from the 2020 estimates base, and the city covers 9.79 square miles.

The Census median value of owner-occupied homes for 2020 to 2024 is $119,900, against $332,700 for the United States as a whole. The city's population peaked in the 1930 census at 82,054 and has fallen in every count since, to 43,963 in 2020.

How did the railroad shape Altoona's houses and streets?

The Pennsylvania Railroad founded Altoona in 1849 as a shop and maintenance site. The borough was incorporated in 1854 and the city in 1868, and at its peak the Altoona Works employed about 15,000 people across 122 buildings. Horseshoe Curve, west of town, remains a National Historic Landmark. In late September 1862 the city hosted the War Governors' Conference of 13 Union state governors.

The housing followed the work. Many older districts mix rowhouses with single homes, built to house workers and managers. The manager houses are narrow and tall, resemble Victorian or Edwardian mansions, and have often been converted to double or triple family apartments. Street names are numbers: Streets run northwest to southeast, and Avenues run northeast to southwest.

Which Altoona neighborhoods should a seller know?

The city's sections and neighborhood names are worth knowing before you describe a house.

  • Downtown and Center City: the Downtown Altoona Historic District, with multistory brick buildings from around 1900 and the Cathedral of the Blessed Sacrament at 13th Street and 13th Avenue.
  • Main sections: Logantown, Fairview, Juniata, Wehnwood, Calvert Hills, the 5th and 6th Wards, Westmont, Eldorado, East End, Dutch Hill, Pleasant Valley, Hileman Heights, Mansion Park, Llyswen, Garden Heights and Highland Park.
  • Named neighborhoods: Little Italy, Gospel Hill, Toy Town, Columbia Park, Knickerbockers and Curtin.
  • Floodplain and zoning: the city website carries a floodplain information page and a zoning and GIS map for checking a parcel.
  • Lakemont, Greenwood, Bellmeade and Newburg: considered parts of Altoona but outside city limits, in Logan Township.

That last group matters: Logan Township surrounds the city, so the tax bill and the codes office depend on which side of the line the parcel sits.

What do Census figures say about Altoona housing?

For 2020 to 2024, 63.9 percent of Altoona homes were owner-occupied, 90.2 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and 17.9 percent were 65 or older. The 2020 census counted 20,672 housing units, 9.7 percent of them vacant, with a rental vacancy rate of 9.1 percent.

What local taxes and transfer costs apply to an Altoona sale?

The city's local tax page lists the charges that touch a home sale. Real estate transfer tax applies to anyone buying or selling property in Altoona and is collected by the Blair County Recorder of Deeds. The page shows a total of 2 percent, with 1 percent going to the state and 1 percent split between the city and the Altoona Area School District.

  • Local real estate tax is listed at 7.129 mils and is collected by H. A. Berkheimer.
  • A 1.70 percent rate applies to persons and entities engaging in business in the city, and 1.40 percent applies to non-residents who work in the city. The Blair County Tax Collection Bureau collects both.
  • Employed residents pay $5.00 annually, assessed by both the city and the Altoona Area School District.

The Blair County Assessment Office is at 423 Allegheny Street, Suite 041, Hollidaysburg, phone 814-693-3110. Ask it for the appeal form and the annual deadline, and ask your closing agent how the transfer tax will be split.

What rental inspection rules apply when the Altoona house is a rental?

Every owner of a leased or non-owner-occupied dwelling in Altoona must hold a Conditional Housing Permit, which becomes a Residential Rental Unit License after the unit passes inspection. Licenses are renewed on or before July 31 each year, and most units are inspected every three years.

  • An inspection takes 20 to 30 minutes, and the owner, tenant or a representative must be present.
  • Inspectors use the International Property Maintenance Code on the interior and exterior.
  • Owners usually get 45 days to repair violations, with extensions in 30-day steps, and life-safety hazards must be corrected immediately.
  • Heat must be supplied from October 1 to May 15, and smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are checked.

A landlord selling a rental should confirm the license status with the Codes and Inspections Department at 1301 12th Street, Suite 103, phone 814-949-2456. The department's page does not describe a separate inspection tied to a sale, so ask it whether one applies to your property.

How does Altoona's mountain climate affect a house?

Altoona's climate is hot in summer and moderately cold in winter, with wide temperature swings. The monthly daily average runs from 28.4 degrees in January to 72.4 in July, and the extremes range from minus 25 in 1904 to 103.

Annual precipitation averages 36.65 inches over about 136 days, and September is the wettest month. Roofs, gutters and basements see regular wear from that many wet days and the winter cold, and the old rowhouse stock shares walls and rooflines between units.

How do jobs, roads and schools affect Altoona buyers?

Health care is the leading field of employment, with UPMC Altoona, a rehabilitation hospital and the James E. Van Zandt VA Medical Center. Sheetz has its headquarters in Altoona, and Boyer, maker of the Mallo Cup, is based here. Penn State Altoona, the third largest of the university's Commonwealth campuses, has bought downtown buildings.

  • I-99 runs north to I-80 and south to the Pennsylvania Turnpike, and US 22 runs east to Harrisburg and west to Pittsburgh.
  • AMTRAN provides local buses, and Amtrak's Pennsylvanian stops once daily in each direction.
  • Altoona-Blair County Airport offers daily flights to Charlotte.
  • The Altoona Area School District serves all of the city, including Altoona Area High School for grades 9 to 12.

What are the ways to sell a house fast in Altoona?

An Altoona owner can list with an agent, sell privately, or take a cash offer. With the median home value near $120,000, the cost of repairs compared with the likely sale price is a fair first question.

For a rental, check the license and inspection status first. For a vacant house, ask the Codes and Inspections Department about any open property maintenance notice before you list. Gather the deed, the tax bills from H. A. Berkheimer and the county, and any permit records before you list.

More questions about Altoona, PA

Does Altoona have a transfer tax when I sell my house?

Yes. The city's local tax page lists a 2 percent real estate transfer tax, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent shared by the city and the school district, collected by the Blair County Recorder of Deeds.

When must Altoona landlords renew their rental license?

On or before July 31 each year. Most units are inspected every three years, and owners generally get 45 days to fix violations found.

Who collects real estate tax on an Altoona home?

H. A. Berkheimer collects the city's local real estate tax, listed at 7.129 mils. Blair County and the school district bill separately.

Is Lakemont inside the city of Altoona?

No. Lakemont, Greenwood, Bellmeade, Newburg and several other areas are treated as parts of Altoona but lie in Logan Township, outside city limits.

Where do I ask about assessment changes in Blair County?

Call the Blair County Assessment Office in Hollidaysburg at 814-693-3110. It handles appeal forms and can tell you the filing deadline for the year.

How does a home sale work in Hempfield Township?

Paperwork is lighter in Hempfield than in many Pennsylvania municipalities, since the township does not ask for a certificate of occupancy at sale. What you do need is a clear view of the septic or sewer setup, the 2 percent transfer tax and the county assessment record.

Hempfield is a township in Westmoreland County, and it is big. Spread over about 77 square miles, it ranks as the Pittsburgh metro's most populous suburb, according to Wikipedia. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 41,421 residents, a 0.2 percent dip from its 2020 base. The township is steady rather than growing, and sellers mostly compete with other established houses.

Whether the buyer arrives through a broker, a yard sign or a direct cash purchase, the paper trail ends at the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds in Greensburg, where the deed is filed and the transfer tax is paid.

Where is Hempfield and what is inside it?

The city of Greensburg and six boroughs sit entirely inside the township: Southwest Greensburg, South Greensburg, Youngwood, New Stanton, Arona and Adamsburg. Hempfield was incorporated on April 6, 1773, and takes its name from the hemp fields of the older Hempfield in Lancaster County.

Named communities within the township include Fort Allen, Grapeville, Hannastown, Carbon, Radebaugh, Maplewood Terrace, West Point and Luxor. Neighbors include Salem, Unity, Mount Pleasant, East Huntingdon, South Huntingdon, Sewickley and North Huntingdon townships, plus the city of Jeannette. The township is large enough that a home near Greensburg and a rural parcel miles away can have very different values.

  • Schools: the Hempfield Area School District, which also serves Adamsburg, Armbrust, Bovard, Grapeville, Hunker, Luxor, Manor, New Stanton and Youngwood.
  • Higher education: the University of Pittsburgh at Greensburg, the Youngwood campus of Westmoreland County Community College, and a Carlow University satellite campus.
  • Policing: the township relies on the Pennsylvania State Police as its sole law enforcement agency.

What shapes the Hempfield economy and home demand?

Hempfield is the retail hub for Westmoreland County and the Laurel Highlands. U.S. Route 30 passes the Westmoreland Mall and the adjoining Live! Casino Pittsburgh, and Greengate Centre is the area's largest big-box center. Light industry operates from several industrial parks, including RIDC Westmoreland, which straddles the Hempfield and East Huntingdon line.

The 2011 tornado is part of local memory. An EF2 tornado touched down on March 23, 2011 southwest of Greensburg and damaged scores of homes in the West Hempfield area and the Fort Allen neighborhood, along with Hempfield Area High School and Harrold Middle School. A buyer may ask whether a house in those areas needed storm repairs.

Age matters for demand too. More than a quarter of residents (26.9 percent) have passed 65, and owners occupy 84.7 percent of homes, so estate sales and downsizing moves are common.

How do Hempfield homes look in the Census data?

Hempfield homes are owner occupied, moderately priced and held for a long time. Over 92 percent of residents stayed put for the previous year.

Few sellers here are racing a mortgage payment. The usual story is a family home held for decades, a parent's estate, or an older house whose repairs the owner is tired of managing.

What local rules apply when a Hempfield house sells?

The township's planning and code department says a certificate of occupancy is not required to sell a home. Two other checks apply depending on how the house drains.

  • On-lot septic. Contact the township's Sewage Enforcement Officer about any dye test the buyer or lender wants.
  • Public sewer. Call the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County at 724-755-5800 for the sewer account and any test or final reading.
  • Permits. Open permits or unpermitted work should be sorted out first. The township says zoning permits take up to 15 business days and building permits up to 30.

The code office is at 1132 Woodward Drive, Suite A, and answers at 724-834-7232. The county assessment office, at 724-830-3409, can explain whether a building permit changes the assessed value. Landlord and tenant disputes go to the Pennsylvania Attorney General's consumer hotline, which the township lists at 1-800-441-2555.

Township property tax is low in dollar terms. The township levies 3 mills for general purposes and 3 mills for a dedicated fire service tax, so a $25,000 assessed value pays $150 a year to the township. School and county taxes are separate and larger. Areas inside a street light district also pay a yearly light district assessment. The township also runs a rebate program that returns part of the general township real estate tax to qualifying senior homeowners, which long-time owners of older houses may already use.

How is the transfer tax split in Hempfield?

The township's own tax page puts the full charge on a sale at 2 percent of the price. One half of that goes to the state's 1 percent, and the rest is divided evenly between the township and the Hempfield Area School District at a quarter of the total each. You pay it when the deed is recorded, and the township lists the recorder at 724-830-3518.

At the $232,100 median home value the full 2 percent comes to about $4,642, and the sales contract says who covers which share. Both parties answer to the recorder for the tax, and state rules exempt certain family transfers and property passing by inheritance.

Ask the title company to show the transfer tax line before you sign. Selling an inherited house? Ask whether the inheritance exemption covers your deed.

How do Westmoreland County assessment appeals work?

The county Tax Assessment Office handles the values that set every property tax bill in the township. Anyone can appeal a change of assessment within 40 days of the mailing of the notice. A yearly appeal has to be on file by August 1 and only changes the next tax year's bill.

Hearings run on the second Thursday of every month, starting at 9:00 in the morning, in Suite 440 of the county building at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue in Greensburg. Forms come from the county website or the assessment office itself.

If you plan to sell, check the assessed value before listing. Lenders look at the current tax amount. If you think the assessment is too high, file by the next August 1.

Which Hempfield houses suit a direct cash sale?

It tends to suit worn houses, estate properties and sellers who want to pick the closing date. It is less useful for a move-in ready home you can list quickly.

Set any cash figure against what a listing would net after commission, transfer tax, repairs and months of waiting. If you want to see a number for your Hempfield house, Cash Home Buyers can quote one, and you can set it beside your other choices.

More questions about Hempfield, PA

Is a certificate of occupancy needed for a Hempfield home sale?

No. The township's planning and code office answers this directly in its FAQ: the sale of a home does not trigger a certificate of occupancy.

Who handles a dye test for a Hempfield home sale?

It depends on the system. For a septic system, contact the township's Sewage Enforcement Officer. For public sewer, call the Municipal Authority of Westmoreland County at 724-755-5800.

Who gets the 2 percent Hempfield transfer tax?

The state receives 1 percent, the township 0.5 percent and the Hempfield Area School District 0.5 percent, for 2 percent in all. The county recorder in Greensburg collects the money when the deed goes on record.

Which school district covers Hempfield Township?

The Hempfield Area School District. It also covers Adamsburg, Armbrust, Bovard, Grapeville, Hunker, Luxor, Manor, New Stanton and Youngwood.

When must a Westmoreland County assessment appeal be filed?

August 1 for a yearly appeal, which affects the following tax year. If a change of assessment notice is mailed, the window is 40 days.

Penn Hills at a glance

  • Penn Hills is in Allegheny County.
Selling in Penn Hills?

What do I need to sell a house in Penn Hills?

You need an Occupancy Permit and a passing dye test before the house changes hands. Penn Hills code enforcement requires the permit for every sale, purchase or deed transfer, whether or not anyone lives in the house. It is a municipal requirement, so it applies to a cash sale as much as to a listing.

The two steps have different owners. The occupancy application goes to the Code Enforcement Department at the Government Center, 102 Duff Road, and a plumber you hire handles the dye test. Starting both early keeps them from becoming the last item standing between you and the closing table.

  • Occupancy Permit: $75 for a single family dwelling and $125 for a commercial property.
  • Dye test: the plumber of your choice runs it, files the form only after the house passes, and you submit it with a $25 filing fee.
  • Septic: a house on a septic system needs an additional septic report.

How does the Penn Hills occupancy permit process work?

You file a three-part carbonless application, signed at the top and listing the new owner's information, and pay with it. The form posted on the municipal website is a sample and will not be accepted, so pick up the real one at the office. Payment can be cash, check or money order payable to the Municipality of Penn Hills, and cards are taken only at the office, where a service charge may apply.

If you mail the application, enclose a copy of a photo ID and name the person the inspector should meet at the property if that is not you. Inspections are scheduled Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m., and the department's own hours are 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The same permit is needed for every change of tenant or occupant, which matters if you are selling a rental with a tenant in place.

Call Code Enforcement at (412) 342-1192 with questions. The municipality's FAQ also lists a building permit as a separate item for new construction or home improvements, so ask before you finish any repair work you started on your own.

What does selling in Penn Hills cost in transfer tax?

Penn Hills sellers deal with a 3% total realty transfer tax: 1.5% to the municipality, 0.5% to the Penn Hills School District and 1% to the Commonwealth. The county's table lists the first two figures and notes that its local rates leave out the state's 1%. Allegheny County collects the tax when the deed is recorded, on a separate check from the recording fees.

On a $150,000 sale the total is $4,500. The municipal share is high compared with most Allegheny County boroughs, where the local share is often one half of one percent, so Penn Hills sellers should price it in early. The sales agreement says which side pays.

What is Penn Hills like for a home seller?

Penn Hills is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, and Wikipedia calls it the county's second-largest municipality. It was formed from the north of Wilkins Township in 1850, carried the name Penn Township, became Penn Hills Township in 1958 and took home rule status in 1976. Its population peaked at 62,886 in 1970 and stood at 41,059 in the 2020 census, down from 42,329 in 2010. The Census Bureau lists no 2025 estimate for Penn Hills.

The municipality covers about 19 square miles, with the Allegheny River on its northern edge and Plum Creek marking the border with Plum Borough. It touches ten neighbors, among them Verona, Oakmont, Monroeville, Churchill and the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of East Hills and Lincoln-Lemington-Belmar. Neighborhood names include Lincoln Park, Milltown, Rosedale, Universal, Verona Hilltop and Frankstown Estates.

  • Owners report a middle home value of $134,700 in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates, and 74.6% of households own.
  • Households: 17,964, averaging 2.23 people.
  • Median gross rent: $1,103.
  • Residents 65 and older make up 24.3% of the population.
  • Commutes average 26.9 minutes.

Interstate 376 crosses the south end, with Penn Hills at exit 81, and Rodi Road (PA 791) connects the interstate to Frankstown Road. PA 130 and PA 380 are the other main routes. The Penn Hills School District runs Penn Hills Elementary, Linton Middle and Penn Hills High School.

How do Allegheny County taxes affect a Penn Hills sale?

Allegheny County uses base year values, and the current base year is 2012, so an assessment is not a present-day market price. The county portal lists parcels, and changes from appeals, permits and corrections post daily. The annual appeal window for tax year 2026 ran from July 1 to September 2, 2025, and the window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026. Both are closed.

Penn Hills tax collection is split among the county, the municipality and the school district. Ask the county treasurer and the Penn Hills tax collector for a paid-to-date statement before you set a closing date. Anything owed at the time of sale is normally settled from the proceeds, and the title company will search for open balances.

The county runs a Homestead exclusion under Act 50 for owner-occupied homes, with the application made through the county. A buyer who will live in the house should apply in their own name after closing.

What disclosures apply when selling a Penn Hills house?

A seller must deliver a signed property disclosure statement to the buyer before the agreement of transfer is signed. The statement must address the roof, basement, structural problems, plumbing, wiring, water and sewage, drainage and other topics listed in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7304. Several creeks run through the municipality, so the land and drainage items deserve a careful answer.

An executor or other fiduciary who sells for an estate falls outside the chapter. Everyone else owes the buyer a truthful form, and a buyer who proves a violation can recover actual damages if the suit is filed within two years after settlement. If something on the form changes before closing, tell the buyer in writing.

How can I prepare a Penn Hills house for a fast sale?

Run the municipal steps first, because they are the ones with set lead times. A dye test needs a plumber's schedule and an occupancy inspection needs a weekday morning or early afternoon slot. Once those are lined up, the rest is the same as anywhere: a clean title, a payoff statement and a realistic price.

  • Book the dye test and, if the house has a septic system, the septic report.
  • Pick up the carbonless occupancy form at the Government Center rather than printing the sample.
  • Cut grass before inspection; the municipality treats grass over 10 inches as high.
  • Ask Code Enforcement whether any open permits or violations are on the address.

A buyer who purchases as-is still needs the municipal permit for the deed to move, so ask whether the buyer or the seller handles it and put the answer in the contract.

More questions about Penn Hills, PA

Does Penn Hills require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. The municipality requires an Occupancy Permit and a dye test for a sale, with an inspection scheduled on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. The permit is $75 for a single family home and the dye test filing fee is $25.

How much is the transfer tax in Penn Hills?

It totals 3%: 1.5% to the municipality, 0.5% to the school district and 1% to the state. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded. The sales agreement decides who pays.

Can I download the Penn Hills occupancy permit form online?

No. The form on the municipal website is only a sample and will not be accepted. Pick up the three-part carbonless form at the Code Enforcement office at 102 Duff Road, or call (412) 342-1192 about other arrangements.

Who does the dye test in Penn Hills?

A plumber of your choice does it. The municipality's contractor list is only a suggestion. The plumber completes the form after the house passes, and you submit it with the $25 fee. A house on septic also needs a septic report.

Is there still time to appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The 2027 window ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026 and has closed. Check the county's real estate portal for the next window.

What should I know before selling a house in Upper Merion, PA?

Upper Merion is a Montgomery County township of about 17 square miles with an estimated 36,674 residents, and the township does not require a use and occupancy permit when a single-family home changes hands. That one rule removes a step that sellers in several neighboring townships still face. What remains is the standard Pennsylvania sequence: disclosure form, agreement of sale, transfer tax, deed recording and tax proration.

The township sits about 16 miles from Philadelphia and takes in the villages of Gulph Mills, King of Prussia, Swedeland and Swedesburg, plus parts of Radnor and Wayne. A house in Swedesburg and a house near the King of Prussia mall draw different buyers, so the first job is matching your street to the right pool of buyers and the right sale route.

What makes the Upper Merion housing market different from nearby townships?

Upper Merion is an employment center as much as a bedroom suburb, which shapes who shops for a home here. The Schuylkill River forms its northern and eastern edge, Valley Forge National Historical Park fills most of the western end, and the King of Prussia retail and office district sits in the middle of the township. The township's 2024 financial report lists Lockheed Martin, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, US Liability Insurance, GlaxoSmithKline and CSL Behring among its largest employers, so many buyers want a short commute rather than a large yard.

Getting around is easy to sell. Buyers will look at these points on a listing:

  • The Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) crosses the middle of the township and meets the Schuylkill Expressway (I-76) at the western edge.
  • US 202 runs parallel to the turnpike and connects to the eastern end of US 422 near the western border.
  • PA 23 runs east to west, and PA 320 runs north to south from its terminus at PA 23.
  • SEPTA's M line stops at Gulph Mills and Hughes Park, and several SEPTA suburban bus routes serve the township.
  • The Rambler community shuttle circles residential areas, the mall, medical sites and the municipal building Monday through Saturday.

How do Upper Merion home values and ownership compare?

Owners here hold higher-priced homes than in the neighboring townships of Upper Moreland and Warminster, and renting is common. The table below uses the Census Bureau's QuickFacts for Upper Merion.

Does Upper Merion require a use and occupancy permit at sale?

No. The township's residential permit page says no Use and Occupancy Permit is required for a change of ownership of a single-family dwelling, as long as the use of the dwelling stays the same. Converting a house into a different use is a separate question for the township.

Permits still matter if you did work on the house. Buyers' inspectors and lenders ask about decks, finished basements, sheds, pools and replaced roofs, and the township's page lists the permit categories for each. Pull your own records before you list:

  • Permit review takes up to 15 business days, and inspections need 24 hours' notice, so finishing open work before listing takes weeks, not days.
  • Residential contractors must be registered with the State and list a Pennsylvania HIC number and a certificate of insurance on the application.
  • Accessory structures have setbacks by zoning district. In R-1 and R-1A a shed or pool sits 10 feet from the side and rear lines, while R-2 and R-3 require four feet from the side and five feet from the rear.

Call the township's safety and code enforcement office if you cannot tell which zoning district your lot is in.

Which school district serves Upper Merion homes?

Public school students in the township attend the Upper Merion Area School District, and its building layout is a talking point in every listing. Children start at one of five K-4 elementary schools: Bridgeport, Caley Road, Candlebrook, Gulph and Roberts. They move on to Upper Merion Area Middle School for grades 5 through 8 and Upper Merion Area High School for grades 9 through 12.

Mother Teresa Regional Catholic School is the parochial option in the township. Because the elementary school assignment depends on your street, confirm it with the district before you put a school name in your listing.

What do I pay and file when I sell in Upper Merion?

The state's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the value of the real estate, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Revenue. Bucks County's recorder describes the full transfer tax as 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, and says buyers and sellers usually split it. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds to confirm the rate that applies to your township and school district before you sign.

The seller's disclosure duty comes from 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. You complete the property disclosure statement and deliver a signed, dated copy to the buyer before the agreement of sale is signed. The form covers the roof, basement, plumbing, wiring, storm water facilities, hazardous substances and flood risk indicators. The Schuylkill runs along two edges of Upper Merion and annual precipitation runs near 48.5 inches, so answer the water questions with care. Act 74 of 2026 amended the land item and added a flood-insurance notice to the chapter.

If property taxes are behind, the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau holds upset sales each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, and buyers at those sales take the property subject to liens. Check with the Board of Assessment Appeals for the annual appeal deadline and forms listed on its page.

Which sale route fits an Upper Merion house best?

The right route depends on how much time and repair money you have. A listing can reach the large employee pool around King of Prussia but brings showings, inspection requests and a financing timeline. A private sale saves an agent's fee and adds legal and marketing work. A direct sale to an as-is buyer shortens the schedule and removes repair negotiations, usually at a lower price.

  • Ask every buyer for proof of funds and a written closing date.
  • Request a net sheet that shows transfer tax, payoff, tax proration and any repair credits.
  • Compare the net figure from each route, not the headline price.

More questions about Upper Merion, PA

Is a certificate needed to sell a house in Upper Merion Township?

No, not for a single-family home whose use stays the same. The township says no use and occupancy permit is required for the change of ownership. Ask the township office first for a multi-unit or non-residential property.

What does a home in Upper Merion cost compared with the rest of the county?

Owners in Upper Merion report a middle home value of $455,300 in the 2020 to 2024 survey. Your house will price off nearby sales, so ask an agent or appraiser for comparable sales on your street.

Who pays the transfer tax when an Upper Merion house sells?

The law does not assign it. Bucks County's recorder notes that most sale agreements split it between buyer and seller, and that the buyer is responsible if the amount paid is questioned. Put the split in writing in your agreement of sale.

Can I sell an Upper Merion house with unpermitted work?

Yes, but disclose what you know. Pennsylvania's disclosure form asks about additions, remodeling and structural changes, and a seller cannot make statements the seller knows are false. Many owners apply for a permit on the open work before listing.

How quickly can a cash sale close in Upper Merion?

A cash sale can close as fast as the title search, the deed and the transfer tax paperwork allow, because no lender is involved. The timeline is set in the agreement of sale, so ask the buyer for a written date and what must happen before it.

What should I know before selling a house in Cranberry Township?

Cranberry is a fast-growing township in southwestern Butler County, about half an hour north of downtown Pittsburgh, and its housing market looks more like a family suburb than a small town. It covers roughly 22.8 square miles with almost no water, and it borders Jackson, Forward and Adams townships, Seven Fields, Pine and Marshall townships in Allegheny County, and New Sewickley Township in Beaver County.

Because Cranberry is a township with no separate city government, nearly every step of a sale runs through three offices: the township for permits and tax certifications, Butler County for assessments, deeds and delinquent taxes, and the Seneca Valley School District for school taxes. Knowing who handles what saves a surprising amount of time at closing.

If you own a house here and want to sell it, you can list it, sell it yourself, or take an as-is offer from a buyer. Each path has the same tax and paperwork steps, so it helps to know them before you compare offers.

Why did Cranberry grow so quickly?

The township was farmland before World War II. It took its name from the wild cranberries that once grew along Brush Creek. Its boundaries were redrawn in 1854, shrinking it from 81 to 25 square miles, and growth only took off after the western section of the Pennsylvania Turnpike opened in 1951 with an exit on Route 19.

Interstate 79 followed in 1966, crossing the Turnpike at the township's southern end, and Interstate 279 opened in 1989, cutting the drive to Pittsburgh to under half an hour. A nonprofit industrial development corporation formed by the township supervisors in the mid-1960s filled an industrial park, and office and retail followed.

  • More than 1,000 businesses operate in the township
  • About 20,500 jobs are located here, and more people commute in than commute out
  • Westinghouse Electric Company has its headquarters in Cranberry
  • Fernway and Fox Run are named neighborhoods that still appear on maps

What do Census figures show about Cranberry homes?

The Census Bureau estimates 35,244 people lived in Cranberry on July 1, 2025, up from 28,098 in 2010. Three out of four households own their home, and the median home value is above $420,000, which puts Cranberry well above most of Butler County.

Cranberry Township housing and income, Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureCranberry Township
Census population, 201028,098
Census population, 202033,096
Owner-occupied housing rate, 2020-202475.3%

Median gross rent$1,708
Median household income$125,126

Some 65.3 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and the mean commute is 27.1 minutes. For sellers, that means buyers are usually working households with mortgages, who care about school district boundaries, move-in condition and inspection results.

What taxes come due when a Cranberry house sells?

The township's own tax page lists a real estate transfer tax of 0.5 percent that goes to Cranberry, noting that the figure leaves out the state and school district shares. The Commonwealth takes 1 percent on top. Ask the Butler County Recorder of Deeds for the school district portion and the total on your deed, since the recorder collects the tax when the deed is filed.

The state Department of Revenue says both buyer and seller are legally responsible for the realty transfer tax, and some transfers are exempt, such as certain transfers between family members and property passed by will or intestacy. Your sales contract decides who pays.

  • County and township property tax: bills mailed March 1
  • Seneca Valley School District tax: bills mailed August 1
  • Township rate for real estate, apart from county and school: 15.75 mills
  • Earned income tax: 1 percent, split between township and school district (this one follows the owner's income, not the sale)

Your closing agent will prorate the current-year taxes between you and the buyer, so having the tax bills handy at the start speeds things up.

How do tax certifications and tax sales work in Cranberry?

An elected tax collector with an office in the Municipal Center on Rochester Road collects township, county and school taxes. The same office issues the certification required when a property or mobile home is sold or refinanced, reviewing the last three years of township, county and school tax records and breaking them down for the closing. The office works with real estate agents and closing attorneys, and appointments are available.

County and township bills offer a 2 percent discount within two months of the notice date. Payments after four months carry a 10 percent penalty. Taxes still unpaid after one year go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau, and a sheriff's sale follows if the balance remains unpaid for an additional year.

The Tax Claim Bureau holds its upset sale on the second Monday of September for properties two years delinquent. If a sale does not happen at that stage, the parcel goes to a judicial sale, then to a repository list. A seller with unpaid taxes should settle them or ask the Bureau for a payoff figure early, because the amount can include added costs.

How does Butler County assess property and handle appeals?

Butler County's Assessment Department builds the tax bills for the county, municipalities and school districts. Cranberry's township page notes that assessments are still based on 1969 dollars, which is why Butler County bills use mills against a base that does not track current market value.

The county assessment page lists the forms an owner may need: a Board of Assessment appeal form, a commercial or industrial appeal form, a mobile home appeal form, a homestead and farmstead exclusion application, and a change of address form. The office also publishes appeal hearing information and millage sheets.

Call the Butler County Assessment office before you assume anything about deadlines. It can confirm the current filing date and whether a recent sale changes how your property is reviewed. Ask the Seneca Valley School District about its homestead application window, since school districts run that program locally.

Which township rules affect the sale of a Cranberry house?

Cranberry's Code Administration staff review and inspect building, zoning, sign and fire permits and enforce the Property Code. The township follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code with the 2018 International Codes, effective October 1, 2018. Inspections are booked through the township's online portal at any hour.

Before you list, look at the work done on the house. Decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences all need residential permits, and a buyer's inspector will notice an unpermitted deck or a finished basement with no paperwork. The township's code of ordinances holds the fee schedule for permits, inspections and rentals.

  • Sidewalks belong to the abutting owner, who must clear debris and handle snow and ice removal
  • Home-based businesses have their own township page and rules
  • Mobile home removal permits come from the tax collector's office

Rental homes have fees in the ordinance schedule, so owners selling a tenant-occupied house should ask the Code Administration office what applies.

What are the ways to sell a Cranberry house?

A listing makes sense for a house in good condition that can wait for showings and a lender's appraisal. An as-is purchase suits an owner who needs a closing date: an inherited house, a relocation, a house with deferred repairs or one with unpaid taxes. In either case, compare offers by your net proceeds after transfer tax, payoffs, prorated taxes and repair credits.

Ask any buyer who is paying cash for proof of funds, the closing date, and who covers title and recording costs. Get the offer in writing before you stop marketing the house.

More questions about Cranberry, PA

Which county handles deeds and assessments for Cranberry Township?

Butler County. Its Recorder of Deeds records the deed and collects transfer tax, and its Assessment Department sets the assessment and prints the tax bills.

Who issues the tax certification when a Cranberry house sells?

The township's elected tax collector, whose office is in the Municipal Center. It reviews three years of township, county and school tax records and returns a breakdown for closing.

Which school district taxes a Cranberry house?

The Seneca Valley School District. Its tax notices are mailed August 1, with a discount through September 30 and face value through November 30, and the year ends December 31.

What happens if I owe back taxes on a Cranberry property?

Unpaid taxes go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau after one year. A sheriff's sale can follow, and the Bureau's upset sale covers properties two years behind. Pay or request a payoff figure before you list.

Does a deck or shed without a permit affect a sale in Cranberry?

It can. Cranberry requires residential permits for decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences, and an inspector may flag unpermitted work. Ask the township's Code Administration staff how to close it out.

What are my options for a fast sale in Lower Makefield Township?

Lower Makefield Township sellers can list with an agent, sell privately, or take a cash offer, and a cash sale is the shortest path because the closing date follows your calendar instead of a buyer's mortgage approval. The township's own sale steps are light: a moving permit, a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, and clean tax and utility balances.

Bucks County homes in this part of the Delaware Valley carry high values, so even a modest delay costs real carrying money in taxes, insurance and utilities. People who want a quick sale here usually have a reason beyond price: an estate that needs to be settled, a relocation, a divorce, a rental that has become a burden, or deferred repairs on a house that no longer fits the owner's plans.

  • Cash purchase: the buyer takes the house in its present condition and you set the closing date.
  • Agent listing: more exposure and often a higher price, with showings, repairs and a longer timeline.
  • For-sale-by-owner: you keep the commission money but handle marketing, contracts and negotiation yourself.

What should I know about Lower Makefield Township before I sell?

The township covers about 18.3 square miles in Bucks County along the Delaware River, facing New Jersey across the water. It wraps around the borough of Yardley on the north, south and west, which is why most addresses carry a Yardley mailing label even though they are in Lower Makefield. Across the river are Hopewell Township, Ewing Township and Trenton, and on the Pennsylvania side the neighbors are Upper Makefield, Newtown, Middletown and Falls townships plus Morrisville.

Brock Creek, Common Creek, Core Creek and Jericho Creek run through it, and Edge Hill is a named local landform. Past and present villages include Schammels Corner and Woodside. The population rose from 25,083 in 1990 to 32,681 in 2000, and later office growth centered on the Stony Hill Road corridor near Interstate 295. Children attend the Pennsbury School District.

Interstate 295 is the main highway and crosses the Delaware on the Scudder Falls Bridge into New Jersey. PA Route 32 follows River Road along the water, PA Route 332 follows Newtown-Yardley Road through the middle, and US Route 1 clips the southern corner. As of 2018, 175.27 miles of public road ran through the township, and 138.20 miles of that were township maintained. SEPTA bus route 127 reaches the southern tip. The West Trenton regional rail line passes through the township without a station inside it, so commuters use Yardley station or Woodbourne station in Middletown Township. The area sits in hardiness zone 7a, so a buyer's inspector will look at roofs, gutters and basements with winter freezes in mind.

What do Census figures say about homes in Lower Makefield Township?

The Census Bureau estimated 34,028 residents on July 1, 2025. Of occupied housing, 87.6 percent is owner occupied, and the median value of an owner-occupied home was $630,200 over 2020 to 2024. Median gross rent was $2,340 and the median household income was $175,206 in 2024 dollars. A bachelor's degree or higher is held by 69.4 percent of adults, and 91.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier.

That profile means most sales are single-family homes where the owner lives, and values are well above most of Pennsylvania. Prices at this level make every percentage point of transfer tax and every month of carrying cost visible, so it pays to compare closing timelines as carefully as the offer price.

What taxes does a Lower Makefield property carry?

Real estate tax comes from three bills: township, county and the Pennsbury School District. The township tax collector page lists the 2025 combined rate at 256.403 mills, and the township levies no earned income tax.

One mill is one tenth of one percent of assessed value. Township and county bills are issued around March 1 for the calendar year, with a 2 percent discount for payment within two months, face amount within four months and a 10 percent penalty afterward. School bills are issued around July 1 for the school year. Unpaid taxes pass to the Bucks County Tax Claim Bureau after the collector's books close. When you sell, prorate these bills at settlement and ask the tax office at 267-274-1116 for current figures.

What does the township require when I sell?

The township's community development office lists three items for a sale, and it states that a resale use and occupancy certificate is not required in Lower Makefield Township. Confirm the current list with the office at 267-274-1100 before you schedule your closing, since a buyer's contract can add its own conditions.

  • A moving permit for both the buyer and the seller.
  • A sewer lateral inspection by the seller, to catch problems with the private line. Questions and submissions go to sewerlateral@lmt.org.
  • Calls to the taxing authorities and utility companies for any additional requirements they impose.

Allow time for a plumber to scope the line and for the township to review the report, since a failed line has to be fixed.

How does a property tax appeal work for Lower Makefield owners?

Bucks County sets annual appeals by a deadline in early August, and the 2026 deadline of August 3 has passed. Any change from a 2026 annual appeal takes effect in the 2027 tax year. Interim appeals follow the date printed on a recent assessment revision notice. The Board of Assessment Appeals meets on the first and third Tuesday of each month at the courthouse in Doylestown, and it can be reached at 215-348-6219.

Owner-occupants can also apply for the homestead and farmstead exclusion, which reduces the assessed value used for school tax. The county lists March 1 as the application deadline for the tax year that begins the following July 1. If you buy or sell an investment property, a Pennsylvania law added in 2026 asks owners to submit contact information to the Board within 30 days of a purchase, with owner-occupied homes excused.

What costs come with selling at closing?

The state transfer tax is 1 percent of the sale value, and the Lower Makefield Township page lists the local share as one half of one percent to the township and one half of one percent to the school district. On a $630,200 house, matching the township's median owner-occupied value, the combined 2 percent equals $12,604, split between buyer and seller by contract. Pennsylvania treats both parties as jointly responsible, so agree on who pays before signing.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain moves among family members and property passed by will or intestacy. Ask a title company to price the statement of value and recording fees at the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, and check whether your sale involves a payoff, a lien or tenants.

More questions about Lower Makefield, PA

Does Lower Makefield Township require a resale certificate?

The township's community development FAQ says a resale use and occupancy certificate is not required. It does require a moving permit for buyer and seller and a sewer lateral inspection by the seller, so call the township office to confirm.

What is the transfer tax in Lower Makefield?

The state charges 1 percent, and the township page lists a local rate of one half percent for the township plus one half percent for the school district. That totals 2 percent of the sale price, divided by contract.

Who is responsible for the sewer lateral inspection?

The seller. The township expects the seller to inspect the private sewer line and submit the result, and its review can take time, so schedule the plumber early in your sale.

When can I appeal my Bucks County assessment?

Annual appeals are due in early August, and the 2026 deadline was August 3, so the next chance is the 2027 cycle. Interim appeals follow the date on an assessment revision notice.

Which school district serves Lower Makefield Township?

Pennsbury School District serves the township, and its 2025-2026 millage of 204.003 is the largest part of the combined 256.403 mills on a Lower Makefield tax bill.

What shapes a house sale in the city of Chester?

Chester is a dense river city in Delaware County, and what drives a sale there is local: an old housing stock, a city under state financial oversight, and a transfer tax that is higher than the county norm. The city covers about 6.0 square miles, of which 4.83 is land, and it lies along the Delaware River's western shore, between Philadelphia and Wilmington.

William Penn landed here in 1682, which makes Chester the oldest city in Pennsylvania. Chester Creek meets the Delaware inside the city limits, and the Port of Chester runs along the waterfront. Streets run on a simple grid: numbered streets go east and west, named streets go north and south, and the main spine is the Avenue of the States, which becomes Edgmont Avenue north of 9th Street.

An owner here has three routes: hire an agent, negotiate privately with a buyer, or take an as-is cash purchase. The right one turns on the roof, plumbing and wiring, any unpaid taxes, and your deadline.

How did Chester's industrial past shape its housing?

Chester grew around shipyards, rolling mills and textile mills along Chester Creek. During the two world wars, factory and dock jobs pulled in workers from southern and eastern Europe and from the American South, and the city's population went from 38,537 in 1910 to 58,030 in 1920. The Census count peaked at 66,039 in 1950.

Since then the city has lost people in nearly every decade, ending at 32,605 in 2020. Much of the housing was built for that larger workforce: rowhouses and twins on narrow lots, many a century old. Buyers and inspectors in Chester tend to look closely at foundations, old heating systems, lead paint and aging sewer laterals.

The waterfront has changed too. The Philadelphia Union plays at Subaru Park beside the Commodore Barry Bridge, Harrah's Philadelphia opened in 2008, and Widener University anchors the west side of the city.

  • 2020 Census count: 32,605

  • Water access that built the economy: the Delaware River and Chester Creek

How do Chester home values and rents compare?
