How does the city's financial recovery status affect a seller?

The effect lands on the tax side more than on the sale. Pennsylvania designated Chester a financially distressed municipality in 1995, declared a fiscal emergency in 2020, and in 2022 the city filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy. The city's website lists meetings of the Municipal Financial Recovery Advisory Committee and identifies a receiver for the city, so the recovery process is still an active part of local government.

The practical points are narrow. Property tax rates and city fees can change as the recovery plan is revised, so an old tax bill is a weak guide to what the next owner will carry. Ask the City of Chester finance office for the current city millage, and ask the Delaware County treasurer for the county and school figures, when you work out your net.

None of this stops a sale. What a title company will want is a clean tax picture, so unpaid city bills, rubbish fees and liens should be sorted out before settlement.

What is the transfer tax on a Chester sale?

Chester is one of four Delaware County municipalities that charge more than the standard local rate: 1.5 percent for the city side, effective September 1, 2023, on top of the 1 percent that goes to the Commonwealth. That is 2.5 percent of the sale price in total, compared with 2 percent in most of the county.

The Delaware County Recorder of Deeds lists only four exceptions to its standard 1 percent local rate: Chester, Radnor, Upper Darby and Upper Providence. On a $90,000 sale, the difference between a 2 percent and a 2.5 percent total is $450.

Under the Commonwealth's rules the grantor and the grantee share legal liability, so the agreement of sale should name who pays. Certain family transfers and inherited property are exempt. For a doubtful case, the county sends questions to the revenue department's realty transfer tax unit at RA-BITRealtyTransferTax@pa.gov.

What city paperwork and rules apply to a Chester house?

The city's Licenses and Inspections department handles permits, rental registration and several exemption forms. Its page lists the forms a seller or landlord is most likely to touch.

  • Building permit application and the residential permit fee schedule
  • Rental registration application, FAQ, letter and a residential rental licensing policy summary
  • Use and occupancy fee schedule and a commercial use and occupancy permit form
  • Contractor license application
  • Homeowner exemption form and a senior citizen disability exemption form for residential property

If the house is rented, find out whether the unit is registered before you list it, because a buyer's lender or title agent may ask. If you did work on the house without a permit, contact L&I at City Hall before you market the property. Open permits are easier to close out while you still control the building.

The city assessor's page also posts the conditions and bid forms for repository properties, which are parcels that did not sell at county tax sales, along with a LERTA application for tax abatement on improvements. Those are useful if your house has sat vacant or you are buying next door.

How do Chester property tax bills and appeals work?

Chester property is assessed by Delaware County. The county's tax bill is mailed on February 1, and paying within 60 days earns a 2 percent discount; after April 1 the bill is due at face value by June 1. Chester Upland School District covers the city, Chester Township and Upland borough, and the city's website carries a link to pay property tax.

The county's Homestead and Farmstead Exclusion lowers the assessed value on a primary residence. The application comes from your school district, and the window runs every year from December 15 to March 1. If you are about to sell, the exclusion matters less to you than to the buyer, who will need to apply in their own name.

An assessment challenge is filed at the Board in Media, on paper with an original signature. Faxed or e-mailed forms are rejected, and because postmarks can lag, the county suggests hand delivery or a counter receipt at the post office. If you disagree with the Board's findings, you have 30 days to go to court. Look at the notice you were mailed for the filing date.

Does Chester's riverfront location affect the condition of a house?

It can. Chester is low and sits where Chester Creek and Ridley Creek reach the Delaware River, so flood exposure varies a lot by block. The climate is humid subtropical, averaging about 43.7 inches of precipitation a year, with July highs near 87 degrees. Damp basements, sump pumps and old drainage are routine inspection topics.

Before you list, find out whether your address is in a mapped flood zone and whether the house carries flood insurance. A buyer's lender will check the same thing.

Interstate 95 has three exits serving Highland Avenue, Kerlin Street and Edgmont Avenue, and U.S. 13 and U.S. 322 also pass through, with the Commodore Barry Bridge linking to New Jersey.

Which sale route fits a Chester owner in a hurry?

Putting the house on the market gives the widest exposure but needs showings, repairs and a lender's approval, which can stretch the timeline by months. An investor or cash purchase gives up some price for speed and certainty, and the buyer generally accepts the property with its flaws.

  • Inherited house with several heirs: confirm who holds title and whether the estate is open before accepting any offer
  • Tenant in place: read the lease and plan for notice requirements
  • Back taxes or city liens: get payoff figures from the county and the city
  • Code or permit issues: ask L&I what is open on the address

Whatever you pick, line up the offers by the check you would actually receive after transfer tax, payoffs and credits.

How much is the transfer tax if I sell a house in Chester?

The combined rate is 2.5 percent: 1 percent to the state and 1.5 percent to the local side, which has applied in Chester since September 1, 2023. The contract decides who pays, though the state holds both parties responsible.

Can I sell a Chester house that has a tenant living in it?

Yes. The lease usually continues with the new owner unless it ends or the tenant agrees to leave. Check whether the unit is registered with the city's L&I department before you list.

Who do I ask about property taxes on a Chester house?

Start with the Delaware County treasurer and Board of Assessment in Media for county and school figures, and the City of Chester finance office for city charges. Both can confirm balances before closing.

Does Chester's bankruptcy stop me from selling?

No. Houses sell in Chester under the same Pennsylvania rules as elsewhere. The recovery process mainly affects city tax rates and fees, so confirm current figures before you price the house.

How do I claim the homestead exclusion on a Chester home?

Request the application from the Chester Upland School District between December 15 and March 1, then send it to the county Board of Assessment in Media. The county replies within 30 days.

Little Lehigh Creek and Swabia Creek drain through it, South Mountain crosses the southern edge just below the boroughs of Macungie and Alburtis, and Alburtis sits entirely inside the township boundary. Which inspection is required before a Lower Macungie house sells?

The township requires a building sewer inspection before a property is sold or transferred. The inspection looks at the private sewer line that runs from the house to the township's sewer lateral, a pipe the owner, not the township, is responsible for.

  • A licensed Journeyman or Master Plumber must perform the video inspection and submit a complete Building Sewer Inspection Report, a copy of the video and proof of licensure to the township.
  • Electronic video files are not accepted. The township keeps a physical copy, preferably on a USB flash drive, in the property file for at least five years.

What bills and taxes come up at a Lower Macungie closing?

  • Local transfer tax: the township ordinance sets its share at one half of one percent, and the township and any other taxing body together may not exceed 1 percent. Ask your title company for the school district's share and who pays what under your contract.

Water is billed separately by Lehigh County Authority, so a final water reading is a separate call. Transfers between certain family members, and property passed by will or intestacy, are among the exempt categories on the state's list, which matters for inherited houses.

How do property taxes and assessment appeals work in Lower Macungie?

Lehigh County assesses at 100 percent of fair market value as of a 2013 base year, the date of its last countywide reassessment, so your assessed value is a figure from that year adjusted for new construction or demolition. The Board of Assessment Appeals accepts only an original signed appeal with the filing fee received on or before August 1 each year. Postmarks and faxed appeals do not count as timely. Interim appeals are due by the date printed on a Change of Assessment Notice.

If you are selling a rental or other property you do not live in, note that a 2026 Pennsylvania law requires non-owner-occupant owners to file contact information with the county within 30 days of buying. Owner-occupied principal residences are exempt, so the rule matters mostly to the investor who buys from you.

What if my Lower Macungie house needs repairs or has tenants?

You can still sell it, and the sewer line is the first item to sort out. Order the video inspection early, because a failed line means repair work before closing and the township mails the pass or fail letter, which takes time. If a buyer will take the house as-is, ask whether that includes sewer repairs and who pays, and put the answer in the contract.

For tenants, review the lease end date and security deposit handling with your attorney, and ask the township office about any rental rules that apply to the address. Keep copies of the sewer inspection letter, the utility certification and the deed, since the buyer's title company will ask for them.

The contract decides, but the law makes buyer and seller jointly liable. The state rate is 1 percent and the township's local rate is one half of one percent, with the county Recorder of Deeds collecting at recording.

How much is the sewer and trash certification in Lower Macungie?

The township charges $50 for a sewer and trash certification used for a sale or refinance. Email the utility billing office and mail the check, which must arrive before processing begins.

Lehigh County takes annual appeals on or before August 1 of each year. The original signed form and filing fee must be received by then, because postmarks and faxes are not accepted.

East Penn School District serves it. High school students go to Emmaus High School, and the township has Eyer Middle School, Lower Macungie Middle School, Wescosville Elementary and Willow Lane Elementary nearby.

Applications go in online, and the department answers questions at 215-443-5423. After that, the sale follows Pennsylvania's normal disclosure, recording and tax steps.

The township has been on the map since 1711, when its borders were set, and it started as farmland under early English and Scotch-Irish settlers. Almost all of its housing came later. As recently as 1955 it had no residential subdivisions and one housing complex, and then the population jumped from 7,127 in 1950 to 34,900 in 1970. Most houses you will see on a listing sheet come from that postwar build-out.

Why did Warminster grow so fast, and what does that mean for sellers?

The Navy's presence at the Johnsville site drove the township's mid-century growth, and that shapes today's housing stock. The U.S. Navy took over an industrial site from Brewster Aeronautical Corporation in 1943, and the Naval Air Warfare Center there operated until 1996. The same site later trained astronauts for the Mercury, Gemini and Apollo programs. Today the township's larger employers include ABB, Burpee Seeds, CRC Industries, Havis and a Penn State research laboratory.

One local issue deserves a straight answer in any sale. Several of the township's groundwater wells have been contaminated with PFOS and PFOA from the former Navy site, the Navy paid for treatment systems, and the Warminster Municipal Authority now buys more water from the North Wales Water Authority. The authority supplies water and sewer to about 10,300 customers. If your house is on public water, buyers may ask about it, so keep a recent water bill and the authority's contact details ready.

You apply through the township's online portal, and the Licenses and Inspections Department handles the review. For commuters, SEPTA's Warminster station is the terminus of the Warminster Line into Center City Philadelphia, and City Bus Route 22 runs south from the township through Willow Grove to North Philadelphia. What do I owe at closing and how do Bucks County rules apply?

Bucks County's recorder says the realty transfer tax is 2 percent, with 1 percent to the state and 1 percent to the municipality and school district, paid when the deed is recorded. It is a tax on the value conveyed, which is not always the sale price, and the sale agreement usually divides it between buyer and seller. Since January 2026 the recorder no longer takes personal checks for the tax: cash in the office, cashier's check, money order or credit card only.

Family transfers can be exempt, but you must still present the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) where the exemption is not stated in the deed. Your attorney or title agent handles that paperwork. The seller must also deliver the property disclosure statement under 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303 before the agreement is signed, and Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information.

On the assessment side, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, which has passed, and annual appeal changes take effect the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year starting July 1. Buyers must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of purchase under Act 29, so tell your buyer.

Should I list or sell as-is in Warminster?

Listing suits a house in good condition on a street with recent sales, and an as-is cash sale suits a house that needs work or a seller on a short clock. Cash buyers usually offer less than a repaired, listed house would bring, in exchange for speed and fewer contingencies. Ask any buyer who takes the house as-is how the township permit will be handled.

  • Ask for a written offer with a closing date and proof of funds.
  • Find out whether the buyer will accept a house that has not yet received the township permit and who handles it.
  • Compare the offer against a net sheet for a listing sale, including permit costs and repairs.

More questions about Warminster, PA

Does Warminster require a permit to sell a house?

Yes. The Licenses and Inspections Department says selling a property needs a permit, and applications are made online. Call 215-443-5423 before applying to confirm the permit type and fee.

What is a typical home value in Warminster?

Warminster owners report a midpoint home value of $418,600 for 2020 to 2024. Your price depends on condition and nearby sales, so the median is only a reference point.

Should I mention the PFOS and PFOA wells to Warminster buyers?

Be ready to discuss it. The Warminster Municipal Authority has closed wells with PFOS and PFOA contamination from the former Navy site, installed treatment systems paid for by the Navy, and buys more water from a neighboring authority. Direct buyers to the authority for current water quality reports.

Where do I record the deed for a Warminster house?

At the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds, usually through your title company or attorney. The recorder collects the 2 percent transfer tax at recording and no longer accepts personal checks for it.

Can I sell a Warminster house that I inherited?

Yes, once the person with authority over the estate signs. Pennsylvania's disclosure chapter exempts transfers by an estate fiduciary, though many sellers still give buyers a condition statement. Ask the estate's attorney who may sign.

What should I know before selling a house in Radnor Township?

Radnor is a Main Line township in Delaware County with high home values, a mandatory township certificate for every resale, and a transfer tax that runs above the county default. A seller who plans around those three items can move quickly, whether the house goes on the market, sells to a neighbor, or goes to a cash buyer.

The township covers about 13.8 square miles and includes Wayne, St. Davids, Rosemont, Ithan, Garrett Hill and Villanova. It is home rule, run by a Board of Commissioners, and it was laid out in 1682 as part of the Welsh Tract. Lancaster Avenue follows the route of the 1794 Philadelphia and Lancaster Turnpike, and the Paoli/Thorndale rail line gave the area its commuter character in the nineteenth century.

Selling fast here mostly comes down to paperwork timing. Buyers, lenders and the township each have steps that can add days, and the sections below set them out in the order you will meet them.

What does the Census say about Radnor homes and owners?

Radnor is an expensive, owner-heavy market, and the figures below explain why pricing and buyer financing look different here than in much of Delaware County.

Do I need a certificate of occupancy to sell in Radnor?

Yes. The township's FAQ confirms that use and occupancy permits are required for resales, and the Engineering Department issues them. No new owner may occupy the property until the certificate is out.

The Engineering Department's transfer page sets the sequence:

  • The seller files the application at least 10 business days before settlement. The owner signs it, and the fee is $150.
  • Filing 10 days or less before settlement triggers a $300 expedite fee.
  • The township inspects for house number display and public sidewalk condition, then sends a violation notice for anything that needs repair.
  • If sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before closing, money goes into escrow with the department, and a sidewalk permit is needed for the work.
  • Sellers and buyers both sign a smoke detector and carbon monoxide certification, and the application is not accepted unless the form, the fee and the signed application arrive together.
  • The owner books an inside look at the sanitary sewer soil pipe to confirm there are no illegal connections, and sump pumps must be disconnected from the sanitary system under Chapter 235 of the township code.

Call the Engineering Department at 610-688-5600, extension 129, to book the sewer appointment. Do it the day you file, because that appointment is the step most likely to push a closing date.

How much is the transfer tax when I sell in Radnor?

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds lists the state share at 1% and the local share at 1%, with Radnor Township named as an exception at 1.5%. On a sale at the median value above, each additional half percent of local tax is about $4,200, so confirm the exact split with the Recorder before you set a net-proceeds number.

The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue explains that the county Recorder collects the state's 1% along with any local tax. Both the seller (grantor) and the buyer (grantee) are jointly liable, which is why a sales agreement states who pays. Certain transfers between family members, and property passed by will or intestate succession, are exempt under state rules, so an inherited house moving to an heir is treated differently from a market sale.

The county's recording office is at the Government Center in Media, and its transfer tax page lists the state's Statement of Value form (REV-183) for deeds that do not state full consideration. If a deed leaves the price off, that form is what carries the value to the Recorder.

When are Radnor property taxes due, and how do appeals work?

Township bills go out on or before February 1, and the face amount is due May 31. According to the township's FAQ, paying by March 31 earns a 2% discount, and a 10% penalty applies after May 31. The Radnor School District bills and collects its own tax separately, with school bills mailed in July.

An unpaid bill becomes a lien if it is not paid by the end of the calendar year, and the Delaware County Tax Claim Bureau adds interest and penalties. When a house sells, the township asks that you return the bill with the new owner's name, because the Recorder can take more than 60 days to process a title transfer.

  • Assessment appeals go to the Delaware County Board of Assessment Appeals before August 1 for a value effective the following January 1.
  • An appeal does not pause the bill. You pay what is billed and receive a refund or credit if the value drops.
  • The county reassessment that ran from December 2017 to 2020 took effect in January 2021, so current values reflect that base year.
  • A tax certification from the township finance office costs $25 per parcel, and title companies typically request one.

Sewer and stormwater are billed together on a separate mailing around April 1, due May 31. The stormwater charge depends on parcel size, and it applies to all developed properties in the township.

Which neighborhoods and schools affect a Radnor sale?

Schools drive demand more than any other local factor. Public students attend the Radnor Township School District, which runs Radnor High School, Radnor Middle School, and Radnor, Ithan and Wayne elementary schools. Private options inside the township include Archbishop John Carroll High School, the Agnes Irwin School, the Hill Top Preparatory School and the Valley Forge Military Academy and College.

Buyer groups differ by area. Downtown Wayne has historic districts, with North Wayne and South Wayne as residential pockets around a commercial core. St. Davids and Ithan are quieter residential neighborhoods, while Villanova and Garrett Hill have long-standing Catholic parish communities. Strafford, Bryn Mawr and Villanova straddle township lines, so a listing's mailing address may not match its municipality, and that matters for transfer tax and the certificate.

Commuting helps resale. The township has SEPTA Regional Rail stops at Wayne, St. Davids, Radnor and Villanova, plus seven Norristown High Speed Line stations. U.S. 30 runs along Lancaster Avenue, Route 320 follows Sproul and Spring Mill Roads, and Interstate 476 meets U.S. 30 inside the township.

Which selling route fits a Radnor house?

Three paths cover most sellers, and each handles the township certificate differently.

  • A traditional listing suits houses in good repair. The agent coordinates the certificate, but showings, inspection requests and buyer financing set the schedule.
  • A for-sale-by-owner sale saves the commission and leaves you running the certificate, the sewer inspection and the transfer tax paperwork yourself.
  • A cash sale to a company that buys as-is removes lender timing and repairs from the buyer side. The seller still files the township application and still schedules the sewer check, so ask any buyer who does the filing and who pays any sidewalk escrow.

Compare offers on net proceeds, not headline price. Subtract the transfer tax, the $150 or $300 township fee, any sidewalk or sewer repairs, and unpaid taxes before you decide.

More questions about Radnor, PA

Who applies for the certificate of occupancy in Radnor?

The seller does. The application goes to the Radnor Engineering Department at least 10 business days before settlement, signed by the owner, with the $150 fee and the smoke detector and carbon monoxide form signed by seller and buyer.

What happens if my sidewalk is damaged at the time of sale?

The township sends a violation notice after its inspection. If the sidewalk blocks cannot be replaced before settlement, money is placed in escrow with the Engineering Department, and a sidewalk permit is required for the repair.

Is Radnor's transfer tax higher than the rest of Delaware County?

Yes. The county's Recorder of Deeds shows most municipalities at the 1% default local share and lists Radnor Township at 1.5%, plus the 1% state tax. Ask the Recorder to confirm the combined figure for your deed.

Can I sell a Radnor house that needs repairs?

Yes, but the sewer connection, sidewalk and house number items flagged by the township still have to be corrected or escrowed before the certificate is released. Cosmetic and structural repairs are a matter between you and the buyer.

Where do I get a Radnor tax certification for closing?

From the Radnor Township finance office at 301 Iven Avenue in Wayne. The township charges $25 per certification, and you need the parcel (folio) number, the owner name and the address.

What should a seller know about Ross Township, PA?

Ross Township is a large suburb on the northern edge of Pittsburgh in Allegheny County, with a retail-heavy McKnight Road corridor, an older population and a transfer tax that is split between the township and the North Hills School District. A sale here is handled through the Allegheny County Division of Real Estate and the township's Building office.

The township was incorporated on June 26, 1809 and was named for James Ross, a Pittsburgh attorney and U.S. Senator. It covers 14.47 square miles, surrounds West View Borough, and shares eleven borders with municipalities including McCandless, Hampton, Shaler, Franklin Park and the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of Perry North and Brighton Heights. Northway Mall opened in 1962 as the first enclosed mall in Pennsylvania, and the Big Mac was created in 1967 at a McDonald's on McKnight Road.

The notes below cover what buyers see, what the township and county require, and how a fast sale compares with a listing.

What do Census figures show about Ross homes and owners?

Ross has a mature, mostly owner-occupied housing market, with a high share of older residents and a population estimate that has slipped since 2020.

Do I need an occupancy certificate to sell a house in Ross Township?

Ask the Building office before you list. The township's Building page says that department handles permit applications, plan review, inspections and Certificates of Occupancy under the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, but it does not describe a separate resale inspection.

Call the Building Inspections office at 412-931-7048, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. at 1000 Ross Municipal Drive, and ask whether your address needs anything for a transfer. If you did work on the house without a permit, resolve it before a buyer's inspector finds it.

  • Permits are applied for online through iWorq.
  • Inspections need 48 hours' notice, and requests must include the permit number, address, inspection type, preferred date and an on-site contact.
  • Plumbing permits and inspections run through the Allegheny County Health Department, and electrical inspections go through the township's third-party agency.
  • For flood questions, the township says it cannot certify flood zones. Properties in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area face added requirements, so check the FEMA map for your parcel.

Projects submitted after January 1, 2026 follow the 2021 International codes as amended by the state, so a buyer's renovation plans will be reviewed under the newer codes.

How much transfer tax do sellers in Ross pay?

Allegheny County says its realty transfer tax runs from 2% to 5% of the price, with 1% going to the state and the rest split between the municipality and the school district. For Ross, ask the Division of Real Estate for the exact municipal and North Hills School District rates, which the county posts on its local rate page.

The county provides two examples. In Shaler Township, a $40,000 house carries 1% state, 0.5% township and 0.5% school tax for a 2% total of $800. In the City of Pittsburgh, the same house carries a total of 5%, which is $2,000. Use those as a guide to the arithmetic only, because Ross has its own rates.

  • The county collects state and local transfer tax when the deed is recorded, paid on a separate check from the recording fees.
  • A Statement of Value (REV-183) is required when the deed does not list the consideration or when an exemption applies.
  • Certain transfers between family members may be exempt, and the deed should say so, for example by stating that the transfer is familial and exempt from realty transfer tax.
  • The Department of Revenue can answer exemption questions at 717-783-8104.

At the Census median value of $268,900, each 1% of tax is about $2,690, so a 2% total would be near $5,400 and a 3% total near $8,100.

How do assessments and appeals work for Ross homeowners?

Allegheny County assesses Ross properties, and the first level of appeal is the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Owners and any taxing body with an interest in the parcel can file. Hearings are held by telephone, and a lawyer is optional, although most school districts and municipalities bring counsel.

If the BPAAR result is unsatisfactory, either side can take the appeal to the second level, the Board of Viewers at the Court of Common Pleas. Only the filing party can withdraw an appeal, using the county's withdrawal form. The county also allows year-round special appeals when the Office of Property Assessments issues a written determination in certain circumstances.

The school district and the township can appeal an assessment too. If you receive a hearing notice for an appeal filed by the school district or the municipality on your home, you may attend but you are not required to. A buyer who learns of a pending taxing-body appeal will ask about it, so mention it during negotiations.

Which neighborhoods, schools and roads matter in Ross?

Ross and West View together form the North Hills School District, which also uses Northland Public Library, shared among several municipalities. North Hills High School is the district's high school, and the school district is a recurring point in listings.

The township's named areas include Perrysville, McKnight, Evergreen Hamlet, Berkeley Hills, Highcliff, Laurel Gardens, North Hills Estates, Kinvara, Greybrooke, Holly Hill, White Oak Heights, Glenshaw, Keown Station and Northway. Commercial districts cluster along McKnight Road, U.S. Route 19 (Perry Highway) and Babcock Boulevard.

The township's population rose from about 15,700 in 1950 to about 35,100 in 1980, so homes in Evergreen Hamlet, Perrysville and the newer plans differ widely in age. Describe your street, lot and era in your listing or offer request, because buyers search by those features.

Should I list or take a cash offer in Ross?

List when the house shows well and you can wait for lender timelines. Take a cash offer when the house needs work, an estate is involved or the date matters more than the last few thousand dollars.

  • Compare offers by net proceeds after transfer tax, any commission, repairs and unpaid taxes.
  • Ask each buyer in writing who pays transfer tax and what happens if an inspection finds a defect.
  • Confirm the closing date and whether the buyer can close without a mortgage contingency.

More questions about Ross, PA

Who issues Certificates of Occupancy in Ross Township?

The township Building department. It handles permits, plan review, inspections and Certificates of Occupancy under the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code, and its inspections line is 412-931-7048.

What is the transfer tax range in Allegheny County?

Allegheny County reports a range of 2% to 5% of the price, with 1% to the state and the remainder to the municipality and school district. Ask the county for the specific Ross and North Hills School District rates.

Can I appeal my Ross assessment before selling?

Yes. The owner or any taxing body can file with the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. A lawyer is not required, and the county lists the appeal forms and a withdrawal form on its Appeals page.

Is a house in a FEMA flood zone harder to sell in Ross?

It can be, because properties in a Special Flood Hazard Area face added requirements. The township cannot certify flood zones, so check the FEMA map for your parcel and tell buyers early.

Which school district serves Ross Township?

The North Hills School District, which also serves West View Borough. North Hills High School is the district's high school.

What kind of community is Bethel Park?

Bethel Park is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, about 7 miles south of Pittsburgh, with an estimated 32,074 residents on July 1, 2025. That is 4.5 percent below the 2020 estimates base, and the borough also has an older population, with 25.5 percent of residents 65 or over.

It began as Bethel Township in 1886, named for Bethel Presbyterian Church, and became a borough on March 17, 1949. The interurban trolley lines of the early 1900s made it an early streetcar suburb, and population doubled from 11,324 in 1950 to 23,650 in 1960. Nine wards each elect one member of the municipal council, and the mayor is elected at large. The municipal building is at 5100 West Library Avenue.

The borough covers 11.70 square miles, all land, and it touches seven neighbors: Castle Shannon, Whitehall, Baldwin, South Park, Upper St. Clair, Mt. Lebanon and Peters Township in Washington County. The primary ZIP code is 15102, while 15234, 15236 and 15241 serve border communities, so confirm the municipality on the parcel record.

Why does coal mining history matter when selling a Bethel Park house?

Bethel Park sits on the Pittsburgh coal seam, and the borough's geology summary, which cites the state environmental agency, says all of Bethel Park was undermined. The Pittsburgh Terminal No. 8 Mine, known as the H Mine and the Coverdale Mine, opened around 1920 and is closed.

Raise mine subsidence early in a sale. Ask your homeowner's insurer whether the policy covers mine subsidence, and ask the buyer's title company what it will search. Land in the borough ranges from 980 feet at the creek junction in the southeast corner to 1,370 feet at Rocky Ridge in the southwest.

What must a Bethel Park seller complete before the deed transfers?

A seller in Bethel Park must complete a dye test and a camera lateral inspection before any deed is transferred. The Camera Lateral Inspections Ordinance took effect on January 1, 2025, and the municipality's dye test page sets the rules.

  • The dye test and camera inspection must be finished 21 days before closing or deed transfer.
  • The municipality charges a $50 processing fee.
  • The camera lateral inspection must come from a contractor certified by the National Association of Sewer Service Companies, and the plumber must be registered through the health department.
  • An Allegheny County licensed plumber performs the dye test, and a municipal building code official signs off if a defect is corrected.
  • A test already performed and certified within the last two years can satisfy the rule.
  • A deed cannot be transferred until needed repairs are made and pass inspection.

Paperwork has a 48-hour turnaround, and the form request goes through the municipal office at 412-831-6800, extension 205. The page also states that an occupancy inspection is not required for a sale. Owners who deeded a property without the test receive an official letter, and non-compliance leads to a citation.

What do Census figures show about Bethel Park housing?

Bethel Park is a market of owners. For 2020 to 2024, 76.4 percent of homes were owner-occupied, the median household income was $107,090, and 53.5 percent of adults 25 and over held a bachelor's degree or higher.

What permits and fees apply to a Bethel Park home?

The municipality's development fee schedule, effective September 9, 2025, lists a Certificate of Occupancy at $50, a written Certificate of Zoning at $50, and a Short-Term Rental Permit at $50 initially and $25 for each annual renewal. Building permits for work under $1,000 cost $50.

Permits go to the Community Development Department on the second floor of the municipal building, or by email to the permits address on the municipality's site. Residential questions go to extension 131 at 412-831-6800. Pennsylvania adopted the 2021 I-Codes under the Uniform Construction Code effective January 1, 2026, so permits for repairs before a sale follow the newer code. Code enforcement also treats grass over 8 inches as a violation, so mow before photos and showings.

How do Allegheny County assessments and appeals work for Bethel Park owners?

Allegheny County's Office of Property Assessments sets values for Bethel Park, and appeals go first to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. A party who disagrees with that result can appeal to the Board of Viewers at the Court of Common Pleas.

  • Hearings take place by telephone.
  • Legal representation is optional, and an authorized representative may appear for the owner.
  • A taxing body, such as a school district or municipality, can also file an appeal on a property.
  • Special Appeals can be filed year-round in response to a written determination notice from the assessment office.

Ask the Office of Property Assessments for the annual filing window, because the county sets it by ordinance. The county's real estate page also covers state and local realty transfer taxes, the municipal and school shares, and recording requirements for deeds.

How do transit, schools and shopping shape Bethel Park?

Pittsburgh Regional Transit's three light rail lines all run through the borough. The Blue and Red lines end at South Hills Village, and the Silver Line passes through the central business district to Library. Park-and-ride lots operate at South Hills Village, West Library, Lytle and Washington Junction.

PA Route 88 and US Route 19 carry most commercial traffic, and the Yellow and Orange Belts of the county belt system serve the borough. Interstate 79 and the Mon-Fayette Expressway stay outside the boundary, each about a 15-minute drive. Bethel Park High School is the comprehensive high school of the Bethel Park School District, and South Hills Village is a two-level mall inside the borough.

What are the ways to sell a house fast in Bethel Park?

An owner here can list the house, sell privately or accept a cash offer. Because the lateral inspection deadline is 21 days before closing, a sale that closes in under three weeks needs the dye test and camera work done before a contract is signed.

Start by requesting the forms from the municipality, hire the certified plumber, and keep the video and paperwork together for the buyer's title company. If the camera finds a defect, price the repair in early, because the deed cannot move until the repair passes inspection.

More questions about Bethel Park, PA

Do I need a dye test to sell my Bethel Park house?

Yes. Bethel Park requires a dye test and a camera lateral inspection before a deed transfers, unless one was done and certified within the last two years.

How much does the Bethel Park lateral paperwork cost?

The municipality charges a $50 processing fee. The plumber's fees are separate and depend on the contractor you hire.

Does Bethel Park require an occupancy inspection when a house is sold?

No. The dye test page states an occupancy inspection is not required for a sale. A $50 Certificate of Occupancy appears on the fee schedule for other situations.

Is Bethel Park built over old coal mines?

Yes. The borough's geology summary says all of Bethel Park was undermined, and part of it lies over the closed Pittsburgh Terminal No. 8 Mine.

Where do I appeal an Allegheny County assessment?

How quickly can a York Township, PA house sell?

Quickly, if the price matches the condition and the paperwork is clean. York Township is a large suburb of the City of York with a steady stream of buyers, and the route you choose (agent listing, owner sale or direct cash purchase) decides how much time you give up and how much price you keep.

Dallastown, Red Lion and Yoe grew out of the township's old southeastern corner, and what remains is the most populous suburb of York. The Census Bureau puts the township at 31,479 residents in mid-2025, a 5.8% rise from a 2020 starting count of 29,748. Growth keeps buyers active, yet a house with liens, tenants or deferred repairs usually waits longer on the open market than a tidy one.

What kind of place is York Township for a seller?

Mostly suburban, with older postwar tracts next to newer streets. Wikipedia dates settlement to 1748 and incorporation to 1753, and says the land stayed largely rural until after World War II. Head counts show the shift: 4,502 residents in 1950, 8,506 in 1960, 12,702 in 1970 and 29,740 in 2020.

About 25 square miles in size, the township contains Queens Gate, Spry and Tyler Run, three census-designated places, and answers to a Board of Supervisors. Many residents drive to work, with an average trip of 24.9 minutes.

Survey figures for 2020 to 2024 sketch the likely buyer pool and the likely sellers:

  • 12,939 households of about 2.3 people each.
  • Seven in ten homes are lived in by their owners, so roughly three in ten are rentals.
  • Household income in the middle of the range is $80,190, and 38.7% of adults 25 and over hold a four year degree.
  • Nearly a quarter of residents (22.5%) are 65 or older, which feeds downsizing and estate sales.

What are houses worth in York Township?

The Census Bureau's middle value for an owner occupied home is $260,800. Owners in the middle pay $1,914 a month in housing costs with a mortgage and $768 with none, while renters in the middle pay $1,389. A township wide figure hides a lot, so a dated ranch and a fully updated home in a newer plan will price far apart.

Which permits and inspections can affect a York Township sale?

The township's Building and Zoning Department issues permits, enforces codes and handles property maintenance. It applies the statewide Uniform Construction Code, adopted locally through Ordinance 2004-7 on May 11, 2004. A finished basement, deck or shed built without a permit may come up when a buyer's inspector or lender looks the house over, so check the file before you list.

  • Plan review is allowed up to 15 business days for a residential building permit and 30 for a commercial one.
  • A zoning permit is due in 10 days, unless a special exception or variance must go before the Zoning Hearing Board.
  • Building inspections are booked on weekdays between 7:30 a.m. and 2:15 p.m. with a day's notice, by calling (717) 428-5641.
  • Plumbing jobs go to a plumber licensed by York Township under Resolution 93-2; swapping a fixture or a water heater on the same fuel needs no permit.
  • Anyone running a business from home registers each year and pays $25.

Zoning and code staff answer questions on weekdays until 4:00 p.m. at (717) 741-3861, and the township asks you to call for an appointment first. The department also lists a LERTA tax assistance program for certain deteriorated areas, worth a question if your parcel might fall inside one.

How does recording work after a York Township closing?

The York County Recorder of Deeds records the deed, since the township does not. County fee notes set the base charge for a deed at $86.25, which covers four pages and four names. Pages past the fourth cost $2 each, extra names cost $0.50 each, and each parcel identification number on the paper adds $20.

Filing a PA Realty Transfer Tax Statement of Value costs $2. Business checks, personal checks and cash are accepted, and a bounced check brings a $50 charge. The county also posts a Common Level Ratio for each stretch from July 1 to June 30; the 2025 to 2026 figure was 1.98.

Pennsylvania taxes the transfer at 1 percent of value, and the Department of Revenue notes the buyer and the seller answer for it together. Municipal and school shares can sit on top, so ask your title company or the county recorder what the total comes to on your deed. Some gifts to family and property passing by will or intestacy are exempt.

Which selling route suits a York Township house?

Three routes cover most cases.

  • Agent listing. Best exposure for a house in good order. You pay a commission, host showings and wait on the buyer's loan, appraisal and inspection.
  • Owner sale. You keep the commission and take on pricing, marketing, contracts and negotiation, and the transfer tax and recording costs still apply.
  • Cash offer. A direct buyer buys the property in its present state, so cleanouts, repairs and tenants stop being obstacles. The price usually runs below a fully prepared retail sale, so compare it against your net after commission and fix-up.

The cash route tends to suit inherited homes, tenants who will not leave, long deferred repairs or a hard deadline such as a job move. To see the gap, request a written offer for your York Township address and set it next to a listing estimate.

What paperwork should a York Township seller gather first?

Begin with the deed and the newest tax bill, then pull permit records for any work done on the house. Request a payoff statement for each mortgage or lien, since those get paid from your proceeds at closing. If the house came from a relative, the estate papers need to show who may sign.

Then walk the property the way an inspector would: roof, furnace, electrical panel, sump area and outbuildings, noting anything built without a permit. Decide whether to repair, offer a credit or sell as is. Once you know the repair bill, choosing between a listing and a direct offer comes down to arithmetic.

More questions about York Township, PA

What is the typical timeline to sell in York Township?

Listed houses commonly take weeks to a few months depending on price, condition and the buyer's loan. A cash sale can close sooner because no lender or appraisal is involved, and the seller often sets the closing date.

Is a permit required before selling a York Township house?

No permit is needed just to sell. Earlier unpermitted work is the concern, because a buyer's inspection can raise it. Call the Building and Zoning Department at (717) 741-3861 to ask what the township file shows.

Which office records the deed for a York Township sale?

The York County Recorder of Deeds. Its base fee for a deed is $86.25 for four pages and four names, plus charges for added pages, names and parcel numbers.

Who owes Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax?

Buyer and seller are both liable, per the Department of Revenue. The state takes 1 percent of the value, and local shares can be added; your sales agreement sets who pays what.

Can a house that needs repairs still be sold here?

Yes. A direct buyer takes it in its current condition, while a financed buyer tends to ask for repairs or a lower price after inspection. A repair estimate up front lets you compare what each path would net.

What should a seller know about Ridley Township, PA?

Ridley Township is a compact, mostly built-out suburb in southeastern Delaware County where owners are long-settled and the housing stock is older. A sale here depends on a short call to the township's Code Enforcement office, the county's 1% local transfer tax default, and a buyer pool that is mostly local.

The township covers about 5.1 square miles of land, with more water along the Delaware River at its southern edge. It includes the communities of Folsom, Woodlyn, Crum Lynne and Holmes, plus parts of Morton and Secane. Rutledge Borough sits entirely inside Ridley's boundaries, and Ridley Park Borough is surrounded on three sides by the township, so the municipal line is not always obvious from a street address.

Ridley was named for Ridley in Cheshire, England, and its tax collectors were appointed as early as 1684. Continental Army troops camped along its roads after the Battle of Brandywine in 1777, and the township grew sharply after World War II, from about 8,600 residents in 1940 to nearly 36,000 by 1960.

What do Census figures show about Ridley homes?

Ridley is a mid-priced Delaware County market, with homes valued well below the Main Line and well above Chester, and with unusually low turnover.

A 93.3% same-house rate means most owners stay put, so houses that do come up often belong to long-term owners, estates or retirees. If you have owned the house for decades, get a repair estimate before you pick a price.

What does Ridley Township require when I sell my home?

Call the Code Enforcement office before you go to settlement. The township's code page says plainly that sellers should contact it for the necessary information, and the phone number is 610-534-4803.

The page also notes that owners of rental units must hold an annual certificate of use for each dwelling unit, whether occupied or empty. If you are selling a duplex or a house that was rented, confirm that the certificate is current so it does not become a closing problem.

  • Ask which inspections or forms the township wants for a sale at your address.
  • Ask whether any open violations, stormwater issues or unpermitted work are on file.
  • Ask for the township's current fee list, since permit and certificate charges are set locally.
  • Keep sidewalks and shared driveways clear of snow and ice within 24 hours after snow stops, because the township enforces that rule and buyers walking a property in winter will notice.

The township also publishes its code book, zoning map and a stormwater management ordinance, which matter if a buyer plans an addition or paving.

How much is transfer tax on a Ridley sale?

Delaware County's Recorder of Deeds lists a default of 1% to the state and 1% to the local municipality, and Ridley Township is not among the exceptions it names. Radnor, Upper Darby, Upper Providence and Chester are the ones that pay more.

At the Census median value of $265,200, 1% is about $2,650, so the combined 2% comes to roughly $5,300. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue says both parties are jointly liable and that some transfers, such as certain family transfers and property passing through an estate, are exempt. The contract should still say who pays.

  • The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 108 of the Government Center at 201 West Front Street in Media, phone 610-891-4152.
  • Recording hours are 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., a full hour before the 4:30 p.m. office close.
  • Ask your closing agent how the recording fee and the two taxes are paid, because the office takes them separately.
  • If the deed does not state the full price, the state's Statement of Value (REV-183) goes with it.

Because deeds for several municipalities are filed in the same office, check that your deed names Ridley Township as the municipality. A mistake there changes the local tax line.

Which schools, roads and neighborhoods shape demand in Ridley?

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District, and Our Lady of Angels Regional School, which formed in 2012 from two parish schools, is the nearby Catholic option. Families searching in this area often use the district as a filter, so a listing's school assignment is worth stating in the first lines.

Access is a selling point. Interstate 95 crosses the southern part of the township, Interstate 476 begins at I-95 and runs northwest across the southwest corner, U.S. 13 follows Chester Pike, PA 291 follows Industrial Highway and PA 420 follows Kedron Avenue. SEPTA city bus route 37 and suburban routes 113 and 114 serve the township. The nearest regional rail stations are in neighboring municipalities, since the Media/Wawa and Wilmington/Newark lines only clip the edges.

The township maintains about 72 miles of road, and PennDOT maintains about 14 miles.

How do property taxes and assessments work for a Ridley seller?

Ridley homeowners pay Delaware County, Ridley Township and the Ridley School District, each on its own bill. Ask the Delaware County Assessment Office for the current appeal deadline and form, and ask the township treasurer for the township's tax certification before closing.

Delaware County's countywide reassessment took effect in January 2021, so values across the county were reset at the same base year. A seller who thinks the assessed value is out of line can appeal, but filing an appeal does not stop the bill from coming due.

Stormwater is its own cost. Ridley adopted a stormwater management ordinance, last updated in September 2022, and publishes a stormwater fee schedule on its code page. Ask the township how the fee is billed on your parcel and whether any credit applies.

Which way to sell is best in Ridley?

A listing makes sense when the house is updated and priced against recent nearby sales. A cash sale works better when the house is dated, an estate is involved or the owner has to move on a deadline.

  • For an estate sale, confirm who has legal authority to sign the deed before listing.
  • For a tenant-occupied house, confirm the annual certificate of use and the lease terms.
  • For a quick sale, ask the buyer to put the closing date and who pays transfer tax in writing.

Whichever route you choose, gather the tax bills, the deed and any township notices before you call anyone. With 73.7% of Ridley homes owner-occupied and few households moving in a given year, a clean file and a firm closing date set one offer apart from another.

More questions about Ridley, PA

Does Ridley Township require an inspection before I sell?

Call the Code Enforcement office at 610-534-4803 to find out. The township's own page tells sellers to contact that office for the necessary information before settlement, so the answer for your address comes from them.

What is the transfer tax rate in Ridley Township?

The county's default is 1% state and 1% local, and Ridley is not listed among Delaware County's higher-rate exceptions. Confirm the figure with the Recorder of Deeds before you finalize your closing numbers.

Can I sell a Ridley rental property with tenants?

Yes. The township requires an annual certificate of use for each rental dwelling unit, occupied or not, so keep that current. Review the lease for how the buyer takes over the tenancy.

Which school district serves Ridley Township?

Students living in the township generally attend the Ridley School District. Parts of Morton and Secane lie inside the township, so check the school district on your tax bill.

Where is the Delaware County Recorder of Deeds?

In Room 108 of the Government Center, 201 West Front Street, Media. Recording hours run 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., and the office phone is 610-891-4152.

How do I sell my house fast in Spring Township, PA?

A direct cash sale is the fastest route for a Spring Township house, but the township's property transfer inspection has to be scheduled either way. Spring Township is in Berks County, west of Reading, and it requires an exterior inspection of every single and multiple family dwelling before title changes hands.

The inspection is the step that most often decides the calendar, so this page puts it first and then covers the township itself: where it sits, what its housing looks like in Census figures, how the creeks and hills affect lots, and what the buyer and seller each pay.

What is the Spring Township property transfer inspection?

It is a required exterior check under the township's Property Transfer Ordinance 341, in effect since August 1, 2007, and the Code Enforcement Officer must inspect before title transfers. The seller, buyer or either side's agent can file the application.

The application goes to the Code and Zoning Office no later than 30 business days before settlement. The fee is $150 per property, and it rises to $250 if the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. After a complete application, the officer inspects within 10 business days.

  • Fences, pools, spas, sheds and decks must be permitted and sit within setback and yard rules. Pool fencing needs a self-closing, latching gate.
  • Sanitary sewer connections must control inflow and infiltration, and sump pump discharge must be properly placed.
  • The number of dwelling units, bedrooms and smoke detectors is checked against township records.

The inspection covers only exterior, observable conditions, and nobody has to be home as long as the inspector can reach the backyard. Add a note with a phone number to the application if you want to be there.

What happens if the inspection finds problems?

Seller and buyer both sign the report to confirm they read it and agree to correct what it lists, and the township then issues a Property Transfer Certificate once the deficiencies are done. That can happen before or after settlement.

You do not have to fix everything before closing. If the buyer is willing to take on the repairs, an addendum to the agreement of sale normally settles who is responsible and how the money works. The township suggests ordering the inspection soon after you decide to sell, because the report has to be disclosed to the buyer and an early look leaves time to permit anything that was built without approval.

Common findings are an unpermitted shed or deck, a fence in an easement, or a pool without the right barrier. Those are fixable, and a cash buyer who plans to renovate will often accept them as part of an as-is purchase.

Where is Spring Township and what is the area like?

Spring Township covers about 18.4 square miles of land in Berks County, west of Reading and next to Wyomissing, Sinking Spring and Adamstown. The Census Bureau counted 28,407 residents in 2020 and estimates 28,873 for 2025, a gain of 1.7 percent. It is the second largest municipality in the county after Reading.

The township was split from Cumru Township in 1850 and takes its name from a large spring that appeared and disappeared with the limestone beneath it, which early settlers called the Sinking Spring. Terrain varies a lot: low ground in the north, with Cacoosing Creek on the northwest edge and Tulpehocken Creek on the northeast, and hills toward the Lancaster County line in the southwest. Communities inside the township include West Lawn, Whitfield, Spring Ridge, Vinemont and Montrose Manor.

Wertz's Covered Bridge, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, is one of the landmarks. The township shares the main western Reading retail district with Wyomissing, and Penn State Berks sits in the northeast corner.

What do Census figures say about Spring Township homes?

Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 show 11,495 households, a 75.3 percent owner-occupied rate and a median owner-occupied home value of $286,900. Median gross rent is $1,416, and median household income is $94,837.

About 17.6 percent of residents speak a language other than English at home, and 9.1 percent are foreign-born. Median selected monthly owner costs are $1,754 with a mortgage and $819 without. About a quarter of homes are rented, so some sellers here are small landlords who should check lease dates before setting a closing date.

How do the roads, bus routes and schools matter to buyers?

Spring Township has 130.6 miles of public roads, of which 112.16 miles are maintained by the township and the rest by PennDOT. U.S. 222, U.S. 422 and Pennsylvania Route 724 cross it, and U.S. 222 south gives expressway access toward the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Lancaster. Mean travel time to work is 23.6 minutes.

BARTA bus routes 12, 14, 15 and 16 serve residential and business areas and connect to the transportation center in Reading. Public schools are in the Wilson School District, which has five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. For a buyer, a house near a bus line or the bypass reads differently from one in a quieter subdivision, so mention it in any listing or offer discussion.

Which township rules can catch a seller by surprise?

Spring Township reviews more than 700 permits a year and enforces its fence, shed and pool rules closely. Fences in a front yard are limited to 4 feet and must be open style, rear-yard fences can reach 6 feet, and sheds are not allowed in required front or side yards.

Residential grass and weeds may not exceed 8 inches. After a verified complaint the township sends a notice, cuts the property after 7 days if the owner does not, and bills the owner, and unpaid amounts become a lien on the real estate. Sidewalks must be cleared of snow and ice within 24 hours after it stops, with the same lien risk. Clear both before you list so the inspection comes back clean.

How are taxes and transfer costs handled in Spring Township?

County and municipal tax payments can be made online through the Berks County Treasurer, and Wilson School District taxes are paid at Fulton Bank, according to the township tax collector's page. Call the tax collector's office for a payoff figure before closing.

Pennsylvania charges a 1 percent state realty transfer tax, collected with any local share by the Berks County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Ask the Recorder for the combined local rate, and expect the buyer and seller to split it unless the sales agreement says otherwise.

More questions about Spring, PA

Does Spring Township require an inspection to sell a house?

Yes. Ordinance 341 requires an exterior property transfer inspection by the Code Enforcement Officer before title changes. Apply at least 30 business days before settlement to pay the $150 fee.

What is the late fee for a Spring Township transfer inspection?

The fee is $250 instead of $150 when the application arrives fewer than 15 business days before settlement. The inspector still responds within 10 business days of a complete application.

Do I have to fix every item before closing?

No. A buyer can agree to make the corrections, and an addendum to the agreement of sale usually covers it. The Property Transfer Certificate is issued once the deficiencies are completed, before or after settlement.

What is the population of Spring Township?

The Census Bureau estimates 28,873 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 28,407 in the 2020 census. It is the second most populous municipality in Berks County.

Which school district serves Spring Township?

The Wilson School District serves the township, with five elementary schools, two middle schools and Wilson High School. School real estate tax is paid separately from county and township tax.

What should I know before selling a house in McCandless?

McCandless is a home rule municipality in Allegheny County, officially called the Town of McCandless, and a sale there carries a 2.5 percent combined transfer tax that is higher than in several neighboring communities. The town also issues its own lien letter and points sellers to the sanitary authority for a dye test.

The town covers about 16.6 square miles in Pittsburgh's North Hills and had 29,709 residents in the 2020 census. It sits on the Allegheny Plateau at roughly 1,024 feet of elevation, and hilly ground defines most streets. Pine Creek cuts a deep valley through the middle of the town, with a floodplain along the creek.

Because of its home rule status, the town no longer operates under the First Class Township Code, although it is treated as a first-class township for certain purposes. McCandless borders Pine Township to the north, Hampton Township to the east, Ross Township to the south and the borough of Franklin Park to the west. Its public schools belong to the North Allegheny School District, and the Northland Public Library is shared with nearby municipalities.

How did McCandless grow into a North Hills suburb?

The first European settler, James Duff, bought 400 acres in 1796, and the area stayed farmland through the 1800s. The township was organized in 1851 as Taylor Township and was renamed McCandless in 1857 after a district judge.

Several events shaped the housing map you see today:

  • A 1908 interurban rail line, the Harmony Line, let residents commute to Pittsburgh until it closed in 1931.
  • Allegheny County created North Park in 1927, and about 1,600 acres of it, roughly 15.2 percent of the town, lie inside McCandless.
  • Population jumped from 2,653 in 1930 to 6,488 in 1950 and 14,582 in 1960.
  • McKnight Road opened in the mid-1950s as the main route into the north suburbs.
  • The Community College of Allegheny County opened a campus in 1972.
  • McCandless Crossing, a mixed-use center with apartments and townhomes, was completed in 2016.

The population has been roughly flat since 1990, with 28,781 residents then and 29,709 in 2020, so listings compete with a mature, established housing supply.

Which McCandless neighborhoods do buyers ask about?

Buyers commonly search by named plan or community, and McCandless has many. Allison Park is one community inside the town, and the list also includes Meadow Oaks, Guyton Farms, Greybrooke, Bennington Woods, Pin Oak, Briarwood, Park Meadows, Foxcroft Village, Sample Manor, Colington Square, Royal Manor, Pinnacle Pointe and Longvue Acres.

Five ZIP codes cover the town: 15237, 15090, 15044, 15101 and 15127. That matters for a listing because a house inside the town can carry more than one postal city. Confirm the municipality on the tax bill, not the postal city, before checking local rules.

Homes near Pine Creek deserve a floodplain check. Ask the town whether your lot sits in the mapped floodplain before you write the listing description.

What is the transfer tax when you sell in McCandless?

The total realty transfer tax on a McCandless sale is 2.5 percent. That figure combines the state's 1 percent, a 1 percent municipal share and a one half of 1 percent North Allegheny School District share, based on the county's published rate table.

The municipal rate is the notable part. Allegheny County's table lists McCandless at 1 percent, the same as Hampton and Pine townships, while Ross Township and Franklin Park borough list one half of 1 percent. On a $300,000 sale, the difference between a 2 percent and a 2.5 percent total is $1,500, so the rate belongs in your net sheet.

The county collects the tax when the deed is recorded. The state says buyer and seller are both liable, and contracts decide the split. Some transfers, including certain deeds between family members and property passed through an estate, are exempt from the state portion, so ask the county's Real Estate office how an exemption is documented.

What does the Town of McCandless need from a seller?

A seller should order a municipal lien letter and arrange a dye test. The lien letter costs $30 by mail or $35 if the results are emailed, and the request needs the owner's name, property address, parcel number and the reason, such as a sale. Checks are payable to the Town of McCandless.

McCandless sale paperwork. Source: Town of McCandless Tax Information FAQ and Allegheny County transfer tax table.

The sanitary authority and the water authority can each file liens for unpaid service, so call both before the closing. The lien letter request is handled by the town's tax office at 412-364-0616.

How are real estate taxes billed in McCandless?

The deputy tax collector, Jordan Tax Service, collects both Town and North Allegheny School District real estate tax. Beginning in 2026, owners receive two separate invoices, one for the Town and one for the school district.

  • The Town millage for 2026 is 1.236 mills.
  • The North Allegheny School District rate is 20.43 mills for the 2025 to 2026 school year, or $2,043 per $100,000 of assessed value.
  • Allegheny County lists 6.43 mills.
  • Taxes unpaid after December 31 are delinquent and can lead to a lien on the property.

An installment plan with three equal payments is open only to owners with a homestead or farmstead exclusion. The first payment is due August 31, followed by October 31 and December 31, and late installments carry a 10 percent penalty. Owners approved for the Act 77 senior citizen discount receive 30 percent off the Town portion. Pay tax on time even while an appeal is pending, because the higher amount must be paid once a deadline passes.

Payments cannot be left in the Town Hall drop box. Send them to Jordan Tax Service or use the options printed on the statement. Jordan representatives also sit at Town Hall on select dates, which are posted on the Town calendar, and owners should bring the full tax statements. Earned income tax and business privilege tax are handled separately by the Keystone Collections Group.

Can I still appeal my Allegheny County assessment?

The 2027 annual appeal window ran from July 1 through September 1, 2026, and it has closed. The Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review hears appeals, and it sends residential hearing notices at least 14 days ahead.

The county set its 2027 common level ratio at 49.3 percent, a factor applied to market value in appeals that started in September 2026. Owners who missed the window should ask the Office of Property Assessments about the next annual period and about special appeals tied to a change notice.

Should I list a McCandless house or accept a cash purchase?

Cash works best when the house needs repairs or the closing date matters more than the last dollar of price. A listing suits a house in good condition in a popular plan, where several buyers may compete.

  • Get the lien letter and dye test started before you accept any offer.
  • Compare offers after the 2.5 percent transfer tax, any payoff and the unpaid portion of the year's Town and school taxes.
  • Ask each buyer how they treat the dye test result if the sewer lateral needs work.

More questions about McCandless, PA

What is the total transfer tax in McCandless?

2.5 percent. The state charges 1 percent, McCandless charges 1 percent, and the North Allegheny School District charges one half of 1 percent.

How do I get a lien letter from the Town of McCandless?

Mail a request with the owner's name, address, parcel number and reason, along with a $30 check. The email option costs $35. Write the check to the Town of McCandless.

Who collects real estate tax in McCandless?

Jordan Tax Service collects both Town and North Allegheny School District real estate tax. Owners receive two separate invoices starting in 2026.

Which school district serves McCandless?

North Allegheny School District. McCandless is also part of the shared Northland Public Library.

Is the 2027 Allegheny County appeal window still open?

No. The 2027 annual appeal period ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026. Contact the county's Office of Property Assessments about later options.

What comes first when a Horsham homeowner decides to sell?

Horsham Township asks every seller of a residential property to complete a township inspection and certification before settlement, so build that step into your timeline from day one. The rest of the sale follows the usual Pennsylvania pattern, with Montgomery County handling assessment, recording and transfer tax.

Horsham sits in Montgomery County about ten miles north of Center City Philadelphia. Its 17.32 square miles held an estimated 27,882 residents by mid-2025, according to the Census Bureau, which is 5.0 percent above 2020. Homes here are worth far more than in older Pennsylvania cities, so a delay of even a few weeks costs real money in carrying costs and interest.

A fast sale to a cash buyer is one route, a listing is another, and a for-sale-by-owner deal is the third. All three need the township certification below, because the rule attaches to the property transfer rather than to the type of buyer.

What is Horsham Township like for homeowners?

It is a suburban home-rule township that grew mostly after World War II. William Penn's surveyors laid out the township's lines, and Horsham was established in 1717. Early settlement clustered around the Friends meeting house at Horsham and Easton Roads, and the township had only about 1,300 people in 1890. The count climbed from 3,663 in 1950 to 8,933 in 1960 and 13,888 in 1970.

Today the township includes the villages of Horsham, Hallowell, Prospectville and Maple Glen. Mail comes through five ZIP codes: 19044 for Horsham, plus parts of the township that use Hatboro, Ambler, Chalfont and North Wales codes. Natural features include Park Creek, Little Neshaminy Creek, Pennypack Creek and Wissahickon Creek.

  • Schools: the Hatboro-Horsham School District, with Keith Valley Middle School and Hatboro-Horsham Senior High School.
  • Parks: about 815 acres of township parkland, a trail network that includes the Power Line Trail, and the 42 acre Graeme Park with its colonial governor's house.
  • Climate: a hot summer humid continental climate, averaging about 32 degrees in January and 77 in July.

Local government is a five-member council elected at large for four-year terms, with a township manager running daily operations and Horsham Fire Company No. 1 providing fire protection. Because the township works under a home rule charter, its rules, including the transfer inspection below, come from its own ordinances rather than the state's township code.

The township's biggest recent land story is the former Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Willow Grove, which closed in 2011 after 68 years. Surplus land from the base is about 8 percent of the township's area and is subject to a redevelopment plan, while the Air National Guard remains on the 200 acre site as Biddle Air National Guard Base.

Which roads and employers shape Horsham home values?

Buyers here shop by commute and by corporate campus. Easton Road (Route 611) runs north to south through the eastern side, Horsham Road (Route 463) crosses the center, and Welsh Road (Route 63), Limekiln Pike (Route 152) and Bethlehem Pike (Route 309) frame the edges. The Willow Grove interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike sits just south in Upper Moreland Township.

SEPTA bus Route 55 follows Route 611, and the township runs a weekday rush hour shuttle called h.o.p.s. between the office parks and the Fort Washington station on the Lansdale/Doylestown Regional Rail line. The Census Bureau reports a mean commute of 28.6 minutes for Horsham workers.

Employers named for the township include Janssen Biotech and Janssen Pharmaceuticals, both Johnson & Johnson subsidiaries, plus corporate offices for Bimbo Bakeries USA, Penn Mutual and SofterWare, and a UPS hub.

How do Horsham's housing numbers compare?

Horsham is a high value, mostly owner occupied township, and the figures below show how far it sits from the state's older cities.

What does Horsham's property transfer certification require?

The township requires an inspection of every residential property before a transfer. The application and fee are submitted to the Horsham Township Municipal Building at 1025 Horsham Road within the 90 days before settlement.

  • A township inspector checks the curb and sidewalk in front of the property.
  • The street address must be posted and easy to see from the road.
  • The seller certifies that working smoke detectors are in the house.

Schedule the inspection early enough to fix a cracked sidewalk slab or a missing house number before settlement. Questions go to the Code Enforcement department at (215) 643-3131.

The township also issues tax certifications through the township tax collector. Send the requester's contact details, the parcel number, the property address, the owner's name and a $30 check per parcel made out to Horsham Township, along with a stamped return envelope if you want it mailed. A title company normally handles this, but a seller handling a sale directly will need to order it.

How do Montgomery County assessments and tax sales touch a Horsham sale?

The county Board of Assessment Appeals sets the values behind county, township and school bills. Yearly appeals are due August 1 and change the tax year after. That same August 1 date applies to real estate tax exemption applications. State law requires annual appeals to be decided by October 31 so changes reach the rolls and taxing bodies by November 15.

The board advises mailing deadline filings with a hand-cancelled postmark, a Certificate of Mailing or certified mail, because postal delays can mark a timely envelope late. You can also hand deliver in Norristown on weekdays between 8:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. The board's phone line is 610-278-3761.

If the house carries unpaid taxes, the county Tax Claim Bureau enters the picture. It holds an upset sale each September and December and a judicial sale at least once a year in August and December. Upset sale buyers take the property subject to its liens, while a judicial sale presents it free and clear. Clear any delinquency before listing so it does not surface at closing.

When is a cash sale the better choice in Horsham?

A cash sale helps most when the property does not fit a conventional buyer's loan, or when the seller cannot wait through showings. Examples are a house with deferred roof or mechanical work, an estate property that needs to close before the next tax bill, or a seller relocating out of the area.

Because Horsham values are high, compare any cash figure with a full net sheet: list price, agent commission, transfer tax, repairs to pass the township inspection, and carrying cost. If you would like a cash figure for your Horsham house, Cash Home Buyers can provide one to set against that sheet.

More questions about Horsham, PA

Is an inspection required to sell a house in Horsham Township?

Yes. The township's Residential Property Transfer Certification Program requires an inspection of every residential property before transfer, covering the curb, the sidewalk and the posted address, plus a seller certification of working smoke detectors. Submit it within 90 days before settlement.

How much does a Horsham tax certification cost?

The township's tax collector charges $30 per parcel, paid by check to Horsham Township. Include the parcel number, property address and owner name, and say how you want the certification returned.

What date closes the yearly Montgomery County assessment appeal?

August 1, and the result applies to the next tax year.

Which school district serves Horsham?

The Hatboro-Horsham School District serves the township, along with neighboring Hatboro. Its schools include Keith Valley Middle School and Hatboro-Horsham Senior High School.

Can I sell a Horsham house with unpaid property taxes?

Yes, but the unpaid amount must be cleared at or before closing. Taxes that reach the county Tax Claim Bureau can put the property into an upset or judicial sale, so settle the balance before then.
