This page covers what is particular to Springettsbury: its history and neighborhoods, the retail and industrial base around the York Galleria and Interstate 83, the two school districts that split the township, and the tax calendar that determines what the closing company asks you for.

What is Springettsbury Township like?

Springettsbury is a supervisor-manager township of about 16.4 square miles, home to the York Galleria mall and a large Harley-Davidson manufacturing campus. The Census Bureau counted 27,058 residents in 2020 and estimates 27,617 for July 1, 2025, a 2.2 percent increase.

The name comes from Springett Penn, a grandson of William Penn, and the township was incorporated on April 20, 1891 out of the northeast part of Spring Garden Township. It includes the census-designated places of East York, Pleasureville, Yorklyn and Stonybrook. East York was first developed in 1903, and the housing built there in the 1930s sits alongside postwar subdivisions such as Fayfield and Haines Acres and newer developments.

Codorus Creek forms the western and northwestern boundary and Mill Creek runs along the southwest. Major roads are Interstate 83, U.S. Route 30, Route 462 (East Market Street), Route 24 and Route 124.

What are the Census numbers for Springettsbury housing?

Census Bureau data for 2020 to 2024 shows 10,202 households, a 72.5 percent owner-occupied rate and a median owner-occupied home value of $243,900. Median gross rent is $1,339, median household income is $86,335 and mean travel time to work is 22.0 minutes.

About 85.8 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, and more than a quarter of homes are rented. Retail sales in 2022 were $1,356,251,000, or $50,118 per resident, which reflects how much shopping in the York area concentrates here.

Which school district is my house in?

Springettsbury is split between the York Suburban and Central York school districts, and your tax bills follow whichever one serves your address. The township tax collector bills school real estate tax for both districts inside the township.

That split matters when you sell. School tax is billed separately from the county and township bill, on a different date, and a closing company needs the right district and the right year to prorate it correctly. Look at your most recent school tax bill, which names the district, before you give a title company the parcel number.

When are Springettsbury tax bills mailed and paid?

Springettsbury tax calendar and fees. Sources: Springettsbury Township property tax page and Real Estate Tax Certification Request Form.

The collector goes by postmark date for mailed payments, so allow time. Cash is not accepted in the drop box. If your mortgage company pays through escrow, forward any bill that reaches you rather than paying twice.

How does the tax certification work for a sale?

The closing company asks the township Tax Collector for a Real Estate Tax Certification, which shows whether York County, township, street light and school taxes are paid, with the year, face amount, discount and penalty for each. The request form lists the property address, parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date and whether the deal is a sale or a refinance.

The fee is $20, payable by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. Delinquent taxes from prior years go through the York County Tax Claim Bureau instead. The township also keeps a sewer account certification request form among its documents, so ask the title company whether a sewer certification is on its list.

What property rules does the township enforce?

Springettsbury employs a full-time Codes Enforcement Officer who responds to complaints about property maintenance. The township's property maintenance page lists the issues that come up most often:

  • Fences, pools, decks, sheds and patios built too close to a property line.
  • Signs of the wrong size, type or location.
  • Cars, RVs, tractors, construction equipment and boats parked on grass, plus abandoned or junk vehicles.
  • Weeds, tall grass, trash, uncleared sidewalks, dilapidated buildings and unsafe structures.

Owners are asked to correct a violation voluntarily, and a finding can sometimes be appealed to the Zoning Hearing Board. If a violation stays open, the township can pursue legal action and the District Magistrate can impose fines for each violation. Fix open notices before listing, or tell a cash buyer about them up front so the price reflects the work.

What happened to the big employers nearby?

Springettsbury has seen several large facilities change hands. A 101-acre Caterpillar plant operated here from 1953 until the 1990s, and the vacant site was sold in 2002 and redeveloped as the York Business Center. The McCrory Stores headquarters was in the township from 1963 until the chain closed in 2002, and Bon-Ton Stores closed its township headquarters in August 2018.

More recently construction of a Post Consumer Brands logistics center on the Harley-Davidson campus finished in January 2017, and Hollywood Casino York opened in August 2021. For a homeowner, these shifts matter mostly through job access and traffic on Market Street and Route 30.

What about transfer tax and recording?

The state realty transfer tax is 1 percent of value, and local governments can add a share, with the York County Recorder of Deeds collecting it at recording. Certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestate succession are among the exemptions the Department of Revenue lists.

Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined local rate for Springettsbury and for current recording fees, then subtract both from your estimate of net proceeds. The sales agreement decides who pays, though both buyer and seller are legally liable if the tax is not paid.

Is a cash sale the right choice in Springettsbury?

A cash sale makes the most sense if the house needs repairs, has an open code violation, is a rental with a tenant leaving, or you need a firm date. Get at least one cash offer in writing, then compare it with the net from a listing after commission, repair credits and the carrying cost of waiting.

Ask any buyer who covers the tax certification fee, the sewer certification and the recording costs, and ask for the closing date in writing.

More questions about Springettsbury, PA

Does Springettsbury Township require an inspection before I sell?

The township's published pages describe code enforcement for complaints and permits, and they list no sale inspection. Check with the township office about any open violation or permit on your address before listing.

How much is the tax certification in Springettsbury?

The fee is $20, paid by check to the Springettsbury Township Tax Collector. The closing company sends the request form with the parcel number, owner, buyer and settlement date.

Which school districts serve Springettsbury Township?

York Suburban and Central York both serve parts of the township. Their tax bills go out July 1 for York Suburban and July 15 for Central York.

What is the population of Springettsbury Township?

The Census Bureau estimates 27,617 residents as of July 1, 2025, up from 27,058 in the 2020 census. The township covers about 16.4 square miles.

Where do I pay back taxes on a Springettsbury house?

Delinquent taxes from prior years go to the York County Tax Claim Bureau at 717-771-9232. Current-year bills are paid to the township Tax Collector, who goes by postmark date.

What shapes a house sale in East Hempfield Township?

East Hempfield is a suburban township west of the city of Lancaster, and a sale there turns on three local facts: Lancaster County is in the middle of a countywide reassessment, the Hempfield School District sets the biggest piece of the tax bill, and the township charges its own transfer tax. Each affects what you net.

The township covers about 21 square miles of land in west-central Lancaster County. It is one of six immediate suburbs that share the Lancaster mailing designation, so many East Hempfield houses carry a Lancaster address. Within the township are Landisville, Mechanicsville, Rohrerstown, Bamford, Centerville, Chestnut Ridge, Donerville, Chestnut View and Wheatland, plus part of Salunga.

This page covers what a seller needs to know about the tax steps, the county assessment cycle and township inspections, followed by the common ways owners here sell.

What is East Hempfield like as a place to sell?

The township's municipal building stands beside Amos Herr House and Park, where a farmhouse dating to 1852 remains. Kellogg's and Y&S Candies are listed among its manufacturers, and Census figures put 2022 retail sales above $1.1 billion.

East Hempfield had 23,522 residents in 2010, 26,304 in 2020 and an estimated 27,287 on July 1, 2025. Growth has been steady, not explosive, and the age mix is older than in many suburbs, with 27.0 percent of residents 65 or over.

  • Households: 11,427 in 2020 through 2024
  • Persons per household: 2.32
  • Average commute: 20.0 minutes
  • Foreign-born residents: 8.6 percent

What do East Hempfield housing figures look like?

About 72 percent of East Hempfield households own their homes. The table below uses the Census Bureau's QuickFacts page.

East Hempfield Township housing and income, Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureEast Hempfield
Residents (2025 estimate)27,287
Households that own their home72.5%
Midpoint value of an owned home$360,500
Midpoint monthly cost for owners with a mortgage$2,098
Midpoint monthly rent$1,383
Midpoint household income$99,384

How do school and county property tax bills work in East Hempfield?

The Lancaster County Treasurer collects county and township real estate taxes for East Hempfield, according to the county's tax collector list, while the Hempfield School District issues the school bill. The district's published rate for 2026-27 is 19.8786 mills, up 4.1 percent from the year before. The district's 2026 school bills were mailed June 30, with a 2 percent discount for payments postmarked by August 31, the base amount due by October 31, and a 10 percent penalty after that, with all payments due by December 31.

If a bill is not paid by year-end, the balance goes to the Lancaster County Tax Claim Bureau. That is also the office to call for questions on delinquent balances.

Tax certifications for closings have a new procedure. Starting July 1, 2026, the Lancaster County Tax Collection Bureau processes them for the school district. The request goes by email and must give the owner's name, the property address, the 13-digit parcel number, the settlement date and a return email or fax number. The fee is $25, and a check payable to LCTCB Real Estate Tax Group goes by mail with the request. Missing information sends the request back and delays closing.

How much transfer tax applies when selling in East Hempfield?

The township's realty transfer tax ordinance levies 1 percent of the value of the real estate, for general township purposes, on top of the 1 percent the Commonwealth charges. The ordinance was adopted in 1987 under the state Tax Reform Code and the Local Tax Enabling Act. It makes the tax payable when the deed is presented for recording, and no later than 30 days after acceptance of the document.

The state Department of Revenue treats the buyer and the seller as jointly liable. Several transfers are exempt in the township ordinance, including transfers to an heir from a decedent and certain transfers to the trustee of an ordinary trust, provided the Recorder of Deeds gets a copy of the trust instrument. Family transfers are also covered in the state's list of exemptions.

Ask the Lancaster County Recorder of Deeds for the total transfer tax on your deed, including the school district portion, before you set your asking price. On a sale at the $360,500 Census median, each 1 percent equals $3,605.

What does the 2027 countywide reassessment mean for a seller?

Lancaster County's Property Assessment Office assesses more than 195,000 parcels across 60 municipalities and 17 school districts. Its last countywide reassessment took effect January 1, 2018, when assessed values were set at market value as of that date with a 100 percent ratio. A new reassessment is underway for 2027, with assessors permitted to make outside-only inspections and photograph exteriors during 2025 and 2026.

The school district's reassessment page says the purpose is to keep taxes fair relative to value and that it does not raise revenue. Taxing bodies must adjust their rates to stay revenue neutral before making other changes, so a higher assessment on your house does not automatically mean a higher bill. A buyer will still compare your assessed value with similar houses.

  • Annual appeals are due August 1
  • In a reassessment year, an owner has 40 days from the date of the reassessment notice
  • The county's page says the next opportunity for an annual appeal after 2027 is 2028
  • Appeals go to a three-member Board of Assessment Appeals

The county warns that no form freezes or eliminates property taxes for seniors. Be cautious of any video or mailer that says otherwise, and contact the Assessment Office at 717-299-8381 for the real programs.

How do township permits and inspections affect a sale?

East Hempfield employs a Building Code Official who reviews permits and carries out inspections, and an inspector who handles property maintenance. Inspections are performed by Code Administrators Inc., which requires 24 hours' notice to schedule. The township's page also lists code enforcement services, a code enforcement complaint form and records research requests.

If you built a deck, finished a basement or replaced a furnace, locate the permit and the final inspection record before you list. Missing paperwork is easier to resolve with the township while you still own the house. The township uses a single generic form for residential building and zoning and another for commercial work, and its zoning map is online.

When a buyer asks about an old addition, the records research request is the route for pulling what the township has on file.

What are the common ways to sell an East Hempfield house?

A listing works well for a house in good shape in a strong school district. An as-is sale suits an estate, a house that needs major repairs, a rental with a difficult tenant or a move that cannot wait for showings and a buyer's financing. Compare offers on net proceeds after the transfer tax, any tax balance, the prorated school and county taxes, and repairs you agree to credit.

Get any offer in writing, ask who pays for title work and recording, and ask when the buyer wants to close.

More questions about East Hempfield, PA

Is East Hempfield part of the City of Lancaster?

No. East Hempfield is a separate township in Lancaster County, though it shares the Lancaster mailing designation with five other suburbs. Permits and zoning come from the township.

Who collects school taxes on an East Hempfield house?

The Hempfield School District handles its own bills, with its 2026-27 rate set at 19.8786 mills. The Lancaster County Treasurer collects county and township taxes.

How do I get a tax certification for an East Hempfield closing?

Email the Lancaster County Tax Collection Bureau with the owner name, address, 13-digit parcel number and settlement date, and mail a $25 check payable to LCTCB Real Estate Tax Group.

When can I appeal my East Hempfield assessment?

Annual appeals are due by August 1. In a reassessment year, you have 40 days from the notice date. The county says the next annual appeal opportunity after the 2027 reassessment is 2028.

Does the township require an inspection before I sell?

The township's page lists permit review, inspections through Code Administrators Inc. and code enforcement. Ask the township's code office whether anything further applies to your address before you list.

  • Shaler is in Allegheny County.
Selling in Shaler?

Get My Cash Offer →

How do I sell my house fast in Shaler, PA?

The quickest way to sell a Shaler house is a direct cash sale, because it avoids the lender and appraisal steps that stretch out a listing. Shaler Township, in Allegheny County, also has its own pre-closing checklist that every seller has to clear, and that checklist is the real schedule driver whichever route you choose.

The township publishes a Selling Your Home guide that lists what the seller does, what the closing company orders, and what the buyer sets up afterward. Knowing it in advance keeps a fast sale from stalling at the last week. Below is how that guide works, along with the township's layout, housing profile and flood and mine issues that can come up in an inspection.

What is Shaler Township, and where is it?

Shaler Township is a first class township in Allegheny County about 11.2 square miles in size, covering much of Glenshaw and part of Allison Park in the North Hills suburbs of Pittsburgh. The 2020 census counted 28,132 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 26,833, a 4.6 percent decline from the 2020 base.

It was decreed in 1847 as Marion Township and renamed Shaler the same day, after a Pittsburgh-area judge. In 1900 it became a township of the first class, and the boundaries have changed little since. After World War II it filled in as a residential suburb, which is why most of its housing is mid-century. Several Pittsburgh mailing addresses fall inside the township, and the area is served by the Shaler Area School District.

The terrain is hilly and cut by three stream valleys that drain north to the Allegheny River: Pine Creek, Little Pine Creek and Girtys Run. Neighbors include Hampton, Ross, O'Hara, Indiana and Reserve townships and the boroughs of Etna, Millvale and Sharpsburg.

What does the Shaler housing market look like on paper?

Census Bureau figures for 2020 to 2024 describe a stable owner-occupied township. 87.0 percent of units are owner-occupied, the median owner-occupied home value is $245,500, and median household income is $95,654 across 12,314 households. Median gross rent is $1,226 a month.

Residents age 65 and over make up 24.6 percent of the population, and 95.8 percent of people lived in the same house a year earlier. With so many long-time residents, a cash buyer who takes the house as it stands suits owners who are downsizing or settling an estate.

What does the township require before I can close?

Shaler requires a dye test, a backflow preventer check and a final water reading from the seller, plus four township letters the closing company orders. The township says every document on its list is required for closing.

  • Dye test. The home must be tested to confirm that downspouts and rain leaders are not tied into the sanitary sewer. Results stay valid for three years. The township asks sellers to request the test at least 14 days before closing.
  • Backflow preventer. At least two weeks before closing, the seller contacts the Hampton Shaler Water Authority at (412) 486-4867 for a visit to confirm a dual check valve and thermal expansion tank are in place.
  • Final meter reading. Sellers and landlords schedule a final reading and send a copy to the closing company so escrowed funds can be released.
  • Trash account. Close the account with the hauler and leave the recycling cart for the new owner.

If the dye test fails, the plumber notifies the township and the owner. Repairs can go to any contractor, but the township's building inspector must be told at least 24 hours before work starts so the work can be inspected.

What do the closing documents cost in Shaler?

Shaler closing documents. Source: Shaler Township, Selling Your Home page.
DocumentIssued byFee

Occupancy permitNot required for a saleNone

The dye test itself is paid separately. Three plumbers under contract with the township charge $30, $35 and $40 per test, and you may hire your own registered plumber if the dye test form and waiver go back to the township office.

How does the tax certification work for a Shaler sale?

For a sale or refinance, the seller gives the closing company three years of township and school district real estate tax receipts. The closing company may use those receipts or order a tax certification letter from the township for $50.

Property tax in Shaler involves the county, the township and the school district, so a bill can come from more than one place. If you have lost old receipts, call the township tax office at 412-486-9700 and ask for copies before the closing company needs them.

What are the transfer tax and recording steps?

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the property's value, and local governments add their own share, all collected by the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds when the deed is recorded. Both buyer and seller are legally liable for the tax, though the sales agreement normally says who pays it.

Some transfers are exempt, including certain moves between family members and property passed by will or intestate succession. If the house is part of an estate, ask the Recorder or the closing company which exemption, if any, fits your deed. Ask the Recorder for the current local rate for Shaler before you work out your net proceeds.

Does flooding or mine subsidence affect Shaler houses?

Both can, depending on the street. The township keeps FEMA flood maps on file and publishes zone maps for Girtys Run, Little Pine Creek and Pine Creek, which the township says flood periodically. The building and zoning office at 300 Wetzel Road will review the maps with you and help work out which flood zone a property is in.

Part of the township sits over land that was mined in the past. The Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection sells mine subsidence insurance because homeowner policies usually leave it out. Coverage of $150,000 costs $41.25 a year, and a buyer needs a new policy of their own because the seller's does not carry over. Sellers who cancel at closing can get unused premium back if they notify DEP within 30 days of the sale.

What does the buyer handle after closing?

Shaler buyers register for the 1 percent earned income tax with Keystone Collections Group and open a water and sewer account with the Hampton Shaler Water Authority, since both charges share one bill. They also set up trash service, which is mandatory under the township code and handled by the township's contracted hauler.

If the property will sit empty for longer than three weeks, the owner can apply for a trash waiver good for up to six months and renewable. A seller who knows the house will be vacant before closing should ask about it.

Is a cash offer a good fit for a Shaler seller?

It is worth pricing when the house needs work, the dye test or backflow check looks like a problem, or the family wants a closing date it can plan around. A cash buyer is usually willing to take on the township checklist, but ask who pays for the dye test, the $50 letters and any repairs before you sign.

Compare the offer against a listing net of commission and the transfer tax. If the gap is small, the speed may be worth it. If it is large and the house is in good shape, a traditional listing may still make sense.

More questions about Shaler, PA

Does Shaler Township require an occupancy permit to sell a house?

No. The township's Selling Your Home page states that occupancy permits are not required for the sale or refinance of a property. A dye test, backflow check and several township letters are required instead.

How long is a Shaler dye test valid?

Three years from the test date, and the township keeps the result on file. Request the test at least 14 days before closing so a failed result can be fixed in time.

Who orders the Shaler no lien letter?

The closing company orders it from the township for $50. It confirms that no municipal liens are unfiled against the property, and the water authority issues its own separate lien letter.

What is the Shaler Township population?

The Census Bureau estimates 26,833 residents as of July 1, 2025, down from 28,132 counted in the 2020 census. The township covers about 11 square miles of land.

Can I sell a vacant or inherited house in Shaler as-is?

Yes, as long as the township's closing requirements are met, because they apply to every sale. Notify the water authority if the house is empty so service can be shut off, and ask about the trash waiver while it sits.

What does a Lebanon seller need to understand first?

Lebanon packs about 26,500 people into a small grid of older homes, many of them rented, with a typical owner's home valued at $156,500. That price level means repairs, taxes and closing costs take a large share of any sale, so the details below are worth reading before you set a price.

The city is also Lebanon County's seat of government, 26 miles east of Harrisburg and 88 miles northwest of Philadelphia. It covers just 4.17 square miles, which works out to about 6,435 people per square mile. The Census Bureau's mid-2025 figure is 26,479, a 1.1 percent drop from 2020. The city had gained 5.2 percent in the previous decade.

A Lebanon owner can use a broker, post the sign personally or take a cash bid for the house. In every case the deed is filed at the courthouse on South 8th Street, and the county treasurer keeps the tax payment records.

How did Lebanon become the city it is?

George Steitz founded the town in 1740 under the name Steitztown. Settlers arrived about 1720, streets were laid out in 1753, a borough charter came in 1821, and city status followed on November 25, 1885. Population passed 14,000 by 1890 and peaked at 30,045 in 1960 before sliding to 24,461 in 2000.

Manufacturing built much of the housing. The Union Canal ran along the north side from 1828 to 1885, San Giorgio pasta has been made here since 1914, and a large Bethlehem Steel mill once operated in the city. Lebanon bologna, first made here before the 1780s, still carries the city's name. The Quittapahilla Creek drains the city westward toward the Susquehanna.

  • Neighboring municipalities: North Lebanon, South Lebanon, West Lebanon and North Cornwall townships.
  • Schools: the Lebanon School District, which serves the city and West Lebanon Township, plus a Harrisburg Area Community College campus and the Lebanon County Career and Technology Center.
  • Weather: about 46 inches of precipitation and 24 inches of snow in a typical year, with January averaging about 30 degrees and July about 74. Gutters, roofs and basements on older homes get tested every winter.

How do Lebanon homes show up in Census data?

Lebanon has more renters than owners, lower incomes than the state's suburbs and a younger, more diverse population. Most homes here are rented, so landlords make up a big part of both the selling and the buying side.

What are the City of Lebanon's rental license rules?

Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the city must be licensed, and each parcel with rental units needs its own application. The rules matter to a seller because a buyer inherits the license history.

  • A $25 penalty is added every 60 days a fee stays unpaid after billing.
  • Renewal is delayed or denied if money is owed to the city or code violations are open.
  • The owner must keep a contract with a licensed trash hauler on file, and a property manager must be within 20 miles of the city limit.
  • Grass and weeds cannot exceed 12 inches, snow and ice must come off sidewalks within 24 hours after a snowfall ends, and inoperable or unlicensed vehicles cannot sit on a premises more than 5 days.
  • Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors are required, and a license revoked for unsafe conditions costs $100 to reinstate.

Questions go to the city's code enforcement office at 717-639-2800, option 2, at 735 Cumberland Street. For a rental, get copies of the current license and any violation notice into your file before you answer a buyer.

What permits and zoning rules can slow a Lebanon sale?

The city's Building and Zoning Division, part of Public Works, runs permits and zoning. A zoning permit is required for building or altering a structure, adding an addition, demolishing or moving one, and putting up fences, decks, sheds and garages. It is also required for a change of use, a swimming pool or hot tub deeper than 18 inches, and a sign.

Construction inspections are done by outside code inspection firms under contract, and the city asks for at least 24 hours' notice. A deck or shed that an earlier owner added without a permit is something an inspector may catch. Settle that question before listing, or ask the zoning office what the city would require.

The city zoning ordinance defines 10 districts. A Zoning Hearing Board hears variance and special exception requests.

How do county taxes and the Tax Claim Bureau affect a Lebanon sale?

The Lebanon County Treasurer collects the county real estate tax, the city tax and, now, the Lebanon City School District bill, so one office can tell you whether anything is owed on a city parcel. The Tax Claim Bureau charges $15 per parcel for a tax certification, and a mailed request must include a stamped return envelope.

Delinquent taxes pass to the Tax Claim Bureau each January. The owner is sent a certified letter showing the balance, interest and costs, along with the date to pay in order to avoid a sale. About 17 months after that first notice the bureau mails a notice of sale. Buyers at the upset sale take the property subject to judgments, liens and mortgages, and bidders must pre-register for a $25 fee. The 2026 upset sale list set the sale date for October 12, 2026, and that date has passed.

A seller behind on taxes should pay or arrange the balance before closing. Once a property is on the sale list, the process follows a fixed bureau and court calendar.

How are assessments appealed and the deed recorded in Lebanon County?

The county's rules set September 1 as the yearly filing date for assessment appeals, with a 4:30 closing time at the Board of Assessment Revision. A notice that arrives late waits for the following year. The filing fee for a residential property of one to four units is $50 and is not refunded. You or an authorized representative must attend the hearing, and the board can raise, lower or keep the assessment.

Filings go to the Assessment Office at 400 South 8th Street, Room 118. The county also lets owners view their records free on DataScout, using the control number and web password printed on the tax bill.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 107 of the same courthouse, open on weekdays, and accepts cash or check only. Most documents come back the following business day, and the Assessment Office must certify the parcel identifier before a deed records. The state transfer tax is 1 percent, and the recorder's office adds any local share when it collects.

Which Lebanon houses suit a cash offer?

A cash sale suits a house with heavy repairs, a rental carrying open code items, a vacant building or an estate. It is also useful when tax delinquency puts the house on a calendar you cannot move.

Price comparison matters here because the median value is modest. Add up the commission, repairs, transfer tax and months of ownership on a listing, and compare that net with a cash figure. To ask for an offer on a Lebanon house in its present state, contact Cash Home Buyers.

Yes. Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the City of Lebanon must be licensed, with a separate application for each parcel that has rental units.

When are Lebanon County assessment appeals due?

September 1 each year, filed with the Board of Assessment Revision at the Assessment Office on South 8th Street. A residential appeal costs $50.

How long can Lebanon County delinquent taxes sit before a sale?

Unpaid taxes move to the Tax Claim Bureau every January, and owners have until the last working day of the next June. A notice of sale follows about 17 months after the first notice.

At the Lebanon County Recorder of Deeds, Room 107 of the courthouse at 400 South 8th Street. The office takes cash or check and can also accept electronic recording.

The Lebanon School District, which covers the city and West Lebanon Township. The county treasurer now collects its tax bill for city parcels.

Warrington is a Bucks County township of 13.7 square miles with an estimated 26,261 residents. Its motto calls it the Gateway to Historic Bucks County, and the township was founded in October 1734 and named for Warrington, England. Its population grew from 2,336 in 1950 to 25,639 in 2020, so a large share of its houses date from the 1980s through the 2000s, the years when the count rose from 10,704 to 23,418.

How does the Warrington occupancy certificate work?

The certificate is a township inspection that confirms a home meets safety and property maintenance requirements before it changes hands. The Permits Office takes applications online or by mail or drop-off at the township building, and the applicant is responsible for making sure the fee is paid and the inspection is scheduled.

The township's program page sets out these terms:

  • Apply at least 30 days before settlement so there is time to fix problems the inspection finds.
  • The residential fee is $140 per unit. Confirm commercial fees before you submit.
  • A certificate is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued, so do not schedule the inspection months before closing.
  • Homes with fire sprinkler systems need a separate inspection and certification by a registered third-party agency, and that sprinkler certification is valid for six months.
  • The township publishes a residential inspection checklist, so you can walk the house before the inspector does.

If a sale falls through and the certificate expires, you would have to apply again for the next buyer. Build that risk into your timeline if your buyer needs financing.

Villages within the township are Warrington, Neshaminy, Tradesville, Eureka, Frog Hollow and Palomino Farms.

Warrington has also had a local fight over land use. In 2010 a pharmaceutical company proposed the largest warehouse facility in Pennsylvania near residential neighborhoods in the township, residents objected loudly, and the company chose a site in Northeast Philadelphia instead. Buyers who care about open land and traffic remember that history, and the township's zoning rules decide what can be built near your street. If a buyer asks about nearby development, point them to the township's Planning and Zoning staff, who work with the Bucks County Planning Commission on zoning updates, and keep a copy of your own survey and any permit records for the closing file.

The humid continental climate brings about 47 inches of precipitation a year, with July the wettest month and seasonal snowfall of 30 to 36 inches. Wet basements and roof wear are therefore the questions inspectors ask most.

What taxes and disclosures apply when I sell in Warrington?

Sellers and buyers usually divide the tax by agreement, and a family transfer may be exempt with a Statement of Value form where the deed does not state the exemption.

The disclosure rule is in 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. Before the agreement of sale is signed, you deliver a signed property disclosure statement covering the roof, basement, drainage, plumbing, wiring and similar items. Act 74 of 2026 adds a flood-insurance notice that sellers provide once the Insurance Department posts its flood information, which matters in a township with several creeks.

For assessment, the Bucks Board of Assessment Appeals set August 3, 2026 as the 2026 annual appeal deadline, and that date has passed. Annual appeal changes apply to the following tax year. The homestead and farmstead exclusion filing deadline is March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1. A new owner must send contact information to the Board within 30 days of buying, so remind your buyer.

Should I fix the house, list it or sell as-is in Warrington?

Warrington's high median values reward a well-presented house, but the 30-day occupancy lead time and a sprinkler certification, if you have one, can slow a quick listing. A cash buyer who accepts the house as-is still has to see the township certificate handled before settlement, so ask how that works before you agree to a date.

It is valid for 60 days from the date it is issued. If settlement slips past that window, you will need a new certificate.

What should I know before selling a house in Lower Providence Township?

Lower Providence Township is a Montgomery County suburb of about 25,600 residents where a sale runs through a township resale certificate, three account certifications and a 1 percent local transfer tax. Those three items set the timeline more than anything else, so sellers who line them up early close faster.

The township covers roughly 15.5 square miles along the Perkiomen Creek valley and includes the Audubon and Evansburg census-designated places. It shares borders with Upper Providence, Skippack, Worcester, West Norriton and Upper Merion townships, plus the borough of Collegeville. The 2020 census count was 25,625 people.

Whether the house goes on the market with an agent, sells by owner or goes to an as-is cash buyer, the same township paperwork applies, and the sections below walk through it.

How did Lower Providence Township develop?

The township was created in 1805, when the old Providence Township was split into Upper and Lower halves along the Perkiomen Creek. The land sits in the historic homeland of the Lenape and was once part of the tract granted to William Penn.

Growth came late and fast. The 1930 census counted 3,189 residents, and the count passed 15,000 by 1970 and 22,000 by 2000. Since 2010 the pace has flattened, with 25,436 residents that year and 25,625 in 2020. The biggest gains came between 1940 and 1980, when the township grew from 3,822 to 18,945 residents.

A few landmarks anchor the township's character and help a listing description:

  • Skippack Bridge, built in 1792 and added to the federal register of historic places in 1970.
  • Evansburg State Park, with trails, fishing and horseback riding.
  • Mill Grove, the first American home of the painter John James Audubon, run by the county as a museum and wildlife sanctuary.
  • A portion of Valley Forge National Historical Park.

Which schools and roads matter to buyers in Lower Providence?

The Methacton School District serves the township, and school boundaries are a common question from out-of-area buyers. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools take students from different sections, while Skyview Upper Elementary and Arcola Intermediate sit inside the township. Methacton High School is across the line in Worcester Township. Visitation B.V.M. School, a Catholic school in West Norriton, is nearby for families who want a parish option.

Commuters look first at U.S. Route 422, the Pottstown Expressway, which crosses the southern part of the township. Route 363 handles local trips along Trooper Road, Ridge Pike and Park Avenue. The township reports 113.66 miles of public road, with 90.11 miles maintained by the township itself and 23.55 miles by PennDOT. SEPTA suburban buses 91, 93, 99 and 131 connect to the Norristown Transportation Center.

What does the township require before a Lower Providence house changes hands?

Sellers need a residential resale use and occupancy certificate, and the township charges $100 for it, which covers the first inspection and one follow-up visit. Re-inspections cost $50 each, starting with the third. The application goes through the township's online permit portal, and residential resale fees are due when the application is filed.

The township finance office also expects tax, sewer and trash accounts to be certified before settlement. The real estate tax certification costs $25 and comes from the elected tax collector. Sewer fees are handled by the sewer authority on Parklane Drive in Eagleville, and trash service is billed by J. P. Mascaro and Sons.

What taxes and closing costs apply to a sale in Lower Providence?

The realty transfer tax on a Lower Providence sale is 2 percent in total: 1 percent to the Commonwealth and 1 percent local. The township's fee schedule splits the local share evenly, one half of a percent to the township and one half to the Methacton School District. The state describes its piece as a 1 percent tax on the value transferred, and both buyer and seller are liable for it. Contracts usually say who pays, and splitting it is common.

Several recurring tax facts matter at the closing table:

  • The township's 2026 real estate levies are 2.1298 mills for the general fund, 0.3727 for the library, 0.7485 for debt service, 0.7614 for emergency services and 0.241 for parks, which together equal 4.2534 mills. County and Methacton school taxes are billed in addition.
  • Tax bills go out on March 1. Payment before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies after July 1.
  • If a mortgage servicer pays your taxes from escrow, forward the bill to the servicer.

Some transfers, such as certain deeds between family members and property passed by inheritance, are exempt from the state tax. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds how an exemption is documented before you sign.

Can I appeal my Montgomery County assessment before I sell?

Yes. The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals takes annual appeals up to an August 1 deadline, and a postmark on or before that date counts. Fax and email filings are rejected.

A single-family appeal carries a $50 processing fee payable to the county treasurer, and the filing needs three copies of supporting documents such as an appraisal, comparable sales or photographs. All appeals must be heard by October 31, and the board grants rescheduling only in extraordinary circumstances. A homestead or farmstead appeal costs nothing. The board's office phone is 610-278-3761.

A lower assessment helps the next owner more than the seller, but a documented appeal can still support a price discussion with a buyer.

What if I am behind on property taxes in Lower Providence?

Unpaid township, school and county taxes are turned over to the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau, which can sell a parcel when taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid. Its upset sales are held each September and December, and the 2026 sale dates have already passed. A buyer at an upset sale takes the property subject to all liens, while a judicial sale presents parcels free and clear.

The practical lesson for a seller is to settle a delinquency before it reaches that stage. Selling before the bureau acts lets the closing pay the arrears from proceeds. Call the bureau at the Norristown office to confirm the payoff figure before you accept an offer.

Is a cash offer or a listing the better route in Lower Providence?

Three things decide it: how fast you must move, what repairs the house needs and how much certainty you want. Marketing the house widens the buyer pool, yet it adds showings, post-inspection repair requests and loan contingencies. A cash buyer usually has no lender to satisfy, so the closing date can follow your schedule.

  • Ask each buyer who orders and pays for the township resale inspection, and put the answer in the contract.
  • Compare net proceeds after the 2 percent transfer tax, any payoff, and your share of the township certifications.
  • Confirm that the buyer will accept the house with its current sewer, trash and tax accounts settled at closing.

Get the township certificates started as soon as you decide to sell. They are the part of a Lower Providence sale that you control.

Does Lower Providence Township require an inspection when I sell?

Yes. Residential sales need a resale use and occupancy certificate, which costs $100 and includes an initial inspection and one follow-up. Apply through the township's online permit portal.

How much is the transfer tax on a Lower Providence home sale?

The total is 2 percent of the value transferred. The state collects 1 percent, and the local 1 percent is split between the township and the Methacton School District. The county recorder collects it at deed recording.

Which school district serves Lower Providence?

Methacton School District. Arrowhead, Eagleville and Woodland elementary schools serve parts of the township, and Methacton High School is in neighboring Worcester Township.

When are Lower Providence property tax bills due?

Bills are mailed March 1. Paying before April 30 earns a 2 percent discount, and a 10 percent penalty applies to payments made after July 1.

When is the Montgomery County assessment appeal deadline?

August 1 each year. The appeal form, three copies of supporting papers and a $50 check for a single-family home must be postmarked or delivered by then.

At 28.57 square miles of land it is the second-largest borough in the state by area. The borough sits northeast of Pittsburgh, with the Allegheny River on its northern edge, and it borders Monroeville, Penn Hills, Oakmont and, across the river, Cheswick, Springdale and Lower Burrell.

The Census Bureau estimates 26,225 residents for July 2025, about 3.4% below the 2020 base of 27,147. The 2020 census counted 27,144 people and 11,869 housing units, 4.7% of them vacant. Postal mail may carry a Pittsburgh address, even though the borough is outside the city limits.

  • Owners report a middle home value of $227,600 in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 estimates, and 80.7% of households own.
  • Median household income: $98,705, well above Pittsburgh's $65,742.
  • Persons per household: 2.45, and 22.8% of residents are 65 or older.
  • Median gross rent: $1,177.
  • Commutes average 31.1 minutes.

The Pennsylvania Turnpike crosses Plum between mile markers 49 and 55. Oakmont Country Club lies mostly within the borough and has hosted ten U.S. Opens. The Plum Borough School District operates five school buildings: O'Block and Pivik elementary schools, Holiday Park Intermediate School, Plum Middle School and Plum Senior High School.

Do Plum Borough zoning and permits matter for a sale?

They can, because a buyer or inspector may notice work that was done without a permit. The Community Development department issues residential building permits for new dwellings, additions, decks, porches and porch roofs, pools deeper than 24 inches, structural alterations and demolitions. Zoning certificates cover front yard fences, sheds, detached garages, carports, gazebos and similar structures under 200 square feet.

If you added a deck or shed yourself, ask Community Development whether a permit or certificate is on file before the inspection. Fixing a paperwork gap before the occupancy visit is simpler than doing it after a buyer raises the question. The department also administers subdivision, conditional use and variance requests, which matter if the lot is large enough to split.

How do Allegheny County taxes and appeals affect a Plum sale?

Plum parcels are assessed by the Allegheny County Office of Property Assessments on a base year of 2012, and the county notes that these figures are not current market values. Appeals go to the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. The annual window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026, so it has closed, and the county says a parcel taxed by the county for the first time in 2027 will not appear on its portal until values are certified in January 2027.

Ask the county treasurer and the Plum tax collectors for a paid-to-date statement before closing. Any balance owed gets paid from the sale proceeds, and a title search will show open amounts. The county also runs a homestead exclusion under Act 50 for owner-occupied homes, and a buyer who will live in the house applies through the county.

What does Pennsylvania require a Plum seller to disclose?

Under 68 Pa.C.S. Chapter 73, the seller must deliver a signed, dated property disclosure statement before the buyer and seller sign the agreement of transfer. The statement covers the roof, basement, structure, plumbing, electrical systems, heating and cooling, water and sewage service, land and drainage, hazardous substances and title issues. It also asks about the condition and location of storm water facilities and whether the owner or someone else maintains them.

The seller does not need to carry out special testing but may not say anything known to be false or leave out a known material defect. The method of delivery can be in person, by first class mail, by certified mail or by fax. A disclosure can be amended in writing before the agreement is signed.

  • Condominium sellers disclose only about their own unit.
  • Estate fiduciaries are outside the chapter.
  • A buyer's damages suit must begin within two years after final settlement.

How can a Plum homeowner sell quickly?

Choose the route first, then line up the permit. A listing gives the widest audience, a sale by owner keeps the commission, and a cash sale usually shortens the schedule. All three still need the Plum occupancy inspection before the deed transfers, so book it as soon as you have a target closing date.

  • Submit the occupancy application at least five business days ahead of the inspection date.
  • Check the borough's inspector checklist and fix small items beforehand.
  • Confirm permits for any deck, porch or shed you built.
  • Ask the settlement agent for the 2% transfer tax figure and the payoff before you accept terms.

More questions about Plum, PA

Does Plum Borough require an occupancy permit to sell a house?

Yes. A Residential Occupancy Permit is required when the occupancy of a home changes. The owner files the application with a $100 fee, an inspector schedules a visit, and a passing inspection gets the permit.

How far ahead must I apply for the Plum occupancy inspection?

Apply at least five business days before the inspection date you want. The application must be signed by the owner and paid by check to the Borough of Plum. An inspector then contacts you to set the day and time.

How much is the transfer tax in Plum Borough?

It is 2% in total: 0.5% to the borough, 0.5% to the Plum School District and 1% to the state. On a $250,000 sale that is $5,000. Allegheny County collects it when the deed is recorded.

Can Plum require a new occupancy permit every time ownership changes?

Not more than once every two years. The borough requires the permit for a change in ownership or residents, but caps it at one every two years regardless of how many changes happen. Ask Community Development how that rule applies if the home changed hands recently.

Is the appeal window for my Allegheny County assessment still open?

No. The window for tax year 2027 ran from July 1 to September 1, 2026 and is closed. Watch the county's real estate portal for the next window if you think your value is off.

How does selling a house in Upper Moreland, PA work?

Selling in Upper Moreland follows the usual Pennsylvania path, with one local advantage: the township's code enforcement department does not require a use and occupancy certificate or any inspection when a residential or commercial property is resold. You sign an agreement of sale, deliver your disclosure statement first, pay transfer tax at recording and settle through a title company or attorney.

Upper Moreland Township is in Montgomery County, about 13 to 15 miles north of Center City Philadelphia, with an estimated 25,880 residents. Most of it is Willow Grove-area housing built during the post-war growth that took the township from 5,103 people in 1940 to 21,032 in 1960. That growth curve points to a stock of mid-century houses, so expect buyers to ask about roof age and original systems.

What is Upper Moreland like for home buyers?

Upper Moreland is a compact, mostly residential township of just under 8 square miles, so almost every house is a short drive from the turnpike, a rail station or a shopping strip. It borders Hatboro, Horsham, Upper Dublin, Abington, Bryn Athyn and Lower Moreland in Montgomery County, and Bucks County lies to the north.

The land has a documented past. William Penn gave the tract to Nicholas More in 1682, when it was called the Manor of Mooreland. In 1916 a line drawn through Pennypack Creek created Upper and Lower Moreland, and in 1930 Upper Moreland was organized as a first-class township. A seven-member board of commissioners, one from each ward, governs it.

Buyers will compare your house on these local points:

  • The Willow Grove interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-276) sits inside the township.
  • PA 611 (Easton Road), PA 263 (York Road) and PA 63 (Moreland Road) carry local traffic, with Davisville, Byberry, Fitzwatertown, Terwood and Blair Mill roads feeding neighborhoods.
  • SEPTA's Warminster Line stops at Willow Grove station, and bus routes 22, 55, 310 and 95 serve the township.
  • Of 85.02 miles of public road, 65.51 miles belong to the township, which also handles trash and recycling through its public works department.
  • PECO supplies power and gas, Aqua Pennsylvania supplies water, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority handles sewage.

What do Census figures show for Upper Moreland housing?

Upper Moreland has the lowest home value among the four Montgomery and Bucks townships that share this Census table, which affects both pricing and who can buy without a large down payment. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts give these figures for the township.

Upper Moreland township figures from Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureUpper Moreland
Count in the 2020 Census26,116
Residents in the 2025 estimate25,880
Number of households10,355
Homes with an owner living in them57.8%
Typical owner's home value$391,600
Typical monthly rent$1,634
Owner costs per month with a mortgage$2,220
Typical household income$99,054
Average commute29.4 minutes

Population has dipped 0.4 percent since the 2020 base, and 89.0 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Low turnover means fewer comparable sales, so a pricing opinion that uses recent sales on nearby streets matters more here than a township average.

Does Upper Moreland require an inspection or certificate before I sell?

No. The code enforcement department states that it does not require a Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of a residential or commercial property, and its FAQ says no inspections are required on resale. Businesses moving into the township do have to file a Zoning Use Registration Permit.

Work you did on the house is a different matter, and buyers' inspectors check it. The department answers permit questions at 117 Park Avenue, Willow Grove, and by phone at 267-607-1032 or 267-607-1033 on weekdays from 7:30 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon Its published rules for open projects are short:

  • Residential permit plans are normally reviewed in about 15 working days, and two sets of plans are required.
  • Only a registered master plumber may submit a plumbing permit. An owner may do electrical work but still needs the permit.
  • A fence needs a permit, with a maximum height of 6 feet in a rear yard and 4 feet in a front yard.
  • Installing a pool requires a building permit.

If you built a fence, deck or pool without a permit, ask the department how to close it out before you list.

Which schools serve Upper Moreland homes?

Upper Moreland Township is served by the Upper Moreland School District, which runs by grade band rather than by neighborhood elementary school. Upper Moreland Primary School takes kindergarten through grade 2, the Intermediate School covers grades 3 to 5, the Middle School covers grades 6 to 8, and Upper Moreland High School serves grades 9 to 12.

The area Catholic option is Queen of Angels Regional Catholic School in Willow Grove. For health care, Jefferson Health-Willow Grove offers outpatient services in the township. Buyers with children often ask about both, so mention them in your listing text.

What taxes and paperwork come with an Upper Moreland sale?

Pennsylvania's realty transfer tax is 1 percent of the value of the property at the state level, and local governments add their own share. Bucks County's recorder describes the combined statewide tax as 2 percent and notes that sellers and buyers usually divide it. Ask the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds what applies to Upper Moreland and how it is collected.

Before the agreement of sale is signed, you deliver a completed property disclosure statement under 68 Pa.C.S. Section 7303. The form asks about roofs, basements, termites, structural problems, plumbing, wiring and storm water facilities. Act 74 of 2026 amended the form's land item and added a flood-insurance notice, so ask your agent or attorney for the current form. If property tax is in arrears, the Montgomery County Tax Claim Bureau runs upset sales each September and December for parcels unpaid from two years earlier. You contest an assessment through the Board of Assessment Appeals, whose page lists the annual appeal deadline document.

Is a cash sale a good fit for an Upper Moreland house?

A cash sale fits best when the house needs repairs you do not want to fund, when you are managing an estate, or when timing matters more than the last dollar. Older houses often carry aging roofs and mechanicals, and a buyer who purchases as-is removes the inspection-repair back and forth. A listing usually fetches more on the open market, with more showings and a financing window.

  • Get at least two written offers and compare closing dates.
  • Confirm who pays transfer tax and whether the buyer covers recording costs.
  • Check that the buyer can show proof of funds before you sign.

More questions about Upper Moreland, PA

Do I need a resale certificate in Upper Moreland?

No. The township's code enforcement department says it does not require a Use and Occupancy Certificate for the sale or resale of residential or commercial property, and it requires no resale inspection. Contractor-built work still needs the permits listed on the township website.

What is the typical home value in Upper Moreland?

Upper Moreland owners report a typical value of $391,600 for 2020 to 2024. That is a township-wide midpoint, so use recent sales close to your house to set a price.

Which county records a deed in Upper Moreland?

Montgomery County records it, through the Recorder of Deeds office. Your title company or attorney handles the filing, so ask them what the recorder needs with the deed, including transfer tax paperwork.

How do I find out who handles trash and sewer for my house?

The township's public works department handles trash and recycling, and the Upper Moreland-Hatboro Joint Sewer Authority provides sewage service. Buyers ask for the latest bills, so gather them before listing.

Can I sell an inherited house in Upper Moreland as-is?

Yes. Pennsylvania's seller disclosure chapter does not apply to transfers by a fiduciary administering a decedent's estate, though the sale still needs proper authority to sign. Ask the estate's attorney to confirm who may sign the deed.

What shapes a house sale in Derry Township and Hershey?

Derry Township is the municipality that contains Hershey, and a sale there is shaped by two things: a very stable local economy built around chocolate, tourism and a major medical center, and a tax setup that runs through Dauphin County rather than a local collector. The township sits in southeastern Dauphin County, east of Harrisburg, with Lebanon County on its eastern edge and Swatara Creek forming most of its northwest border.

It covers about 27.4 square miles, almost all of it land. The unincorporated communities inside it include Hershey, Palmdale, Swatara, Hockersville, Oakmont, Waltonville and part of Stoverdale. When people say they live in Hershey, their deed usually says Derry Township.

This page walks through what a seller here should line up: who bills the taxes, what transfer tax applies, how assessments and appeals work in Dauphin County, and what the township's Community Development office handles.

How has Hershey shaped Derry Township?

The township was incorporated on August 1, 1729, by the sons of William Penn, back when it was much larger and part of Lancaster County. It joined Dauphin County when that county was created in 1785. In 2002, township supervisors proposed renaming it Hershey Township, and voters turned that down, with 54 percent opposed.

The township's own website describes Hershey as a model town that Milton S. Hershey set out to build for the needs of the factory workers. That planning still shows: the community has its own police department, public works department and public library, and the Hershey Medical Center and Children's Hospital stand on a large tract inside its borders.

  • Hersheypark and other attractions are run by Hershey Entertainment and Resorts
  • The township levies an amusement tax tied to those attractions
  • The climate is hot-summer humid continental, with monthly averages from about 30 degrees in January to about 75 in July

How do Derry Township homes and incomes measure up?

The Census Bureau estimates 25,179 residents for July 1, 2025, only slightly above the 2010 count of 24,679. This is a mature community that grows slowly. Nearly one in five residents is 65 or older.

Derry Township housing and income, Census Bureau QuickFacts
MeasureDerry Township
Residents counted in 202024,715
Share aged 65 and over19.5%
Households that own their home63.1%
Midpoint value of an owned home$390,000
Midpoint monthly rent$1,361
Midpoint household income$97,025
Average commute18.5 minutes

Health care receipts of about $2.5 billion in 2022 and accommodation and food service sales of $354 million show how much of the local economy rests on the medical center and visitors.

Who bills property tax in Derry Township, and at what rates?

Since January 1, 2023, the Dauphin County Treasurer's Office collects both township and Derry Township School District real estate taxes. The township's Tax Association Office closed that day, and occupation and local services taxes moved to Keystone Collections Group. The county's tax collector list also shows the county treasurer handling Derry bills.

The township's tax page lists these real estate millage rates: 2.53810 mills for the township, 20.3387 mills for the school district and 9.193 mills for Dauphin County. Rates change when budgets pass, so confirm the current numbers with the county treasurer before you build a net sheet.

Other township taxes depend on the person, not the house. Earned income tax is 1 percent, split evenly between the township and the school district, and the township also receives $250 from each employed resident earning over $12,000. A buyer moving into Derry will pay those, but they do not affect your proceeds.

What does a Derry Township sale cost in transfer tax?

The total is 2 percent of the sale price. Dauphin County's Recorder of Deeds explains that the state's Department of Revenue receives 1 percent, and the municipality and the school district each receive half of one percent. The township's tax page confirms the township share: 0.5 percent of the purchase price.

On a $390,000 sale, which matches the Census median value, 2 percent comes to $7,800. The sales agreement determines which side pays, and the state holds both parties responsible. Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt, though the Dauphin recorder suggests checking with an attorney or the Department of Revenue for other exemptions.

The Recorder of Deeds is at the Dauphin County Courthouse in Harrisburg, and its records begin in 1785. Fees for recording are set by the state legislature.

How do assessments, appeals and relief programs work in Dauphin County?

The Dauphin County Office of Tax Assessment values real property, keeps ownership records and runs the county's homestead and farmstead exclusion, its Clean and Green preferential assessment program and its tax deferral program. Its office is on the second floor of the County Administration Building at 2 South Second Street in Harrisburg, and its parcel data is online.

The office does not set tax rates. The county, the township and the school district do that after assessments are in. If you think your assessment is too high, ask the office for the appeal rules and the filing date that applies to your parcel.

A new state law matters for owners of rental houses. Act 29 of 2026 creates a county-kept contact registry for properties that are not owner-occupied, effective September 18, 2026. Owners, and lenders after a foreclosure, must give the county a name, address, phone and email for someone authorized to resolve code violations, within 30 days of taking ownership and within 30 days of any change. A failure to comply can bring a $500 fine, and owner-occupied principal residences are exempt.

What does the township's Community Development office handle?

The township municipal complex at 600 Clearwater Road in Hershey is where you ask about permits, zoning and any open code issue on an address. Do that before you list, because a buyer's lender or inspector may ask for the same paperwork.

  • Check whether any past work on the house, such as a finished basement, a deck or a pool, had a permit
  • Ask which zoning district the lot is in if your buyer plans a business, an addition or a rental
  • Confirm that street light assessments and other township charges on the account are current
  • Sign up for the township's eNews to follow notices that affect your street

A little time spent on these items before you list keeps surprises away from the closing table.

What are my choices for selling a Derry Township house?

With a median home value near $390,000 and strong local employers, a house in good order can sell through a normal listing. An as-is sale makes more sense when you are settling an estate, relocating, or facing repairs you would rather not finance.

Whichever path you choose, ask for the net figure in writing: price, less 2 percent transfer tax if you agree to pay it, payoffs, prorated county, township and school taxes, and any repair credit. Request the buyer's proof of funds and closing date before you take the house off the market.

More questions about Derry, PA

Is Hershey a separate town from Derry Township?

No. Hershey is an unincorporated community inside Derry Township, so deeds, permits and taxes for a Hershey address go through the township and Dauphin County.

What is the transfer tax on a house sale in Derry Township?

It totals 2 percent: 1 percent to the state, 0.5 percent to the township and 0.5 percent to the school district, collected by the Dauphin County Recorder of Deeds.

Who collects real estate taxes on a Derry Township house?

The Dauphin County Treasurer's Office collects both township and school district real estate taxes. Call the treasurer for balances before closing.

Do I need to register a rental house I am selling in Dauphin County?

Act 29 of 2026 requires owners of non-owner-occupied property to give the county contact details, effective September 18, 2026, with updates within 30 days of any change. Your buyer takes on that duty when they become the owner.

Are family transfers exempt from realty transfer tax in Dauphin County?

Transfers between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings are generally exempt, though other exemptions exist. Confirm with an attorney or the Department of Revenue.
